It Was first narrated in the principal netespePers at the time of the murder. and Some years afterwards the late' Dr. Aber- . - litembie was enabled, by the kindness of a :medical friend, to obtain an account cf it from the gentleman to whom the circumstance occurred. It was afterwards 'published by Dr. Abercrombie in his "Observations on the Intellectual Powers." :The facts are simply as, fol- low :--In the night of the 11th of May, 1112, Mr. V,Vil- ime „barns, of Scorner House, Bedruth, Cornwall, dreamed that,he was standing in the lobby of the House of Corn. : qc ' more, when a short gentleman entered, dressed in a blue coat and white waistcoat; immediately afterwards he saw a man, in a brown coat with. yellow basket-metal buttons, -draw a pistol from under his Coat and dis- charge it' at the former, who instantly fell, the blood issuing from a wound a little below the left breast. He saw the murderer seized- be some gentlemen who were standing by, and dreamed that he was told that the murdered man was the Chancellor. He awoke in great terror, arid, rousing his wife, related the dream to her. She, .however, made light of it, and he went to sleep .:. again-. Twice again, however, during the.night were the same drendful events presented to his-iniagination. In the morning Mr. Williams made his strange dream known to his acquaintances, and so great was the im- pression it made on his owe mind that it was with much . difficulty his friends dissuaded him from travelling to London to make it known to the Chancellor himself. • Alter being the talk of the neighbourhood for some few day,,, the matter rested, until the news was received that on that very day Mr. Perceval was shot in the lobby of the House of Commons, by a man named Bellingham. Some time afterwards, Mr. Williams went to !London, where he was shown the pictures of the murder (which were then publishedy, and also the scene of the event it- ( ; self. And it was found that the whole of the details of ' the dream corresponded with those of the real on- FI ' . co rre oe —Old and AreT London for -herv. ,

GLADSTONE. • ' Mr. Gladstone's letter to Mr. Thomas Gee on the ques- tion of Welsh Disestablishment was considered at a meet- ing of the Executive Committee of the North Wales Liberal Federation„ held at Rhyl, on Saturday. Ministers have caused it to be made known amongst their supporters that they are resolved to carry :out their intention of summoning Parliament in No' ' ember and further agitation on that side of the House is deprecated. We understand that both Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain are person- ally strongly in favour of the proposed arrange- ment.

Everyone has heard of the famous "Punch' dinner, but on Tuesday night was inaugurated a "Daily News" dinner—in other words, the *hole literary staff of the “ Daily sews" dined 'with Mr. Oppenheim. Among the guests were Mr. Glad4tone, Lord R6sebery, and Mr. John Morley. The whole staff was present, and a very charming evening was spent.

--- Empress Frederick would become a powerful factor at Court if she remained long in England. During the last three weeks her influence has been successfully exerted with the Queen to induce her Majesty to allow the Guards' band to play ou the gest Terrace at Windsor Castle on Sunday after- noons, and she has also obtained the Queen's; per- mission for Princess Beatrice to make a iengthy tour abroad.

The report set afloat on Wednesday to the effect that Sir Michael Hicks Beach. is likely to be ap- pointed Governor of New South Wales, in succession to Lord Carrington, whose term of office expires in September, was interesting, but unfounded. Sir Michael's eyesight is again giving him some trouble, and his general health is not strong, but there is a high official post yet waiting for him at home.:

• The Comte de Paris intends to remain for still antler week at Folkestone, where he is lodged in royal style at the Pavilion Hotel. He is accompanied by a suite of twenty persons, and holds a sort of leVee, a constant stream of Royalists coming over from France to pay their respects. By 'a curious coincidence M. Henri Rochefort spent Sunday to Monday at Folkestone, but the local report that he called upon the Count is inaccurate.

A London,news agency says that tbe lestal ar- rangements were completed, on Saturday, for, buy- ing out Mr. T. P. O'Connor's interests in the" Star newspaper. Under the agreement. Mr. O'Connor receives in all £17,000, £5OO representing Money invested in the company, the balance being r‘mun- ,eßtion for services, and for the surrender of inter- est. -Mr. O'Connor took leave of the chief mem- bers of the" Star " staff on Saturday.

A nineteenth century Oliver Cromwell has just died. We refer to the late manager of a Sheffield theatre, Mr. William Oliver Cromwell. This gentle- man had a rather adventurous career, for: he began , life as a postilion to the Prince of Wales and page to Sir George Armitage, was afterwards almost eaten by, sharks in the West Indies, acted at both covent Garden and Drury Lane, and finally was connected with the Sheffield stage for some twenty-five or thirty years.

From the pages of some of my daily contempor- arieS I learn that the great advantage which Bisley is likely to have over Wimbledon will lie in the sub- ordination of festivity to business, and in the more soldierly tone of the whole meeting. This is a good news, and it bears out the principal argument that used to show that the Duke of Cambridge really did:the best thing possible for the Volunteers and the National Rifle Association when he signed the death-warrant of the Wimbledon picnic.

Sir renry Halford deserves to be congratulated upon the manner in which be laid the rifle for the first shot at Bisley, on Saturday. The aim was so true that the Princess of Wales struck the target only an inch from the absolute centre of the bull's eye. This was far better than in 1860, when the Queen similarly fired the shot which inaugurated Wimbledon, for on that occasion the rifle was so laid that it missed the bull's eve and scored only a "centre," which at that time ranked next " the bull "in counting points.

A man known as the Bird of Death in the Vienna General Hospital has met with his fate in the dis- charge of his gruesome hospital duties. His name was Alois Pakes. He was a man of Herculean build, and for thirty-three years had carried all the corpses to and from the mortuary chamber. Hence the weird name the howital jesters give him. He died a few days ago of blood poisoning caused by handling the body of a patient who had died of an infectious disease. He had sold his skeleton to an itinerant musenm many years age, and spent the money in drink, and his remains have been banded over to the Purchaser.

One of the veterans at the Peace Congress is M. Fr&laic Passy, the celebrated French economisi. M. Passy is one of the ()Mast friends of free trade in France. He helped Cobden to get the reciprocity treaty with France under the Empire, and has for thirty years written much in books and journals, and spoken at many meetings throughout France, in support of the principles of free trade. In 1867 he helped to found the international Peace League. In politics M. Passy is a Conservative Repablican. He was elected as one of the deputies for Paris in 1881, but was defeated at the last general election. He was born in 1822.

The larg,cst tan ever paid to a Scotch advocate was l".1:lat of a thousand guineas sent to the Lord o cate with his brief in the recent action with reference to the Murthly estates. Five hundred guineas was the fee at first sent, but this was not enough to induce his lordship to leave his duties in Parliament. Some time ago the Lord. Advocate Yeciived a fee of eight hundred guineas in a court of sessions case—till then the highest fee known in Scotland. It is curious that both fees should have been supplied by American millionaires, Mr. Ken- nedy and Me. Ross Winans, and it is equally curious that both of them lost their actions in the court.

Flint locks are generally supposed to be entirely things of the past. How, then, are we to explain the fact that at Brandon, in Suffolk, at this moment, no fewer than thirty-five men are still employed in ,fashioning gun flints, or "flint-knapping," as it is generally called ? No less a number than thirty millinns Of gun flints of various qualities and sizes areofficialty stated to have left the workshop of one Brandon man. alone during the last ten years. What has become of them? Some light is thrown on this puzzling question by the information that their des- tination lb the West Coast of Africa, whence they are distributed among the savage tribes of the in- terior.

It is always good to take a hint from the enemy. The "St. James's Gazette" said the other day, with reference to the subscriptions to its Balaclava fund, that many of the cheques and money orders had b6en carelessly sent in open or half-open envelopes, but that in no one case was there any sign of decal- tents having been tampered]with. This is only one testimony out of a thousand to the honesty of the men to whom Mr. Raikes awards the lowest sweat- ing rates known in London. Honesty, intelligence, experience—all bought up dirt cheap for IBs. a week! , And this is the class who are denied by a depart- mental order the right of combination which the law guarantees to the poorest Wage-slave in great Britain.

The charming little ceremony in E Committee- room; on Monday afternoon, has added a fresh link to the ties of affection which more and more bind together the English and Irish peoples. ,Mr. and Mrs. William O'Brien, both of whom were present, were given a set of wedding presents by a number of their English friends in the House, the Irish members simply attending as spectators. The gifts, which were admirably selected by Mr. Schwann, consisted of a silver inkstand, silver candlesticks, Ruskin's works, copies of the original "Spectator and Tatler," Swift's and Pope's works, and other volumes. The presentation was made by Mr. Stans- feld in one of those beautiful little speeches in which this good and sympathetic man excels. div.head: LABOUR CAUSE.
div.p: THE LABOUR CAUSE.
HOW THEY BOYCOTT IN CALIFORNIA.
BY H. WHITHAIf.

I can fancy my last letter needs a further one as a sort of explanation. Allow me to say first, that trade seems to have brightened up a little, and I think, and hope, the letter referred to has marked the turning point. I trust I am not too sanguine when I say further, that thera is just the least little,bit of silver lining beginning to appear from behind the very dark cloud. You know it is a long lane that has no turning. The lane I have ' been treading along for many years has been rather monotonous, and I begin to think that Dame Fortune might do a worse thing than intro- duce just a little variety into the business, if it I was only to make life worth living. It seems from the above, my explanation is only a statement of a more favourable character. Well, any way that's good, because I know readers of the "Examiner" will only be too pleased to/ know that in our leap from the frying pan we cleared the fire and alight- ed on something like solid ground. Before I take up the question I wish to write of, allow me to say

div.head: A-WORD FITRTHER AS TO THE FANCILY.
div.p: A-WORD FITRTHER AS TO THE FANCILY.

There is an impression in the world, outside Cali- fornia,that this State is a wonderfully healthy tate. Well this may be so in theory, and even according to figures California can be proved the healthiest place in the world. That's all right, but according to hard facts (his city is decidedly unhealthy. For doctors and cemeteries I back the place against t any other in thesworld, for its size, and in the latter the preponderance of babies graves over those of adults is quite a feature. Pneumonia and diptheria are the coinmonest and ?most fatal complaints ; of the, latter we have a case next door, and one in the basement under us. I think corruption in municipal matters to blame for this. Whether it be draining a district, or build- ing a city hall, all is corrupt. Another intolerable nuisance is a wild plant, which grows in great abundance all round the city, the Poisen Oak. One of my children (Ruby) is kept almost a prisoner. If she goes out into the country, She is sure to suffer afterwards from the results of this poison. ,It is not necessary to go nearit. If the wind blows over the plant, and towards her it is enough, and the appearance of the whole body within a day or two can only be compared to that of one suffering from small-pox. During the past week, she has been al- most blind with it, and now she is Ordered for a six months course of medicine. We, have also the trade winds, which blow steadily .rbut very persis- tently every afternoon and evening during six months of the year. These have affected the sight of ray wife and me very much, so that now I can- not correct letters in pica type, whereas when I left Warrington I could easily read pearl. These winds also cause evenings to be very cold; one needs blankets and top-coats all the year reund, and I don't think many cities outside Russia can boast so many sealskin clad ladies. But enough of all this, and let us get to the most burning question of all questions in America, as in Europe—

div.head: TUB LABOUR giTREITION.
div.p: TUB LABOUR giTREITION.

I We all remember the question of Trades Unions ' used to be, twenty and thirty years ago, a standard subject for discussion in Mutual 'lmprovement Classes. What was then mere theory for most.of us has since assumed a very practical shape. From Adam Smith to Malthus, to Ricardo, and Stuart Mill, 'a politico-economical science was given to the manufacturing interest which would, undoubt-, edly, have reduced the labouring population to , mere serfs, had it not received, a check. This check made itself felt on the repeat of the Combination Laws. It was seen by workmen that a mere 'alma faire, or 'do-nothing policy did not, and Could not suit the workman's needs, however it might 'suit the employer ; therefore they combined and formed their Unions, since when the struggle bet been carried on as if between mortal enemies rather than joint producers. From Trade Unionism to Socialism may seem, to English workmen, a wide step ;on the Continent of Europe it is not so. Karl Marx's book on Capital has bridged the seeming gulf. The Continental Trade Unionist is a Socialist of an advanced type; and as such he comes to this country. As a member of

div.head: TRIFEDICIIATBD MAIMS COUNCIL
div.p: TRIFEDICIIATBD MAIMS COUNCIL

I have good opportunities for noting the peculiarities of the various (and they are many) nationalities represented. I notice, first, that the native American is a poor Unionist. He seems to be toosuspicious of everything, and everybody. He will neither trust, no can he be trusted ;hence a very small percentage of native Americans ever become Trade Unionists. Next, I find that Germany sends the pure. unadulter- ated Trade Unionists. The German workman finds, at home, no constitutional outlet for his social aspiration; the iron hand has, hitherto, held the safety valve down; therefore it is Socialist steam that is always blowing off in the Fatherland, or, in other words, extreme measures on the one hand produce extreme results on the other hand. The Scandinavian is here also in large,numbers, but like the Englishman, he has been reared in freedom, looks on Socialism with a philosophic' eye, makes a good Trade Unionist, and does not go into ecstatics over everything that is American. Of course what I say on this subject, has reference only to Califormia I know nothing of the Eastern States : it may, or inaynot apply to them, although I fancy it does. We have in this city a great variety in trades. Sausage makers combine, and so do candy makers. The gentlemen from behind the counters combine, , and also the newsboys on the streets. The plasterers and bricklayers combine and manage to get out of it, I—and the public—five dollars for an eight hours day. By the way, I should say that the two latter trades will afford good op?ortunities, during the next two or three years, for single young fellows to come out and make lots a money. i It matters not how insignificant the trade, combination is the rule, with representation in the Federated Council. In the Council, all sorts of disputes are discussed. Each trade tries its best to settle its own disputes; failing this, the matter is referred to the Council, and the trade concerned ceases to have any more control over the dispute in question. A deputation is appoint& to wait upon the refractory employer,who, if he is wise comes to terms ; if not, the failure to settle is reported back. This is followed by a boy- cott being declared, and next morning every paper announces the fact of such a &dr being boycotted.

div.head: I see
div.p: I see

BOWE CURIOUS THINGS at times—as for instance,the shoe-makers are carry- ing on a vigorous boycott against Chinese and Eastern made shoes. I can understand boycotting all and everything that is Chinese, although it does not always mean that everything these people make is nasty because it's cheap; but I cannot understand boycotting Eastern made goods which may be the workof men who are members t f the, same Union. The brewers, for instance, have a rule compelling each member to hold his boots up when requested, and woe be to him if he cannot show the trade. stamp, for a five dollar,flne is inflicted. The same fine is inflicted if they are caught Brooking a cigar which does not come out of a box showing the White Labour stamp. , A short time ago the brewers determined to boycott one of the breweries. Hand- bills were spread all over the city to that effect, and dogs pailided'the streets with black cloth covers on . which appeared in large white letters "Boycott Frederic urgHeer." Just fancy how it would look in Warrington—" Boycott Greenalfs Beer." The boycott is resorted to, in the first instance, in- stead of strikes. Suppose the coopers tohave a dis- pute with their employers: instead of calling the men out they boycott the shop. Everyone, who is known to 'use a barrel,oianything from this cooper's shop is waited upon and urged to take his custom away. If he refuses, he is in turn threatened with the boycott. A while ago, one of the theatres would employ a scab band. Musicians get five dollars. a day. Immediately the streets were littered with handbills declaring a boycott. The management didn't appreciate an empty treasury, r gave in. One of the Sunday picnic steam-boats hired a scab band, but it has just given in. Again, Should a restaurant employ a waiter who refuses to join the Union, the boss is requested to discharge him. Should he refuse, a boycott is at once declared. A man will stand at the door giving out handbills to that effect. Anyone seen entering is " shadowed," and if he is found to belong to a Union, down comes a fine on his poor head. There are no laws pro- hibiting this sort of thing, for this is a free country "don't cher ?now ?" I must candidly say this way of lighting capital has very little of my sympathy. it is destruetive at the beginning, the middle, and the end ; there is nothing constructive about it. It seems to me that such a course of action can have no satisfactory ending. German Socialism, like the new American "fad, National- ism, seems impracticable, because it ignores the fixed laws of evolution. In England you have bonc2-fide workmen in Parliament; you have the same in your Town Council; you will have the same in your County Councils. Your proletariat have only to ask to receive; you will nationalise the land, and your industries, before we, in this free and enlightened country have ever begun to think about sending or trusting a working-man out of

div.head: BABY WORRIED BY A PIG.
div.p: A BABY WORRIED BY A PIG.

A horrible affairbas occurred at Llandyosil, a small village in Montogoniervshire A woman named Rogers went to Montogomery market, leaving her baby, two months old, in clam of its brother and sistev. The babe/ was lying in its cradle, and the other children were !play- ing outside the house., when a pig entered through the open door, and began to worry the poor child. Its pierc- ing screams attractedattention, and the pig was driven away, but not beforethe baby's nose, face, and hands had been terribly bitrau. It is not thought likely that the child can recover, and if it does it will be disfigured for life.

The National Liberal Club on Wednesday evening gave albanquet at the Club Rims° to Mr. Sehnadhorst on his return from South Africa-, where he haalately spent six months in re-establishing his health. Sir. William Har- court, who presided, proposed the healthiof the guest of the evening, and in the coarse of his speech alluded, to the great successes of the Liberal party. He went onto criticise the proposals of the Government in the Proce- dure Committee, and avued that thv would have effected a resolution fatal asid disastrous to the authority of the House of Commons, a resolution calculated) to give the whole initiation and control of legislation to the House of Lords. Mr. Schnadhorst, in reply; expressed a confidentopinion that at tha next election two divi. sions of Birmingham would be represented by working- men. The Liberal Federatiorr were prepared with can- didates for every election that might take place, thosigh they did not always deem it advisable to rad them I:on- ward beforehand. • .1
PEOPLE BOUND TO THE SIAKE.

The great majority of people have to work for a 1117, ing with hands or head, or both. Very well: To make our living we must be able to labour, so marry hours in a day, days in a week, weeks in a,year. Very good again. But suppose we each had an enemy who possessed the power to tie us up with a rope when he pleased. To-day he ties only the left arreiy.,.te-morrow the right, the next day a leg,..and so on.. Once in a while he ties us to our beds and keeps up there a week.. How much would he cost us in hard cash irka year P. and how much would it be worth to us if we could chain him to a rock or hang him with his -own rope?. Let us have a rough illustration or two. A man was working on the Midland Railway aa,. at signalman. We all know what the position is and have some idea of the labour and responsibility: Well, he kept at it for several years, never missing a day. He knew his busines, nobody better, and nothing want wrong on his section of the line;, but by-and-by his enemy began to tie him up. Somehow he- couldn't eat with a relish any more ; when he tried he was taken with such a distress it took all the life clad. him. Then he would have times when he was so giddy, that every- thing went round and round like a whirligig. If this had happened when he had a signal to set, a collision inight, have come of it: happily it did not. Other- ropes wore tied around him: he had pains in the chest and sides, his bowels became costive, tongue coated, bad taste in, the mouth, heartburn, weakness,. Sic. The doctors said, he would have to give up his situation;, but he couldn't. There were the wife and children to be looked out for, and only his earnings to do it with. But finally he broke down altogether, and was laid up for weeks, unconscious part of the time. Then, we may say,ile was tied hand and foot. His enemy had him fast, and came nigh kill- ing him. One day, after the doctors had given him up,. his mind was clear, and he remembered a xnedicine—halil the bottle full—he had hidden away in a locker in a signal box and forgotten all about it. He sent for it and took a dose. In less than a month he-was a well: mart ; the ropes were all cut away. If you write to him (Andrew Agge, Culgaith, Cumberland) he will tell you this medicine was Mother Seigere Carative Syrup, and his ailment was indigestion and dyspepsia. But,. whilst he was ill with it, he might as well,—yes,. better'—have been tied to a stake. _ .

There are lots of cases of this sort all over England— all over the world. A few of them we hearof of them we never hear of. Sometimes it is heart disease; sometimes rheumatism; sometimes consumption.; some- times general debility ;, sometirnss kidney and bladder complaint; sometimes nervous prostration ; sometimes liver disorder. That is,. the doctors call it byall these hard names, but at the bottom it is indigestion and dyspepsia, and all these other so-called disea.ses are just tokens and symptoms of that—neither more nor less. If man never had any trouble with his ,-,tomach, he might live for ever, for aught we can. tell.. Yet how„in Mercy's name, can a man or woman work with death and cor- ruption inside, of the body—with the stomach full of decaying food, sending poisan throughtheblood to every joint, muscle', and nerve ? This is what dyspepsia dam. Indigestion is a slow but sure poison,lust as taking so many grains of arsenic every day would be. Here is another case, that of a railway fireman, who writes from Hurlford. He says : "I have been a suf- ferer from indigestion and dyspepsia for three yews; I tried several doctors, bat got worse all the time. At last I went to a chemist and he promised to cure m& in a week or two. He sold me three very expensive bottles of medicine, and all the effect I felt from.it was the loss of' my money. Then I got hold of a bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup, and was better almost at ones. How sorry lam I didn't use it years ago ! " We can give this man's name if you care to have it. He didn't want it printed. But he was as good as tied up for a long while. Illnessis a strong rope.

Hers is onomore illustration. Mr. R. B. Hopton, of Long Weston, says : "1 am sixty-eight years old, Mother Seigells44:rtm has not quite made me a young man again, but it has cured me of asthma, nervous pros- tration,and the throat ailment arising from impureblood. I was too ill to labour, yet can now do my work, thanks to that great remedy. You may publish the fact. The whole complication came first from indigestion." And this is the way people are bound. until Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup sets them free.

She did not intend to remain in'quarters . with, her husband all her life.- - Lucy had, she argued, been born for better thing; and, therefore, she saved all she could to enable her to livo in some Sanatarium in the hot season'as a "lady."' ! • Her husband was appointed acting quartermaster, and now she felt mere satisfied, but 'the old feeling that she had been a vietim still remained supreine. • He was ordered to another station, and then MI s. Layton came out in quite a different character. She did not care to accompany him. She had a little house of her own, and, by some female strategy,. managed to court attention without giving rise to scandal. New arrivals,, who were- not? particular, ' pronounced her a ",jolly little woman," and in the deadly Want of occupatim at times Mrs. Layton Managed to secure a flirtation with the sulialterns. . . .

So i'hings went on mall her industrious, and per- severing partner was put 011' the staff, transferred to a distant station, and, then el2u came out in her true colours.. As an officer's wife), as she said, she could ruffle it with the best, and atain loans from tho bank when she got into dsbt. These debts were seSured upon her husband's pay. Ile had to insure his life in consequence for the- benefit of tho bank. But Lney did not care. She determined to boa lady, and so she carried on all sail, ,regardless of the leo fill' re to which she was &if tinst . .

Thus it came to pass that she found herself at Mussuri at the beginning of the hot seasom—and quite ready to iiirt in moderation—though quite capable of inspiring a grande passion in some of the idlerawho came up on sick leave ttatlae station i t/ao

AN EXPLOSION. - THE Mall at Mussuri is or was, at!the date of' any ' story, the great meeting place for the society of the 'station. It was the drive before-Mentioned whieh is .not free from danger to quick' riders for it is only a, few feet wide and not more than half a mile long in the level- It is not given to everyone to gallop along such, a, road with a mountain ons one side and a precipice en the other. Between. five and six o'clock in therafternoon ins Mall is crowded, We have ladies in janpans and ladies on horseback, with plenty of men in curious costumes te,carry the former, and some on hotseback, to escort the bitter. Tiffin ha., passe&and everyone is at liberty to .idc in the Mall. Some amble, sorne canter, a low gallop, and nearly all ass flirting, ler what else can, you do in Mussuri The enamoured embaltern who had :despised the Major's advii-e Were tittin, was now in. f till flirtation with Mrs. lasyirn. Shy, had taken him with her that morning. to,the milliner's, and ho hav assisted her to ; snake a choice of a n4w bonnet, anti had even given her to trades-stand tlist sire need not mind the ; expense for he owid.rel. it ripresent'to her, And now Shl3 is C.21:01./ili.;;Eg nhn ii. a manner which, if flirtation were not su common, and furious love- making rather . fatter° of the station, would have been prono-inesa atelrleoly "marked." Major Dean., nho was up on short sick leave, pending the issue of the threatening rumours that were flying in all dirieti,:ns concerning the native regiments, warch.3.l the pair, and being indirectly related to lina foolis't young man, determined to put a: stop to his folly Were a duel end vandal ensued. But tho pass 'widow, who peroeived that hr admirer had a long parrs. had made op her mind to dip into it, and encouraged the young man so openly that older "hands," though porhers not a whit less .intragante, turned up their eyes end 'wonder how she. could. Mrs. Layton rvotild doubtless not have.carried on such a flirtation 'rod she been aware of the probable consequences, fer duelling had by no means gone:out.. of fashion in Mussuri. Many a quarrel at tho club had ended in a meeting, and Major Deane deter, mined to- save his young friend's character, and protect the foolish woman, who was running her Lead, into a noose, for her husband's sake at any rate. And thus some weeks passed. He spoke seriously to Frank Soutar,..and made such a point Of being attentive to Mrs. Layton that she became quite flattered. The Major saw only one way out of the trouble, and took it.. He called on the young "grass widow," who gave no quarter to her enemies, and was graciously receive& "I have heard of you, Major Deane," said...the beauty, "'from Mr. Soutar. I feel; quite as-if you were An old friend." _ _

"I regret I can scarcely count myself a friend," replied the Major, gallantly. "I wish koeukl; but you see—' ' Welli„Major ; pray oceed." "1 acam Itely know ether/I ought. You see, Mrs. Layton., lam peculiar in my views, and wish my friends Mbe really friends. Now yo-a are so young, so—pardon me—so handsome, that I cannot dare to aepire—l beg your pardon, I'm sure—l didn't meaer*" tr

Here the-Major' who was scarcely forty,. sighed, and continuesl the conversation in a melaneholytone. I must:save Mai*, he thought; this woman would swallow.me as the whale did Jonah; but he only sighed, and continued— • • Yoey.my dear Mrs. Layton, but I see your time is.so occupied---" " Oh.dea.r no; I'm quite disengaged. My dear Major ,Ii sball be charmed to see you at anytime." "B.at Mx. Soutar —" began the Major. "Never mind Frank Soutar. He is young and silly. 'A good boy enough I allow: but my friends, MajaarDeane, must be older and steadier men." • "Shall you be at the Mall to-morrow, Mrs. Layton,? " "Certainly; and you will be there, too?" "Yes. I hope so. But my chances are so very emelLin. comparison—" " I will keep myself disengaged omptrpose ts) rido with you. Major. There T." "•lt, hall be charmed, I'm sure; nay, am charmed alrsady," responded the diplomatic Major, as he took his leave.. "Au platar
right," responded the lady. "Never mind. pleueure to see you. And, Major, I will be thoro at five." _ _ _

The assignation was made, mak the gallant 4or who was a.,married man,. laughed heartily when he thought of how he had, "cut out" his young relative, anti‘ what a lessonhe w.ould read the grass widow. Bat he little knew the nature with which he had be deal. Mrs. Layton cared little for any man.; !, except her husband; but to have -the- commander of the detachment M which lies' hasbend was, or ha/ been serving, at her feet wae. for her a triumph.. All her native coquetry returned,.and she made up her mind to plague the Major.. And he? Could he have, told, or in any way : ;messed the raiaery in store far him from the time when he atttempted to save two young people from scandal, I rather think he would have let them take . their own path and the =sequences at the same time. . . It is no part of our story tesdetect the means- and ways whereby in a few days the astute Major:lt:quid the weak side of the grass wide's!, and befoolact her. Bhe snulabed the youngen man, and appeared: quite delighted at the success- whTeh she had gained. While congratulating herself, did not fcrget the main chance, and she probably would have succeeded had net her husband get a hint of the eirermstances, and roadside unexpected. appearance on the scene. There was a suddeuly-organised dance at the club that evening, and yeung b'outar, whose name had been mentioned pretty-freely in connection with Mrs. Layton, was madly jealeue of the " He had perceived his Oiend's tactics, and had resented the, interference. He had told the lady, and her pride had been se/merely wounded. Bigh words had passed. The elder officer had been obliged to con- fess his well-meant but somewhat clumsy endeavour to save appearance which had only resulted in a ' worse fate for himself. P

It was at the dance that evening that Layton appeared in civilian costume and met Soutar at the supper table, He had learnt enough to make him angry, and the other had had enough champagne to make 'him quarrelsome. We can, perhaps, ima- gine the meeting. The first supper had passed over. The ladies had gone home, and at an early hour of fhb morning the men sat down to their roar supper, and a very noisy one it was. The young non-commissioned officei bided his ; time. Ho had. watched Soutar and ids wife, and had taxed her with her misconduct. Soutar was too tipsy to be discreet, and when during supper he was boasting ofl his influence in a certain quarter, Layton turned, and coolly and deliberately gave him the lie direct. t "What did you say t" cried Soutar, angrily

"I Say that's a lief" repeated the injured hus4 band. No more was needed. Soutar sprang at his enemy, as he deemed him, and an unseemly struggle would have taken place had not both the men been held back by main force. The Major, who was preeouto was obliged to orders both combatants under arrcst,, but they heeded him not Soutar turned Upon L'un. violently, and a tetritle uproar ensued: The principals in the quarrel were with ddlcultr kept apart; and at length,losinw all command over himself, Layton ruidied suddenli3forward and struck his antagonist a:heavy blow. "Take that, you lying scoundrel!" he crd. "It will teach you to, traduce. men's wives again. MY' name is Layton. lam that lady's husband." A dread silence fell upon all wbo heard theses-re/Tin' and witnessed the affair. . Not a sound was heard as Soutar, completely sobered by the blow, was, his face and with a smile of savage satisfaction,' replied: "Very well, Sergeant Layton. / know you now. You will consider yourself under arrest. I call tilon.' you all here to bear witness he has struck his - superior officer, and ;he will be tried by, court- martial. You know the result most probably." Layton turned pale as death as he aoted the yin' distive glance-that accompanied this speech. The- whole truth was now disclosed.' Mrs.. Layton was' after all only the wife of a quartermaster-pergeant, and her future at Mussuri was quite untenable. The circumstances were, however, not known generanY until' the following morning, and then the occurrence of the evening before Was th'e talk of the whole

station, - How had the husband obtained the admittance to the club? How was it possible that Layton had left his carps and. come up unannounced and unexpected to Mustairi just at that time? No one could answer these questions, and yet it is certain that he had received some information which led to his sudden. appearance. What would Mrs. Layton do ?,I Her name was now bandied about.in a most unceremonious way, and being only a non - commissioned officer's wife, a course her offence was dreadful. She had also , thrust herself into a situation and endeavoured to gain a position amongst her betters, and even if, as a. people said, her husband had been lately advanced " to commissioned rank as quartermaster, he had not been gazetted. Of course ladies could nob associate with Mrs. Layton. Her character western to shreds before she left , Mussuri. Those who had not fancied her at anr time were now, of course:: exceedingly bitter, and , even the ,men—the civilians up there—no longer cared to net her. Major Deane was the ondr. person who showed her any kindness; but Mrs. Layton, believing he had been the cause of all the scandal, spurned him, and said. some very indignant' and cruel things. - "You have ruined my life amongst you. If you lad not interfered with me I might have been, at , any rate, spared the humiliation •I am now suffering • from. Go—l don't want to see you again." But hear me for your husband' d sake, if not for , your own, for your future is clouded at present." "Yes, and you have clouded it. Leave me, please+ Major Deane. I can hate pretty well, and it is to you I owe my humiliation. lam going to join nal husband, but depend upon it, if ever I can revenge . myself upon you, I will.' "Nonsense," was the somewhat stern reply. "Val had better join your husband at Sealkote as soon you can. He will be tried by court-martial, but no , doubt under the circumstances will be acquitted or let off easily. Let me help you."' "I tell you I hate and detest you, and if I were starving, which thank goodness 1 am not, or in want of money, I would not accept a rupee from you or yours. Why couldn't you leave me alone?" "I acted for the best. I wished to save that Or Soutar from making a fool of himself and you. 1 am pledged to look after him, and I have onlY carried out my trust. You seem.to forget that you are married, and he is a boy." "I forget nothing—l never she'll, and you shall . some day learn that I can hated My husband is quite assured, and you know that no harm ever came from my flirtation. Every woman flirts here. Whr should I have been alone humiliated? Leave thie house if you please or I will write to your wife and , tell her how you gave sought me. That would be a sweet revenge." The Major started. He, had certainly committed " himself a little in appearance, but all with the best intentions. It is those who act with the best into- tions, without considering whether their interference is necessary or not, who get into scrapes. "You are a bad, wicked woman, I am afraid," be- answered hotly, "and I wash my hands of you." "Your hands are not' so clean after all, she re" " I torted. "We shall yet meet, and I will pay my debt ' I if I die for it." All the etfl in her nature appeared to- have 1)03131 roused, and she stood flushed and angry before the , abashed officer like a beautiful fairy. Opening the' door she motioned to the well-meaning but over- zealous Major to leave the house. . By October most of the residents were thinking en returning to the plains. The season has had its victims of play and passion. More than one duel had. been fought, and one of the combatants had bean. killed. Elopements were also well represented in the list of casualties. Two ladies who had been special'. angry with "that Mrs. Layton, as she calls herself,' had left their husbands, and Soutar congratulated himself, when he was summoned to Calcutta as 6.- witness in one action, that he had not egured as-°' principal in another. He had learnt his lesson. Meantime sentence had been pronounced ul°l'. Layton, who, however, had been permitted to resial°, with his wife in quarters pending the assembling' 0' the court-martial. She had the candour to confess, her share in the business, and told him all the truth. He forgave her, and then the Court atsembled and sat for many days. The evidence was conclusive" The soldier had struck his superior officer. The' penalty in such eases was DEATH ! The Court had no choice but to find the cattail penalty, but they added a rider to the finding, an' the whole of the proceedings were forwarded to the' .Gkwernor-General. 'The forwarding and considerse tion of the documents, with the return of the opiaioa confirming or quashing the sentence, occupied a log time, and the prisoner 1-1123 still detained. His wife' and he was quite reconciled, and he was fully ar!,i pared for his fate. Soutar, who had repented, explained all the circumstances to the ptisonea, he had received his excuses. At length the sentences arrived, and with it Cato° WI g a memorandum and the approval of the executioruo a native officer who had been found guilty of mutinous language.asalinciting the native infantli: to revolt, with a view to promote rebellion again" tite State, and to subvert the British Governueente The finding of the Court in both cases had: beet; gailty, and the sentences had been approved, an° confirmed. The,native was to be blown from a git`a. after the "usual good character "- of the prison' had been taken into consideration. The Ear°- peen was ordered to be shot, and the young officer; cashiered for their, respective shames in the biainesn at Mussuri. Of the time people implicated the native scented the least affected. The sentence upon the men-cote' missioned officer was felt to be harsh, but the cir eumstances were peculiar. The whole Indam were mutinous, or verging on mutiny., and example was called for. Short shift was given the prisoners, There much sympathy evoked for poor Mrs. Layton, On tor. eve of her confinement too, and Lieutenant Sou was scarcely pitied. But there was a. surprise for in store, yet sympathy gave way to indignation ,disgusta when, on the nightbefora the executton to take place, the disgraced officer was observeaan'la earneehconeersation with,the sergeant's wife. they were planning something waa supposed. Next- morning the garrison was startled br report that the lieutenant and the woman hal 71 away together. At least no trace could be foanan either, and circumstances pointed to the fact.. gross indecency was everywhere condemned, P iawas certain that Mrs. Layton had gone. ...„4 At half-past four p.m. the rumbling of the .67,1376- on to the parade-ground broke the silence phice, and the spectators assembled to see the stc`it'ed tion which ended in a tragedy totally unexPe blia by all, and worked E, wonderful change in Pn. . . . At the Leigh Police Court on Mowl3ay, John Worsley, a boy, of Bell Vuo, Lowton, ho resides with his parents, was charged with setting fire to a haystack belonging to Mr. Joseph Wood, of Byrom Hall, Lowton. Joseph Wood, farmer, eaid he was going into one or his shippons to milk the cows, and Worsley was going in the stockyard. Shortly afterwards witness-saw that one of the bhaystacks was on fire. The strsok-was one of between 2E and 30 tons, and eight or eine tons were damaged. J ssistance was rendered by the servants of the adjoiwing farm and a number ot neighbours, and water was thrown on the

_ burning hay. lie estimated the damage done at £5O. Andrew Carney, labourer in the erhploy of Wood, said he was carting 'hay on the afternoon an question, and saw the boy Worsley sitting at one cower of a stack of old hay. Soon afterwards Wchalev ran out, and a mo- ment later witness saw flames at the bottom of the hay- stack, and in loss than a miahte they spread from the bottom to the top,—Cross-examined by Worsley's ;mother, witness said belted not seen the boy playing with thatches. There had been another man at the place during the afternoon, and a jacket Was burnedby the stack. div.head: LIVERPOOL MANCHESTER, &c., AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: LIVERPOOL MANCHESTER, &c., AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agri- cultural Society,—.called principally for the purpose of fixing the place 43f next year's show, and of award- ing the prizes for farms, cottages, and gardens, was held on Thursday, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington. There was a large attendance, the chair being occupied by Mr.. J. W. Fair, of Wigan. Amongst those also present were Messrs. John White, W. Scotson, R. Webster, T. Parson, J. Southern, James Hatton, James Birch, C. R. Linaker, F. Robinson, J. animal, W. Darlss shire, R.. Lonsdale, T. Fairhurst, and T. Rigby {Secretary). '

div.head: NEXT YEAR'S-EHOW.
div.p: NEXT YEAR'S-EHOW.

After several new members had been elected, Mr. Rigby explained that at previous meetings of the mem- bers overtures had been received from the authorities of the towns of Bury and Bolton, asking the society to hold their show of 1291 in those places. Deputations had been received on the subject, the gentlemen composing which had set forth the claims of their respective towns. Ulti- mately a cominitteeof inspection was appointed. The committee met at Bury in June, and saw three sites in that neighbourhood. They then proceeded to Bolton, ' and visited the site of the show held there in 1872. The result of the inspections was that there was a tacit understanding that each member of the coin- mitten shculd individually express his views as to the most desirable site at the meeting then being held. Two of the members of the inspection Committee had written their opinions to the meeting. One, Mr. J. C. 1 Hale, wrote that his opinion was decidedly in favour of the Bury number 2site. Amongst other advantages it possessed was the one that it would require very little fencing, and it was in other respects well situated. Mr. Brockholes wrote acquiescing in the recommendation that the site mentioned should be chosen, and Mr. Scot- son,also a member of. the Committee, said that after tak-1 lug all circumstances into consideration, he was inclined to vote for Bury. On the other hand, Mr. Helsel], also , one of the Committee, pointed outthat the larger popula-1 tion of Bolton gave prospect of a better financial success, and that the means of access to the town were favourable to exhibitions. He thought that the ' interests and the safety of the society would be better consulted by going to Bolton rather than to Bury. The Mayor of Bolton, Alderman John Barrett, then introduced an influential deputation.from that borough, which, he said, waseoxious that the society should hold its next year's show there. When the show was held there be- fore it was a success, though the population was only 90,000, whereas now itamounted t 0120,000. There were also populous districts round about. The General Pur- poses Committee of the 'Town Council, which included the whole body, met the other day to consider the mat- ter of a guarantee fund. Though they could not vote a sum direct to the society, it was almost unan- imously decided that £5OO should be voted to the Mayor next year for the purpose of the show. Spon- taneous offers of donations had also been received and he had,not the slightest doubt that the sum men- tioned would be doubled. Other members of the depute- ion having spoken, a deputation from Bury was intro- Itluced by the Mayor of that town, Alderman Brierley, who stated that every effort would be made to secure a successful show at that place. He thought there •would lise no eiifficulty in raising an .adequate sum for local prizes, as well as the usual guarantee fund. If £5OO or .13.,000 were required, it would be forthcoming. Mr. Thomas Stetter, jun., president of the Radcliffe and Pilkington Agricultural Society; also introduced a depu- tation representative of that body' which urgently desiles that the show should be held at Bury. On a vote being taken, the meeting decided in favour of Bury, 20 voteobeing recorded for that town, and 18 for Bolton.

'each, itnd until Warrington vOsS reached there was no bridge across the river from the sea, and again for some miles higher up the riper them was no 'other bridge, and accordingly the streets of Warrington were, if he might use the expression, ilooded with traffic consequent upon its being focussed from the enormous stretch of country. The main street of Warrington was, in fa.ct,the high road between Lancashire said Cheshire, and it crossed the river at the town an& found its way by roads north and south. Consequentiy there was a connection between the outside districts on the north and south banks of the river and Warrington which they did notrind to the same extent in most.oeher towns.

A DIVIDED BOROUGH.. • The river divFided the borough into t'VVO portions, the lower portion‘being in the county of Chester, and the upper portion in the county of Lancashire. To some extant the inconvenience had been cured by the legisla- tion of 1888, but hitherto the fact he had referred to had been attended by many inconveniences which would be Obvious. t ,et him mention one or two: If an offence I was committed on one bank of the river it would be dealt with by one set of justices, and if it was committed .on the ether bank of the river it would be dealt with by a different set of justices. Then if anybody fell into the river td was drowned, it woald depend upon the bank of theliiver to which his body was brought whether he wouhobbe sat upon by the coroner of Lancashire or the coroner of Cheshire, obviossly two different persons. Those and other matters it was sought to remedy by the propcsed Bill. It was not necessary for him to point out thattven in a borough sitnated as this was, natural extension ought to followthe lines of the main roads, butevenif the matter stood there would be a claim fora reskjustmentof the boandaries of Warrington. Some- thing had, however, arisen in recent years which had accentuated the need or this re-arrangement of the berandaries. The hon.members of the Committee knew Well that the

how wining or considerate.. Therefore, economically and on other grounds, it we desirable that the water tinder- taking should be in 1.1... e hands of authorities, and the Committee would tind from good figures that would be handed in that, having regard to other transactions , which had taken place,notably in the Windsor and Stock- I ton, and Middlesbrough cases, the terms of the transfer would compare favourably with what had been done in such cases. A graduated scale had been arrived at, so as to deal adequately with the different classes of stock , in the water undertaking, compensation being arranged in proportion to the value of each stock. It was hoped, taking into account the arrangement proposed as to a sinking fend, that the great object would be secured to the town without any unreasonable burden being cast at all upon it. ARGITMENTS FOR TIM EXTENSION. There had been no opposition on the part of the owners of property or ratepayers to the proposed extension— that was a significant and a happy feature of the present case. The area of the township of Latchford proposed to be added was 1711 acres, and the rateable value £1,577 or thereabouts. In Appleton there were 45 acres, and the rateable value £3,041; in Walton Inferior the area was 231 acres, and a rateable value £250; so that the Com- mittee would see that none of these were in any degree large interests to be dealt with. The population pro- posed to be taken of Latchford was 86, of Appleton 463, of Walton Inferior 45, so that again there was no great disturbance of existing interests. But the necessity for dealing with those districts was independent of this, that they would be absolutely cut off from the remainder of their own township by the Manchester Ship Canal. They would be on the opposite bank, and it would be more convenient for them to be part of Warrington,than to remain the existing territories, because they could be only approached by ocgasional means of getting across the Manchester Ship Canal; whereas being connected with the town on the same bank as they would be with Warrington it would be much more convenient. Evi- dence would be given to show that the Warrington Union and the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority were in favour of the extension.

--- --- Warrington was a borough which sinceits constitution bad increased very largcly in population and ratable value, and in all-the materials winch go to constitute the prosperity and the importance of a town,. In 1847;wthen Ithe boundaries e the borough were origmally fixed, the Ilpopulation was only '22,800, and taking it by stases it would be found that in 1361 it had grown to 26,00 U—he merely gave the round numbers—in 11 to 32,000, in 1881 to 41,000, and in-1800 the popniation was estimated at 50,000. Therefore it would be • seen that 'since the question of boundaries was last dealt with the-borough had more than doubled its population. The houses again exhibited the same rate of increase. In 1851 the number of houses was 4,f301) in round figures ; in 1861 they were 5,200; in 1871, 6,2001 in 1881. -sow; and in /890 the, estimated number was 0,137. Then again it would be seen that this increase corresponded with the actual increase of population, the increase 'being 9,137 in 1890 as against 4,634 in 1851. But the increase in ratable value was still more remarkable, because in 'lB5l the ratable value was £52,000; in Tam it was £62;000: in 1871 it was £97,000; in 1881 it was £137,000: and in 1890 £150,000. Returns would be submitted which would show those increases in detail, but the summary he had given was a short and convenient one.
TREPORTLET

Large staple industrios were carried on in- the town which were principally connected with the manufacture of iron, wire and cotton goods, and goods of 'that class. It was also obviously a place ot oorisiderable interest to the railway companies, and that was a very good test of the importance and trade of the town, because' the Com- mittee would see by the map that 'limes intersected it hi various directions. He was told that those-aompanies, either by lines of their own or by .running powers that connected it with Manchester and other places, were the London and North-Western, the Great Western, the Mid- kind, the Great Northern, the Manchester,Sheßield, and Lincolnshire, and the combined system known as the Cheshire Lines. Obviously, therefore, Warrington was a place of great commercial activity and interest, and he thought one might say of great \value to the ,railway companies. There was one feature about Warrington which he thought marked it out frem almost any other borough—indeed, he thought it would be difficult to find the case ef any other borough which was exactly on all fours with that of Warrington—the Committee would see that traversing, in fact, boundingiene might almost say, the present Borough of Warrington, was the river Mersey, Which flowed in a loop-like course through the borough. The town was as nearly-as possible fialf-way between Liverpool and Manchester, about 18 miles from

Sometimes Arpley Meal dows were five or six inches under water at high tide when a westerly wind prevailed, but there would not bti much difficulty in preventing flooding. Be did not, think that the Mersey Dock Board would object to an' abstract of such tidal area. Though the Manchester , Ship Canal might own a considerable proportion of the Arpley Meadows, he denied that the sole or any object of the Corporation was to secure an increase of the ratable value at the expense of the Manchester Ship Canal. rhe Corporation thought this was a proper time, owing to the congested state of some parts tat the borough, to seek a permanent extension of the borough. In reply to Mr. Clifford.—The Corporation had origin- ally fixed the boundary as the centre of the canal, but in endeavouring to come to terms with the Ship Canal Company they altered the boundary to the north bank. While the whole of Warrington was in Lancashire for administrative purposes the persons in the added areas of Appleton and Walton would still be Parliamentary votefs in one of the divisions of Cheshire, and the 'Bill did not propose to remedy this anomaly. He understood that there was a public meeting in Appleton to protest against the annexation, and calling upon the Cheshire County Council to oppose it, but so far as he knew none of the inhabitants affected were present. lie ckuld not say whether a similar meeting was held and a similar resolution adopted in the Walton township. Re-examined by Mr. Fitzgerald.—The Corporation only adopted the canal as a boundary because it made an excellent one physically. For police purpeses all ther canal would still be in the county of Cheshire.

FRAECOME, Mayor of Warrington, in reply to Mr. Balfour Browne, said he lived at Wilderspool in Appleton, and owned property in that neighbourhood, a' portion of which was proposed to be annexed to the borough. He concurred with what Mr. Longdin, the borough surveyor, had said as to the canal being the rational physical boundary. Witness's place of business was at 'Warrington, and a great number of people living in Appleton had business interests in the borough. Mr. CLIFFORD: Is your feeling as to annexation shared by your fellow inhabitants? I did not attend the meet- ing which has been mentioned; but I think the only thing they object to is paying the higher rate. That is the difference between Zs. 4d. and ss. 10d. ? Yes. That is a very important matter, isn't it? Yes. How long have you resided in Appleton? Since January of this year. Where did you re3ide before? In Warrington. Witness further admitted that it was possibly open to the Corporation to have proceeded by Provisional Order, but it was a matter for their legal adviser. Mr. BALFOUR BROWNE : I am very glad this has been mentioned. We communicated with the Local Govern- ment Board, but we found we could not proceed by means of a Provisional Order because of the contemplated purchase of the water undertaking.

div.head: GENERAL POSITION OP THE TOWN.
div.p: THE GENERAL POSITION OP THE TOWN.

- - The learned counsel then detailed at some length the work done by the Corporation for the benefit of Warring- ton in the way of its public library, art gallery, its police arrangements, fever hospital, and other matters. He pointed out also that the Corporation were the owners of the Gas Works, which had been in their hands for some considerable time, The price of gas had, in consequence, been reduced, and the Corporation hoped to go further in that direction. As regards finance the Borough of Warrington was, in comparison with other towns, in a satisfactory position. They had borrowed for what he might call the general purposes of the town, as distinct from purposes which were remunerative, roundly £152,000, and some £46,000 or £47,000 of that had been I paid off by the operation of a sinking fund, leaving a lbalance practically of £104,000. The present rateable value of the town without an extension was £150,000. Therefore the Committee would see that there was noth- ing in that direction which need cause anxiety. There was a further debt, an originaldebt of £202,000, borrowed for the purpose of the purchase if the gas undertaking, £31,000 of which had:been Todd off, leaving something like £170,000 due under that head. That was not properly a charge upon the property of thetown, because that had been borrowed for'the purpose of the gas sup- ply in the same sense as other borrowings, which was money spent for remunerative purposes. Of course it was well-known, too, that the existence of outside dis- tricts such as these in close proximity to a town led to increased value in the land for letting and selling pur- poses or otherwise. Thestreets in the area to be added were not at present lighted, and in some partslhere are notve-laws for the regulation oi buildings. gm In his opinion the whole of the drainage of the added •district could be efficiently dealt with by the Warrington Cor- poration, andlie added that frequent complaints had been made of the pollution of the Sankey Brook, and the 'Corporation believed that if more of it wereinoluded within the borough they would be able to prevent its palkition. ME. JAMES MANsaaorf, C.E., of Great George-St., Westminster, who stated that he had large experience of extension schemes and water undertakings, said that he had gone over the whole of the district concerned in the proposed extension, and he was of opinion that the Ship Canal constituted an admirable boundary. It was a well-defined physical feature in the country separating one part from another. He also inspected the Water Works, and considered the terms of transfer fair and reasonable between the parties. Ile thought it very desirable that they should be vested in the hand of the Corporation. In reply to Mr. Clifford: He believed the money derived from increased rate would be expended on the district. Re-examined by Mr. Pembroke Stephens.—The objec- tion might be met by a scheme for differential rating. It seemed to him that the clause providing for arbitra- tion between the Cheshire County Council and the Cor- poration would settle any financial questions arising from the addition to the municipal area, and was sufficient. Alderman J. E. Wright and Alderman T. B. Sutton, of Warrington, were also examined in favour of the Bill, and the Committee adjourned until the next day.

div.head: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
This Bill again came before the Committee of the House of Commons on Wednesday, Mr. Mounts presid- ing. .
ALDERMAN BURGESS SPEAKS IN FAVOUR OF TUE BILL.

Alderman Jonx Bunging, of Warrington, examined by Mr. Pembroke Stephens, Q.C., said that he had filled the office of Mayor, and for a number of years had been an active member of the Corporation. He had taken a great interest in the sanitary affairs of the borough, and had been connected with many important works which had been carried out. Warrington was an active manu- facturing centre, outside of which there was a large agricultural district. It was a place to which these out- siders came for purposes of their own, using the streets, markets, Szc. The borough of Warrington possessed several public buildings, and had control of its own gas supply. There was also baths, a library and museum in Warnngton, all of which were available for the people outside the borough boundary. Notwithstanding all this activity and the growth of the town, there had been no extension of the borough boundary since its incor- poration in 1847. At that time there was an idea of incorporating the Arpley meadows, and the Boundary Commissioners approved of the proposal; but the three or four owners of the land at the time were adverse, and the district consequently was not included. As matters now stand, are you in any way cramped? We are very much cramped. There has been a consider- able change in the district owing to the Mar.hester Ship Canal, which has, I think, caused an additiona: uopula- non of about 3000.

In the neighbourhood of A rpley Meadows there are some" buildings, are there not? Yes. The Wilderspool Brewery, is that in full work? Yes, breweries generally are. (Laughter.) There is consider- able business carried on there' and I think the whole of the work people are resident immediately around the boundary. Along the main roads out of Warrington building is actively going on? Yes. Do you find that those outside the borough take advan- tage of your institutions such as markets, recreation grounds, baths, museum, library, and others? They have the use of all these. They are as much at their ser- vice as at anyone's in the town. Do you think that in all these matters there is a die- tinct community of interest between the borough and outsiders? Outsiders have all the advantages the inha- bitants have in these matters, the only difference being that they have the advantage, whereas up to the present Warrington has paid for the whole of it. Do you think that if the outsiders are brought in there will be advantage to them in any way as to sanitary matters? I think there would be great advantage, very great ; and I think, too, if a poll were taken upon this question that they feel and know that. In the first place, I think you have an efficient police force in Warrington. This, of course, at present has nothing to do with the outside districts. Yes. Then in the same way they would share in the advan- tage of your fire brigade without anything to pay for it? Yes.

_ Would they also have the benefit of your hospital, upon which you have spent a large sum of money? Yes And last, not least, would they be entitled to use on equal terms with the citizens the cemetery? Yes. (A laugh.) It is a fact that not merely is Warrington built up, but the houses in Warrington are well filled at the present ? Yes, the houses in Warrington are crowded. We have perhapsnot fifty houses unoccupied. We have immense overcrowding in some parts. It there ever is to be an extension of borough boun- Idaries would you say that in this case specially the time I has come? I never knew of a place whie.h required an extension of boundaries more than Warrington does. Cross-examined by Mr. Cripps, QC., witness said that lin-1847 the proposal to incorporate Arplev Meadows in the borough was not adopted; except for the Manchester Ship Canal the had been no very great change since. There had been some change, however, as the Bank Quay Foundry Company had since built some works there. He thought the Manchester Ship Canal formed the natural southern boundary of the borough. Now you have mentioned the value of Warrington to these districts, what would be the advantage to the dis- tricts themselves? They will be better governed, they will be more within civilisation, and enjoy the benefits of Warrington. They will not be a lost people as they are now. (Laughter.) Do the people of Latchford use your sewage system? Yes. _
_ And do they pay for it? Yes, they pay for that part of the district which is outside the borough.

It is not a-clesfialale thing, however, ti; have to take ether people's sewage, but it is a matter dealt with in the Public Health Act, and I suppose occurs in every other borough in England ? I suppose it does, but that does not make it desirable. One rather serious matter was mentioned by you as to the cemetery ; there is no difficulty in burials there? I cannot tell ; I have not experienced that yet. (Laughter.) Do you rely upon this cemetery matter? I don't, per- haps, vet. (Renewed laughter.) Cross-examined by Mr. Worsley Taylor, witness said that the present scheme was elaborated by a Committee of very able gentlemen. Who were they? It would be rather invidions to. Have I the pleasure of seeing one before me? Yes. (Laughter.) Who else? Mr. Frederick Monks. He is a Cheshire squire? He does not live in War- rington. Another was Mr. Alderman Joseph Davies, awl there were also fifteen or sixteen members of the General Purposes Committee. Cross-examined by Mr. Clifford: Witness said that the average rate in Warrington for the last five years was. 5E% 74.(1 . in the £ ; but the last rate collected was 58. 10d.; or thereabout.

War is a remnant as a matter of fact, of barbarism --- the time when men settled their differences, as the brutes do still, by "tooth and claw." In view ' of the vast and ever-iner3asing standing armies Which are organised on the continent, it seem absurd to many people to talk of getting rid of 'var. But the darkest hour is before tho dawn; and it is not unlikely that the ago of universal armament will immediately precede the age of universal arbitration. This much progress has already been made, that it is not now customary, even amongst Tories, to sneer at arbitration as was the case when Mr. GLADSTONE, to his lasting honour, brought about, by this method, a settle- inent of the Alabama claims. Distant as the end 'nay be, that was at any rate the beginning of the end of the old bad system of settling disputes by force of arms. Civilisation has got thus far that ' it is regarded as brutal and disreputable for two men who have quarrelled to go into the street and " fight it out." The community insists upon it that, if men cannot agree, the' shall appeal to ' courts of law ; and it takes upon itself to punish those Who, as the phrase goes, take the law into their own hands. We have only to carry this Principle a little further, and war between nations will be, in a similar way, regarded as brutal and disreputable. Let the feeling be followed up by International Courts, with international officers, or soldiers, to enforce the decrees of the courts, and there is an end of war; for resistance in such a case would be as hopeless then as individual re- 'stance to the police is to-day. Why go to war? The question is now being asked by nations; and that is a great step in ad- vance. The Hon. D. D. FIELD (United States). Win presided at the formal opening of the Peace Congress on Monday afternoon, said :—" An Inter- national Conference of all the independent States of North and South America was held in Wash- -ington from October of last year to the following May, and they adopted with unanimity, excepting Chili and one other, a series of resolutions designed to substitute arbitration for war. They undertook to show that most of the disagreements which arose between the Governments of the world could and should be, settled by disinterested arbiters." tut the Government of the United States, ever in the van of progress, have done more than this. They have come to a resolution whereby it is understood the President of the Republic is invited to communicate with the representatives of 'other countries in order to secure the adoption of Permanent treaties of arbitration "under which no War would be possible among the countries that eigned." And why should not such treaties be ad- opted? They can only be objected to by nations Who prefer might to right, or by monarchs and statesmen who have interests to serve which are not public interests. Unfortunately, the governing classes—" Kings and archdukes and other tremendous personages "—as Lord DERBY once called them—are interested, in the main, not in promoting peace, but in provoking war. War to them means promotion and pay, honour and glory. It is to the democracy, as Sir Wu- ?nth LAwqoN observed at Tuesday's meeting, that We must look for the enforcement of peace Principles. The democracy of the United States have gone through a terrible war, but they will not be hampered with a war debt. They have cleared that off; and, instead of having a million of Ineo in arms, they content themselves with a standing army of 25,000. If the working-classes Of this country properly realised the burden of our military expenditure, they would insist upon every candidate at the next election being pledged to support the adoption of permanent treaties of arbitration, as proposed by the United States. calculation has been made with a view of showing how each pound of the National Debt of. England has been spent during the present century ; and it is found that there has been spent out of each pound :—on war and preparations for War, 16s. 31d.; on all expenses of civil government, as. 81d. A startling result such as this should be constantly associated in men's minds with the question—Why go to war? FREDERICK the GREAT once said that if his soldiers were Philosophers they would not fight. But men need Dot be philosophers to object to fighting; it ought to be sufficient that they are one degree removed from the category of fools.

The TUE Warrington Extension, Water Improvement and Improvement Bill has this Bill. week passed through Committee of the House of Commons; but it is shorn of its fair proportions. To begin with, the clauses relat- ing to police and sanitary matters were dropped, as they would have had to be considered by a separate Committee, and it would have imperilled the bill to persevere with them so late in the ses- -Bion. The loss in this respect cannot, however, be regarded as permanent, as there is reason to believe that most of the powers sought to be obtained will be conferred by an Act which is to apply to the 'Whole country. The most serious miscarriage relates to the proposed extension of the borough ; the failure is not complete, but it is almost complete. Except on the northern side, the boundary is not to be extended at all. Instead cf having, on the south, the natural division that is provided by the making of the Ship Canal, the boundary is to remain untouched. Wilders- Pool will not be brought in, nor the works of Messrs. MONKS, HALL & Co.; and even Arpley Meadows, which are on the Lancashire side of the liver, are still t outside the borough of War.. o b e e rington. All this is very disappointing, but, as we Pointed out the other week, Parliamentary Com- rnittees have shown themselves difficult to deal With in proposals for extension; and besides, this the Corporation have had to contend with power- opponents. It has been a mistake to trust so lauch to the tender mercies of the Ship Canal Com- -13,er137. If the Corporation had stood out against 'co Company, as they should have dame, in the case 'ef the Latchford roads and bridges, they /liculd in all probability have brought them to terms. As it is, the weakness of the Corporation 'Lea resulted in the Ship Canal Company having Pretty much their own way, whilst they have given Zothing in return. We are told that the Ship Canal Ceropany backed out; at the last moment, of 171 engagement into which they had entered as to 'ne borough boundary. If this be so, the circum- atances should be made known, so that the public 'flay judge whether or not there has been a gross breach of faith. The chief feature of the bill as it linw stands is the sanction of the provisions for the Purchase of the Warrington Water Works; and 4.11 this connection it is very satisfactory to be able , to state that the Select Committee have granted a Zl,l,spension of the Sinking Fund for five years. means that the purchase, if the growth of the .o"vr:ter revenue keeps up to the average, will be little burden upon the rates. We understand, too, ‘uat power is being given under the bill to roake Lib a further levy* for Museum and rarY purposes, thus enabling the Committee ,w,,Take the Library a Free Lending Library. This 43,.."-,1 be accer ted as a great boon to the inhabitants; coupled, as it is with the purchase of the Water
