Sorry for Stanley. Dame Nature shows herself at times a peevish jade. Gastritis on one's wedding day is a poor sort of wedding present.

The Government have determined to commence the next session in November. They will take their text from Shakespere—" Now is the winter of our discontent." There is a sort of fitness of things in a bemuddled Ministry beginning business in November. There will be fog without and fog within.

It is to the credit of the Speaker, and of the Chairman of Committees, that they decline to be made use of as Tory tools. Mr. Courtney has, on three occasions, refused to closure discussion on Irish votes; while Mr. • Peel has refused to allow references to be made by ministers to the so-called intimidation of the Postmen's Union.

It is obvious from the collapse of the strike amongst the postmen that they were not prepared for the struggle upon which they entered. It is hard upon those who showed courage by "coming out" that they should be victimised by dismissal. The Union ought to assist them until they find other situations. The telegraphists are profiting by the strike; they are getting better pay which will cost the country £200,000 a year. Why not devote the increase, for a time, to the strikers who have been dismissed?

The ratepayers of Earlestown are good at elec- tioneering. They don't believe in anybody having "a walk over," and they are in the right in seek- ing a change when they want a change. They keep an eye on the doings of their representatives, and when those doings don't suit them they speak out plainly. This shows a healthy state of public feeling ; and it would be well if larger places showed as lively an interest in town's affairs.

There was a public meeting at Earlestown on Monday evening, and three candidates were adopted to be nominated in place of retiring members of the Board. The inhabitants want to know what is to be done about the Public Hall; and they want fuller representation than is accorded to them at present. Representation ought to be based upon population; and the case for Earlestown is good alike as to assessment and number of inhabit- ants.

A number of glass-workers at Cowley Hill Glassworks, belonging to Messrs. Pilkington Bros., are out on strike, and at a meeting on Saturday afternoon, all sections of glass-workers were strongly urged to combine in looking after their own interests. It was incidentally mentioned that the Chemical Workers' Union now numbers 4,500 members. That "union is strength" is a very old proverb, but it needs enforcing every genera- tion—especially amongst working-men.

In another column will be found a letter from Mr. Whitham. It will be seen that he regards his outlook as improving somewhat; and it is to be hoped that he will soon see the end of "dark days." His daughter Harriet, who wrote our readers a lively letter some time ago, has just succeeded in gaining" the first school medal, and one of tho medals given by the city to the three first scholars." Well done, Harriet! And we may add —well done Warrington!

Mr. John Roche, M.P., delivered a rousing ad- dress at the Nationalist meeting which was held at Warrington, on Sunday evening. Referring to Lord Clanricarde, he said as much as £lO,OOO had been spent on his estate during the last four years in evictions, and the protection of emergency men and bailiffs. Over 100 families had been evicted, and 100 more were to be evicted, from houses which they had themselves built. Coercion had failed ; they wanted Home Rule to give peace to Ireland.

Prince Bismarck has made it known that he does not approve of the course taken by the German Emperor on the labour question. He regards the international protection of labour as a chimera, but would guarantee workmen against the dangers of illness, accidents and old age. The ex-Chan- cellor may not speak of himself as a Socialist; but what's in a name? It is Socialistic all the same, and a very good thing, too, to "guarantee work- men against the dangers of illness, accidents, and old age."

"The Gentlewoman" is a new candidate for public favour which is likely to make headway. It is a sixpenny illustrated weekly "for gentle- women," which, speaking of the first number, is as full of good things as an egg is full of meat. The illustrations are numerous, and most of them are highly-finished and artistic. The bill of fare is a large one ; there is plenty for the money, and the quality is good. It has only to be kept up, to ensure "The Gentlewoman" being in great de- mand.

July has been so cold in this country as to sug- gest haymaking in overcoats. On the continent the weather has been worse, for, on Monday, the streets of Innsbruck were white with snow. The English Lake District has been wet. It is often wet. It was wet once when the late Edwin Waugh, was staying at Willie Ritson's in Wastdale. Grow- ing impatient, Waugh asked one morning: "Willie, does it always rain here ? " " Nae, nae," replied the quick-witted dalesman, 'it sometimes snaws." It need hardly be said that the Lancashire poet was delighted at being "bested."

Mr. W. Whitlow made nothing of it in his " exposure " of the way in which members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians were fed, at the Workhouse, at the expense of the ratepayers. He would not go forward with his motion on the sub- ject, and when asked to do that, or apologise, he said: "You have got the wrong pig by the ear to ask such a question." It was hinted that Mr. Whitlow was lacking in knowledge of lamb ; but his suggestive reference to the ways of the pig passed unchallenged.

It is much to be regretted that Mr. Eli Hey- worth does not feel himself at liberty to accept the pressing invitation of the Liberals to oppose Lord Hartington in the Rossendale Division. He is a solid, sensible and effective speaker ; In admirable business man; and would therefore make a capital representative for a manufacturing constituency. Mr. Heyworth is a leading manufacturer of Black- burn, and President of the Blackburn Liberal Association. He is one of the Directors of the National Telephone Company; and it is understood that his numerous business engagements prevent his devoting himself to politics.

A large number of Tory M.P.'s were at a garden party given by the Prince of Wales, on Monday afternoon; and, an early division being taken on the Scotch Police Committee, the Government had another narrow escape from defeat, the majo- rity being reduced to eight. The "Standard" calls it "a dirty trick" to try to steal a march on the Government in this way; but complaint of this kind is childish. It is the duty of the Oppo- sition to defeat the Government whenever it can. If Tories will let it be seen that they care less for the Government than for Ascot Races and garden parties' the Opposition ought not, on the other hand, to be blamed for attending to business.

Mr. Coningsby Disraeli has been delivering him- self at Bramhall, near Stockport, on the political situation. He said :—" He had been thinking a great deal lately about the business of the House of Commons, and it seemed to him it was like a beautiful machine which started well oiled, and which worked beautiful at first, the wheels spinning and the straps moving splendidly; but suddenly there came a jerk, a bang, and a crash. What has happened? Mr. Labouchere has put his finger in the pie. The machine goes on, and there comes another crash. Sir William Harcourt has fallen in, and so on with all the members of the Parnellite fry, until the beautiful working of a perfect machine became the jerky action of mere mechani-

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
ANOTHER CHANCE FOR AMBROSE.

Ambrose Bate was brought before the Runcorn magis- trates, on Monday, charged under a warrant with having been drunk and disorderly in Greenway-road, on the 21st June. P.C. Woodrow proved the case.—Ambrose denied that he was drunk, and said, being a boiler maker, he naturally talked very loud. He appealed to have another chance.—Mr. Brundrit said ho had been fined three times in five months, and he would be fined 20s. and costs 165., or a month's imprisonment.

div.head: FATAL FALL AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL FALL AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy-Coroner, on Monday held an inquest at the Simm's Cross Hotel, Widnes, on the body of Arthur Evans, aged nine years, son of Rich. Evans, labourer, 8, Gladstone-st. On Sunday, the 29th ult., the deceased was swinging on a rail, when a com- panion shouted that a policeman was coming, and he dropped, alighting on his head. He,afterwards com- plained of severe pains in his head, and Dr. MacLennan attended him ; but in spite of that gentleman's skill, he died on Friday evening. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

RUNCORN PARISH CHIIRCIT. The annual school sermons were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. Canon Greenall, rector of Grappenhall, who occupied the pulpit morning and evening. There were good congregations at each service. In the afternoon a flower service was held, the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of Halton, delivering an appropriate address to the young people. The scholars brought floral offerings, which were afterwards distributed to sick persons in the town, and a quantity of the flowers were sent to the hospital at Dut- ton 'Workhouse. The choir rendered specially selected music at the various services.

COMPLIMENT TO A WIDNES POLICE SERGEANT. At an inquest held at Widnes, on Thursday, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, said he had received a letter from Mr. Brighouse as follows :—" The Police Sergeant who has made the report (of this case) makes the best report of any police sergeant in my district." Mr. Husband said this coming from Mr. Brighouse, who had the best possible right to speak on this matter, was a very great compliment, and he thought Superintendent Noblett ought to know—in fact it ought to be made public. He asked who had made the report.—lnspector Keighley : P.S. McGregor. It is very complimentary, and I hope you will thank Mr. Brighouse on his behalf, Mr. Husband said he would do so, ATTACK ON A WIDNES WATCHNIAN _ ' - -

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before. Mr. 11. Gaskell, jun. and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell, a labourer named Christopher Daley, 9, Caroline-st., was brought up under a warrant, charged with having assaulted Jas. Williamson, a watchman at the Widnes Alkali Works. On Tuesday the watchman reported the prisDner for leaving the works for the purpose of obtaining drink. On Wednesday, while he was walking along Ann-st. East, the prisoner came up to him and struck him a vio- lent blow over the eye. The defendant alleged that he only struck in self-defence. Inspector Keighley said there were several convictions recorded against the prisoner, who was a very violent character. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sun- dayin St. Paul's Chapel. The preacher was the Rev. W. L. Watkinson, of Manchester, ex-president of the conference and he delivered two eloquent and convincing discourses to large congregations. In the morning the sacred edi- fice was well filled, and in the evening there was not room for all those who wished to take part in the service and a large number had to be turned away. A pleas- ing feature of the day's proceedings was the singing of the scholars and choir, the anthems and hymns being rendered with admirable effect. Mr. Grice presided at the organ, and the scholars had been trained by Mr. 3. Birkett. The services were continued on Monday evert- ing, when the Rev. G. Garrett, of Liverpool occupied the pulpit, and preached a characteristic sermon. The collec- tions realised an amount in excess of previous years. IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES.

A meeting of the members of the Widnes Branch of the Irish liational League was held in St. Paul's Chambers, on Sunday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. John Howlin. There was a good attendance. Mr. Thomas Delaney proposed, and Mr. McKindlan, of St. Helens, seconded the following resolution :—" That we, the people of Widnes in meeting asse:nbled, fail to find words sufficiently strong to condemn the cruel adminis- tration of coercion in Ireland by the present Tory Government, a law which was brought forward and forced through the House of Commons by the combined action of the Tory nul Unionist members, aimed not only against combiaati in but against those who seek by legal and legitimate means to redress the wrongs under which Ireland is at present suffering. We assure Mr. Balfour that in spite of his Coercion Act, and in spite of his mean and cowardly system of shadowing people, the Irish cause is marching on to victory." Mr. John Roche, MT., supported the resolution in an impassioned speech, and it was carried unanimously. SUMMER SALE now on at a. lc W. Dunes's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt._

div.head: HALTON LADIES' CLUB,
div.p: HALTON LADIES' CLUB,

The members of this club celebrated their 74th anniver- sary on Monday afternoon, when about 200 assembled in the Parish Church to listen to a sermon by the Rev. S. Wilkinson. vicar a St. Paul's, Warrington. The rev. gentleman delivered an appropriate discourse from the text "Is it well with thee, is it well with thy husband, is it well with the child." After service the members, headed by the Runcorn Volunteer Brass Band, walked in procession through the village to the Castle Green. They were accompanied by Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P., Mr. J. 11. Gannon, Mr. T. Wright, Dr. Carrathers, and the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar; Lady Brooke, Mrs. C. Reynolds, Mrs. Cox, Mrs. Dixon, Mrs. Wray, the Misses Dixon, and the Misses Reynolds. A capital tea was provided in a mar- quee erected by Mr. Cooper, of Runcorn, Lady Brooke occupying a seat at the head of the table. Subsequently Mr. T. Wright, the secretary, presented a balance sheet which showed that the member's subscriptions for the year amounted to £145 2s. 6d., and the income from other sources was £35 6s. 10d.. ; total, £lBO Bs. 4d. There had been paid a balance due to the trnsurer, £l2 13s. 6d.: sick allowance fund to members, £69 6s. ; funeral money, £10; medical attendance, £37 16s. ; leaving a balance in the treasurer's hands of £l5 7s. T he total funds of the society amounted to Z 1,103118. 9d., which was invested in various securities. The accounts were passed, and appropriate addresses were delivered by Lady Brooke, Mr. C. Reynolds, &c. In the evening the band played for dancing, and there was a largeatten- dance of persons from Runcorn and district.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1890

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. The monthly sitting of this Court was held on Tuesday by his Honour Judge Wynne Flounces. There were set down for hearing one adjourned plaint, two default sum- monses, 81 original plaints, and eight judgment eummonses. The only case of interest was one in which T. Ainsworth, of Marsh Green, Frodsham, farmer, sued Thos. Davies, timber merchant and farmer, of Frodsham, for £3 Bs. 7d., the balance of an account for manure and a man's wages. The defendant denied the debt and had filed a counter claim for £l9 3s. 9d. balance of an account for goods supplied.—Mr. Burton appeared for Ainsworth, and Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys for the defendant. The case turned upon the question of the price agreed upon for the manure and the rate of the man's wages. The plaintiff stated the price of the man- ure was 7s. 6d. per ton, and the man's wages 2s. 9{l. per day, and against his uncorroborated testimony the defendant called his sons to show that the price of the manure was 7s. per ton, and the man's wages 2s. per day. His Honour gave judgment for Davies on both claim and counter claim. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DurroN's Sankoy-st., Warrington.—Advt. COAL AND SALT FOUND NEAR ALTCAR. During the past few weeks a number of experts have been boring for salt on Barton Moss, seven miles from Southport, and adjoining the Waterloo coursing ground. It is stated that not only has salt been discovered, but also coal. Further searcli will be made. •.. •

--- GARDEN TOOLS.—J. S. Garland, :Ironmonger, Warrington & Earlestown. AN EPIDEMIC OF SUICIDES IN CHESHIRE. At Winsforci and Middlewich this week -.here have been two suicides and an attempt-'d suicide. The latest tragedy took place at the White Lion Middlewich, where Mr. Robert Rowlands, the landlord, who has been receiving medical attendance for some time, took a razor and neatly severed his head from his body. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt. A BURGLAR OVERCOME BY ClismPArotf. An unusual case of burglary was before the St. Helens magistrates on Monday, when John Roddy. a labourer, living at Gerard's Bridge, was charged with breaking into the Grey Horse public-house, 143, College-st., and stealing four bottles of cham- paign, three pints of ale, half-a-pint of whiskey and a quart jug, together of the value of £1 4s. 3d., the property of Ellen Hall. It appeared that early on Sunday morning the prisoner was lying near some steps in the backyard which lead down to the cellar. He was drunk and speechless, and he had three full bottles of champaign in his pockets. The door of the cellar was partly open, the lock having been forced. There were four bottles of champaign miss- ing.—lnformation was given to the police, and Con- stable Williams apprehended the prisoner who was in a helpless state of drunkenness. Prisoner was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions. TRAVELLING TRUNllS.—Garland, Ironmonger, Si, Bridge- at., Warrington.

FARM FIRE AT NEWTON. A serious fire broke out on the farm of Mr. J. Cowley, Crow-lane, Newton, on Tuesday morning. A new stack of hay had been erected last week, and early on the day named flames and smoke were seen issuing from one of the corners. Before the out- break could be suppressed, another stack some yards away got ignited and burned fiercely for a considerable period. Information was conveyed to the bottle works of Messrs. Borron and Company, and an effort was made to put out the flames by , means of a hose pipe and buckets of water. The hay however, was almost entirely destroyed, and the damage was estimated at about £7O. The orig- ination of the fire was not known,but it is supposed that the hay was accidentally ignited by some children playing in the neighbourhood. summF.a SALit now on rt J, S 4 W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington,—Advt. THEFT AT VULCAN FOUNDRY. Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and T. D. Grimk4 at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday. John James Tatlock, a young man, was charged with stealing a silver watch, valued at 12s. 6d., the property of Robert Henry Birkby. at Vulcan iron foundry, on the previous Thursday. Prosecutor stated that he resided at Derby-row, Vulcan. Prisoner was a fellow workman in the forge. He placed his vest,in one of the pockets of which was the watch pro- duced, on a nail in the works, He afterwards missed the watch and gave information to the police. Police Constable Hughes said he appre- hended the prisoner and, on searching him, he found the watch produced concealed in his stocking. He charged the prisoner with the offence and the reply was "The top and bottom of it is I was going to Liverpool to-day to pawn the watch for to help me to pay my lodging money."—The prisoner who had previously been an inmate of the Liverpool Farm Reformatory School was committed for trial at the Sessions. BKIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Union, American. and other lines.— John Walker, agent, " Examinee,' Office, Bewsey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. _ _

ASTOUNDING IGNORANCE AT NEWTON. At the Newton Patty Sessions, on Saturday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie and other magistrates Thomas Hughes, of Earlestown, was summoned for keeping a dog without a license on the 24th June. Defendant pleaded not guilty and alleged that the dog was not six months old. Defendant called an Ashton-in-Mak erfield collier, from whom he received the animal, and witness said it was born in Febru- ary last. Superintendent Weir asked how he knew that,—Witneskl ;, I do know.—Mr. Weir : What month are we in now ?—Witness: I don't know. I can neither read nor write.—The Chairman : Then how do you know it is six months old ?—Witness : Take it to any dogman and he will tell you.—The Clerk: Can you tell us what the last month was? —Witness: No; I cannot read nor write.—The Clerk : Nor the month before that ?—Witness: No. —The Clerk: Nor the month before that P—Witness: No I cannot. It's no use asking me what month they are when I cannot read or write.—The Chair- , man : Then how did you mention the 26th Febru- ary P—Witness : Because my landlord put it down. The Bench ultimately imposed a fine of 2s. Gd. and costs. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. Burrow's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPLAR& A district convention of Good Templars was held at Hindley, on Saturday afternoon, under the aus- pices of the Hope of Ilindley lodge. In the unavoid- able absence of the C.C.T. (Bro. Colour-Sergeant Devlin, of Warrington) the chair was occupied by Bro. J. Brockbank (St. Helens). The C. Sec. re- ported on the position of the various lodges in the convention area, after which the reports from the lodges were received. During the business Brother Morris Jones, D.C.T., Bro. R. D. Petterson, D.S., and Bro. F. L. Sedgwick, L.D., arrived from Liverpool, and were received with Templar honours. The D.O.T. was invited to preside over the subsequent business, and lie accepted the invitation. A general discussion took place on Templar mission work, and addresses were given by the gentlemen named. Brother Sedgwick offered to present the convention with 100 Templar periodicals, and they were ac- cepted with thanks. For the next place of meet- ing St..l-lelens, Earlestown, and Ashton-in-Maker- field were nominated. It was ultimately decided to meet at St. Helens, under the auspices of the Great Heart lodge. After the business had concluded, a tea party Was held and a large number of members sat downs A public meeting and entertainment followed. IRON BRDSTELDS & BRDDING.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. THE NEW ARCHDEACON OF MANCHESTER

In succession to the late Dean Oakley, the Queen has approved the appointment of the Rev. Canon Maclure, vicar of Rochdale and Archdeacon of Man- chester. A Miitichesttr correspondent says the new dean is the eldest brother of Mr. J. W. Maclure, M.P. Me was edutated at the Manchester Grammar School, where he was the exhibitioner of his year. He graduated B.A. and 31:A. at Brasenose College, Oxford, of which he was a scholar and Hulme ex- hibitioner. After octupying curacies at St. Jbhn's, Ladywood, Birmingham, and St. Pancras, Middlesex, he became vicar of Burnley in 1863, and held that position for fourteen years. During one half the time he was chairman of the Burnley School Board: On the death of Dr. Molesworth, in 1877, Mr.Macl ure was appointed Vicar of Rochdale by the late Bishop of Manchester. Iti'll3tB he became Honorary Canon of Manchester, and in 1879, Rural Dean. Canon] Maclure has always undertaken a very considerable ' ' share of diocesan work, being honorary secretary of the Diocesan Conference and the Diocesan Board of Education. Ile is also honorary secretary to the Training College at Warrington. In 1888, he was one of the hon. secretaries of the Church Congress in Manchester. SUMMER SALE now on at Jo & IV. Din-rotes Sankey-st.,• Warrington.—Adrt. -

Damage estimated at 1,000,000d015. has been caused at Minneapolis by afire in the peat repository fer furni- ture and valuables. Alden Carter Weston, who recently figured in the action concerning a' cliegne for £3OO purporting to be drawn by Mr. Wertheimer in favour of Lady Dunlo, was, on Wednesday, committed for trial by the Marylebone magistrate on a, charge 'of forging and utttering the document.-
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUT9ORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Hey. J. W. IN. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Heywood, Brandreth. W. Whitlow, John Whitlow, James Vvhitlow, H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).

_ THE POLLUTION OF REKEWICII BROOK. The Deputy-Clerk said a letter had been forwarded to the Local Government Board with regard to the pollution Kekewick Brook and the Board had replied that the matter should have their attention. The authority could do nothing until they heard further from the Board.— Inspector Farrington reported that he had taken two more samples of the water in Kekewick Brook, as directed, but he had not ye.; received the analysts report.

THE WARRINGTON EXTENSION BILL. The Deputy-Clerk reported that the Committee ap- pointed to deal with the proposed extension of the borough of Warrington had resolved that a petition be Presented to the House of Lords against the Bill. A draft had been submitted to the Parliamentary agents, who had written as follows to Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, the solicitors to the Authority. Dear sir,--Warrington Extension, kc.—We have re- ceived your letter and the draft petition, and have wired you that it is impossible at present to settle the petitions. The promoters are making very extensive alterativis in their Bill, and are proposing a new description cf the extension, the effect of which (although apparently not very much as regards you' districts) we cannot judge of. The main object of the alteration seems to be to exclude the Ship Canal. The numbers of the sections, and the title of the Bill will also be altered so that the settlement of the petitions had better wait until the Bill is through the Commons Committee. We only got notice this morning of the alterations. In the meantime we should advise that you should bring the matter before your clients and take an authority from them to seal the petitions, leaving the actual settlement of the term of the petition until we get a reprint of the Bill after the Commons Committee. We will send you on Monday a a copy of the new descriptions of the boundary if we can get one.—Yours truly, Graham, Currey, and Spens." —Mr. Aaron proposed that the Chairman be authorised to attach the seal of the Authority to the petition when it was ready.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the motion, which was carried.—The Deputy Clerk said the parliamentary agents had stated that the petition of the Rural Sanitary Authority and of the Board of Guardians could be ?re- sented in one. This course would says expense.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended the payments of accounts amounting to £l3 13s. ed., and reported that the treasurer's balance was £9O 4s. 3d.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting on Tuesday, when there were present the. Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, E. Aaron, J. Brandreth, W. Whitlow, J. Mclntyre, John Whitlow, James Whitlow, and 11. G Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: WARRINGTON EXTENSION BILL.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON EXTENSION BILL.

Mr. A. Linaker, solicitor to the Union, attended and made a statement with regard to the Warrington Exten- sion Bill, and on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Maclntyre, the Chairman was empowered to attach the seal of the Board to the petition against the Bill when it was ready.

div.head: MAINTENANCE OP DESTITUTE PARENTS.
div.p: THE MAINTENANCE OP DESTITUTE PARENTS.

On the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, seconded by Mr. Mclntyre, it was resolved,to forward to the House of Commons, through Mr. Tollemache, M.P. for Frodsham Division, a petition in favour of the Maintenance of Destitute Parents Bill.
THE INCREASES OP SALARY.
A letter was read from the Local Government Board, approving of the increase of the Master's salary from £BO to £9O per year, and of the Matron's from LIO to £5O a year.
THE ALLEGED CHEAP DINNERS.

Mr. Whitlow had given notice that he would move that the price of the dinners supplied to the Guardians should be increased from is. to 2s. He said he had con- sidered the matter, and he would withdraw the motion on the condition that the Guardians had a shillings worth for a shilling, and not half-a-crown's worth for a shilling, which he was satisfied was the case. It was a great convenience to members coming from a distance to have lunch, but he objected to the ratepayers who supported that house paying for an elaborate spread for a shilling. When the lunch was first established, there was just ft :plain joint, with vegetables and a glass of beer; now it had got to what he might call a first-class ordinary. There was no lamb nor fowls mentioned in the contract :for the supply of the House, and as the Master and Matron were pleading poverty a few weeks since when I they were applying for an Advance of salary, he was surprised how they got in the House.—Mr. Heywood : There is lamb in the contract.—Mr. Whitlow : There is beef, mutton,and pork.—Mr. Brandreth:: Is Mr. Whitlow going to withdraw his motion or is he not.—Mr. Whit- low: A cheap feed just suits some fellows. (Laughter.) —The Chairman : You must either move the resolution or withdraw it unconditionally.—Mr. Whitlow : Then I will withdraw it, and give notice of motion that we have only a plain lunch.—The Chairman : Had not you better thrash it out now.—Mr. Whitlow: No, I will not. It shall be understood what the motion is.—Mr. Taylor said to withdraw the motion in this fashion, after the insinuations he had thrown out, was like stabbing a man in the dark. He had used the extraordinary statement that the members had been in the habit of having a lunch for which they did not adequately pay, and he moved that the Master be called in and asked the cost of the dinners.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion, for the reason that it had gone through the papers that the Guardians were eating £l9 of the ratepayers' good money and this should be cleared up.—Mr. Whitlow said he was a carterer himself and he knew the value of the dinners in question, and he I was prepared to substantiate every word he had said.— Mr. Heywood said a licensed victualler had not the same chance.—Mr. Whitlow : It is all very well to feed at the parishioners' expense, which I am satisfied you are doing. This lunch is like all other good things ; it wasestablished for a very good purpose, but now it is abused.—Mr. Mclntyre said Mr. Dansey, the Local Government .Board Inspector, allowed the Guardians to have dinner in. the house because there was no place of refreshment within reach.—Mr. Aaron said he had been a member of the Board for 26 years, and he had quite as good a dinner 26 years ago as he had at an time.—The Chairman said he had been credited with Mr. Whitlow's motion in a leader in a Liverpool newspaper, and he should like to state that he had never dined in the House, and he did not know whether the Guardians got value for their money or not.—Mr. Taylor's motion was carried, and the Master (Mr. Cunnah) was called in.—The Master said the late inciter calculated that the dinner for the Guardians cost 7d. each, and the members paid that amount, the various items being set forth. The auditor said lie thought it would be fairer if the Guardians paid a reasonable amount per head, and then it would not be necessary to go into the items. He considered that a shilling would be a, fair price to pay fora dinner. In 1883 the Guar- dians commenced to pay is. each. They had just a plain dinner ; nothing was specified by die auditor.— Mr. Brandreth : It was all right so long as there was no loss to the ratepayers 9—The Master : Yes.—Mr. Brandreth : There is no toss to the ratepayers.—The Master : No.—He added that the dinner referred 'to specially by Mr. Whitlow cost Bs. 7d., and he re- ceived 10s. being a profit of is. sd. to the ratepayers. The cost of the dinner last Board day was 7s. lid., being a profit, and he received 33. I(l.—Mr. Whitlow asked if lamb and fowls were contracted for.—The Master replied that at the beginning of the quarter an order was issued for fowls, and only two had been supplied, and these were put on the Guardians' table. One was used by them, and the officers had the other. As to butchers meat, the contract was for so much of the best, and no mention was made of special joints. He received what the butcher sent,lls. and he had no complaint to make.—The Chairman : If he sends a quarter of lamb, you don't complain. (Laughter.)—The Master: No. (Laughter.) He charges the same price for lamb as mutton.—Mr. Whitlow: I spend a hundred pounds a year in butcher's meat, and he is more lenient with you than me.—The Master : I don't order anything special for the Guardians and officers. The only order he gave was the quantity, and when it is to come, and he sends it. If he sends anything special, / don't refuse it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Brandreth said the butcher sometimes killed too much of beef, mutton, or iamb, and then he sent on to the House whatever he had too much of.—Mr. Taylor said Mr. Whitlow had made a serious charge against the Guardians who spent a whole day at the House once a fortnight, and as little as he could do, after the explanations given, was to apologise to the members for the accusation he had made.—Mr. Whitlow: You have got the wrong pig by the ear to ask ,me such a question.—Mr. Taylor said Mr. Whitlow's accusation was most contemptible. He would take care that lie (Mr. Taylor) did not dine at the ratepayers' expense. He was quite as sensitive as Mr. Whitlow, and if hehad thought that he had eaten one pennyworth more than he had paid for he would not have done like Mr. ' Whitlow—enjoyed his dinner and then found fault at the Board. He would have paid the 29., and this is not what Mr. Whitiovestender conscience prompted him to do.—'Mr. Brandreth We have had the Master's explana- tion, and it is clear the question has arisen through Mr. WhitlOw's ignorance. He did not know the price of the ineat'supplied.—Mr. Whitlow : I won't sit here to be insulted.—The Chairman: Perhaps you will act upon Mr. Taylor's suggestion. (Laughter.)—Mr. Whitlow : It suits some gentlemen to come here and have a cheap feed ; :the'cheaper the better. They will lose a day if they can have a cheap feed.—The Chairman : Order, order.--Mr. Taylor: If you will allow Inc a word— The Chairman : I cannot unless there is a motion.—Dr. Gastildi : Move a vote 'of censure upon Mr. Whitlow. (Laughter).—The Chairman r We shall be here all day. —Mr.'Aaron : And want tea: (Laughter).—The subject then dropped.
FINANCE.
Oh the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £3Ol 193. 5d were passed for paphent.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Union Workhouse, Winston, on Thurs- day afternoon. There were present Major J. W. Wareing (chairman), Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. C. B. Johnson, E. Syder, J. Birchall, J. Whalley, W. Borrows, W. Lowe, J. Poover, J. Ranson, J. Kenwright, W. Daine, and S. 11. Hartley (clerk). A GUARDIAN'S BEREAVESIENT.—The Chairman alluded to the loss sustained by Mr. Chadwick, one of the Guar- dians for Bold, by the death of his wife, and said he was sure they would all sympathise with him. He moved that a vote of condolence be forwarded to Mr. Chadwick. —The Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester seconded the motion which was adopted. RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 482 inmates of the house this week, 478 last week, and 483 in the corresponding period last year. Vagrants relieved during the week 52, corresponding week last year 54. COAL MINES' RATINO.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board requesting to be furnished with particulars relating to the rating of coal, ironstone and other mines (if any) in the Union.—The Clerk stated that the information had been supplied. THE UNION OFFICERS.—The Local Government Board wrote asking to be furnished with a list of the guardians and of all the paid officers of the Union.—The Clerk mid lie had given the information. Tirm ECCLESTON AND WINDLE TOWNSHIPS.—The Local Government Board wrote on the 14th July enclosing copies of an order which they had issued directing the Guardians to invest the sum of £330 Bs. 63., being the amount received in respect of the redemption of the £3 per cent. Consolidated Bank Annuities formerly held by the Guardians on behalf of the townships of Eccles- ton and Windle. When the investment had been made the stock receipt relating thereto should be forwarded to the Local Government Board for registration, together with a statement showing how the stock purchased had been apportioned between the townships interested there- in. The Clerk said the Local Government Board would not permit the Guardians to give the money to those who were entitled to it. They must continue to act as trustees, and under those circumstances he recommend- ed the signing of cheques for the amounts due to each township. The Chairman moved and Mr. Daine seconded a resolution to the effect, which was adopted. 1 THE MAINTENANCE OF DESTITUTE PARENTS.—The Clerk read the following letters :—" House of Commons, July 16th, 1390. Dear Sir,—Yours to hand re Maintenance of Destitute Parents' Bill, which has my best attention. —Yours faithfully, H. SETON-KARR." "House of Com- mons, July 16th, 1890. Dear Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter of yesterday's date, and shall be glad to sup- port the principle of the Maintenance of Destitute Parents' Bill when it comes before the House of Com- mons for the second reading. It is down for Friday, the 25th.—Yours truly, T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS." A letter was also received from Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., acknowledging receipt of the communication. Poon Law CONFERENCE.—The Clerk reported that he and the Chairman and Mr. Middlehurst had attended the preliminary Poor Law Conference at Manchester for making arrangements for the :annual conference. This was all the business.

div.head: SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES:
div.p: SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES:

An accident of a shocking description occurred at the chemical works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., on Tuesday morning, when a labourer named Thos. Kennelly, 40 years of age, who resided at 3, Victoria- road, met with his death. The deceased and three other men were employed in the construction of a plant for the recovery of sulphur. In an excavation a number of brick pillars had been built, and the tops of these were about nine inches or a foot below the surface of the ground. The men were engaged in placing blocks of stone on the tops of these pillars and a number had been so fixed. While in the act of moving one, weighing about newts., the deceased slipped from the pillar and fell into the excavation. His companions were then unable to retain control of the stone, which crashed ' through a plank and fell upon the deceased. The stone was removed as quickly as possible, and Dr. Hutchinson summoned, but Kennelly was frightfully injured about ; the head and body, and death occurred in a few minutes. The inquest on the body, was held on Thursday, at Anderson's Hotel, by Mr. Husband, the deputy coroner, Mr. NV. Towers, manager of the works, appeared on be- half of the firm, and Mr. Mearns, solicitor, of St. Helens. watched the proceedings on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, and of the Chemical Labourers' Union. Mr. P. T. King, the president of the union, was also present. —Mary Kennelly, of Northwich, sister of the deceased, gave evidence of identification.—John O'Brien, a yard foreman, made a statement as to the work of the de- ceased.—Thomas Westhead, 48, Wareing-street, said he was a labourer at the works, and was engaged in the construction of the sulphur plant. He, the deceased, and two other men were moving a stone along a plank on to a pillar by means of rollers. The deceased was standing on a pillar in front of the stone and witness stood on another pillar, nearer the bank. The other two men were at the back side of the stone. Whether the de3eased forgot he was on the pillar and stepped too far back, or whether his feet slipped from under him, he could not tell, but the deceased fell on his back into the excavation, which was about five feet deep. The stone then came with a rush, as witness could not hold it, from the rollers and fell upon the deceased, who died in a few minutes.—By Mr. Mearns : They had usually to I get on the top of the pillar to put the stone in the posi- tion. There was no protecticn round the pillar to pre- vent anyone from falling off.—By Mr. Brookes: They I had no rope round the stone. They had put three on that morning. It would have been right enough if de- ceased had not fallen off the pillar.—By Mr. Chapman : We did not require a rope. The deceased did not come to work until breakfast time, and he was sober.—Thomas Oxley gave corroborative evidence.—The Coroner, having summed up, the jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental Death."
THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS AT RUNCORN. ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES.

In the House of Commons, on Thursday, Mr. Brunner asked the President of the Local Govern- ment Board whether his attention had been called to irregularities in connection with the last election of guardians of the poor for the township of Run- corn ; whether he was aware that a considerable number of qualified electors received no voting rapers ; that many mistakes in the distribution and collection of voting papers occurred owing to the fact that the numbers Of the houses in any street were not entered on the papers, and that the per- sons employed by the returning officer to assist in the counting of the Voting papers were two of his own sons and the workhouse master, who had been for many years his own clerk ; whether the irregularities affected the result of the election ; and whether the Local Govern- ment Board made inquiry into the conduct of the elec- tion, so as to fix the responsibility for and prevent the recurrence of such irregularities. Mr. Ritchie in reply, said : I have received complaints as to irregularities in connection with the last election of guardians for the township of Runcorn. At the last elec- tion five guardians were to be elected, and there were nine candidates. lam not able to give the precise num- ber of persons who were entitled to vote in the election, but it must have been very large, as one candidate re- ceived as many as 946 votes. In communications which I have received from one of the candidates it is alleged that in thirty-seven cases there was a failure either to distribute or to collect voting papers. I have made in- quiry as to each of these uses, and find that in some of them a satisfactory explanation has been given. For , instance, there are cases where persons had left the house in respect to which they were assessed prior to the election. In others, the collectors were unable to obtain an answer when they called with the voting papers. There are other cases in which mistakes have occurred through inadvertence in preparing the voting papers or otherwise. It is, however, to be observed that in the public notice which is given of the election the attention of the electors is distinctly called to the fact that if any voter fails to receive a voting paper on the day of the distribution, or if any voting paper is not collected through the default of the return- ing officer or any person employed to collect the voting papers, the voter is entitled to attend at the place fixed by the returning officer, and there personally hand in a voting paper filled up by himself. I learn from the returning officer that in one case a messenger who asked for certain electors was informed that if the electors wished to vote' it would be necessary that they should attend before the returning office for the purpose. In none of the cases, however, did the elector avail himself of this right. It is impos- sible for me to say whether the result of the election would have been effected if the persons in the case re- ferred to had availed themselves of the right to which I have alluded. I have no definite information as to whether or not the sons of the returning officer and the Workhouse master assisted the returning officer in count- ing the votes, but the officer was entitled to have assist- ance in this duty, and it does not appear to me that there was any objection to the employment of these persons. It is a matter for regret that irregularities should have occurred in any of these cases ; but I a.,in not satisfied that there was any wilful neglect; and after full consider- ation, the Local Government Board arrived at the con- , clusian that the circumstances were not such as to require that the heavy expenses of a new election should be incurred. . _

The preamble of the North-West Central Railway Bill, which proposes to construct a railway from Keighley to Preston, was passed by a Select Committee of the House of Commons on Wednesday. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned on Wednesday by a Bootle jury with reference to the shoot- ing of GeorgeCornett, on board the steamer Sigyn, on the 6th inst., by his friend Mr. J. E. Johannessen. The Master of the Rolls and Mr. Justice Lindley, on Wednesday, refused anApplication on behalf of the trus- tee in bankruptcy of the Jubilee Plunger's estate, to pre- vent an officer of the I.l„th Hussars from leaving the 'country. It appeared that judgment had been obtained against the officer for £13,000 ecieLt A similar application was refused in another court several. days ago.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. That the members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians will continue to be supplied with dinners at the usual rate of Is. That " us farmers" *ere at home minding their own business, and Mr. Whitlow, finding his usual supporters absent.thought discretion the better part of valour, and withdrew his motion, but he did not moderate the strength of Ins language. That it was not deemed wise that the price paid for butchers meat should be made public, but the rate is wonderfully cheap, and the master calculated that on the dinner which Mr. Whitlow had described as sumptuous, there was a profit of Is. sd. That it is evident Mr. Whitlow had been calcula- ting the price of the dinners on the system he carries out in his own business, but he indignantly protested that he would not be insulted, when Mr. Brandreth said the whole question had arisen through his ignorance, and Mr. Taylor's demand for an apology, met with no better reception. That if Mr. Taylor had the pig by the ear he could not make it squeak ; and he contented himself with describing Mr. Whitlow's conduct in accusing the Guardians of dining at the ratepayers expense as contemptible. That no reasonable ratepayer will begrudge the Guardians their shilling dinner, when they are away from home spending a whole day in the transaction of public affairs. That considerable satisfaction is expressed that the Warrington Corporation have failed in securing those parts of Cheshire which they desired to in- clude in the borough, as theloss of part of Appleton and Lower Walton would have been a serious one to the Runcorn Union. That Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., and Mr. H. Linaker, the clerk to the Union, have been in London ready to give evidence against the proposal, but the House of Commons Committee decided the question without calling witnesses for the oppon- ents of the Bill. That had Wilderspool Brewery been included in Borough it would have meant many extra hundreds of pounds a year in rates, and, although the wealthy baronet did not oppose the Bill, be will probably be glad, in a commercial sense, that the project has failed. That the Vicar of Runcorn has been appointed an honorary canon of Chester Cathedral, and his work in the diocese for about a quarter of a century fully entitles him to that honour. That the people of Runcorn ought to be grateful to him for one thing, it for nothing else, and that is the introduction of the district nurse, who has done and is doing so much good amongst the poorer folks, and is winning their hearts by her unvarying kind- ness and tact. That the Vicar has protested on more than one occasion that the movement is unsectarian, and certainly the nurse visits the sick and needy irrespec- tive of class or creed, but the subscribers to the fund number amongst their ranks very few Noncon- formists. That it is a pity the Nonconformists do not sub- scribe to the fund, and thus place themselves in a position to take an active art in its manage- ment.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

- ---- FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—The monthly meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees was held in the lawn Hall, Fred- sham, last evening week. There were present—Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P. (chairman), Dr. Robinson, Messrs. John Ashton, H. E. Heywood, Thomas Lewis. James Percival, W. C. Collinson, H. G. Linaker, and James Farrington.—The Clerk reported that the Frodsham Gas and Water Company, Limited, had been supplied with a copy of the letter from the Vicar of Frodsham having reference to the water supply of Frodsham.—After some discussion it was proposed by Mr. J. Ashton, seconded by Mr. H. E. Heywood, and resolved, that the Frodsham Gas and Water Company, Limited, be requested to provide a supply of water to the inhabitants of Frodsham. —The Inspector reported that the contractors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company had abated the pollu- tion of the watercourse on Frodsham Marsh, as requested by the Committee.—Plans were produced from Mr. John Jones, of Frodsham, of two cottages which he proposed to have erected at Five Crosses, when it was resolved that the same be passed and recommended to the Authority for approval, on his producing the necessary specification as to the materials to be used in the erection of such cottages.

PENKETE TOVIVI MIN'S CrtursrrAil Assonivrolkt. Last evening week the annual meeting of this society was held at Bethany House, the residence of Mrs. Coop. Mr. C. E. Parker presided. After prayer, Mrs. Coop (the president of the association), gave a short address, and said she was glad to see so many of the old faces before her, and that the young men who had joined the association at the start had still continued to come to the weekly meetings, and had not allowed other attractions to draw them away. Mr. J. Simpson, the secretary, in his report stated that they had 22 members, and an average weekly attendance of 12. From time to. time the members had given essays on various sub- jects, and they had also had a lecture on chemistry. Mr. J. T. Budden, the treasurer, presented his report, which showed there was a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £3 Gs. 10d. The election of officers for the ensuing year was next proceeded with. Mrs. Coop was unanim- ously re-fleeted president; vice-presidents, Messrs. C. •E. Parker, j. Watson, W. J. Wigfield, T A. Robinson, T. Gandy, , E. Winder, con- ditional on the secretary obtaining 1";.!ii consent: Mr.. J. Simpson was re-eltcted secretary. ass:....fn! secretary, Mr. J. Randall. Mr. J. T. Budden having resigned his post as treasurer, Mr. A. Tucker was unanimously elected to the position. The follow- ing were elected members of the committee : Messrs. W. J. Holden. Fred II ughes, Philip Hughes, T. Oliver, and W. T. Wilkinson. The business part of the meeting having closed, refreshments, supplied by Mrs. Coop, were served, and a very pleasant evening was spent. Mr. A. Robinson gave a recita- tion entitled" Shamus O'Brien," and Mr. A. Dunabin gave two readings in a capital manner.

div.head: LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS.

At the Liverpool County Sessions on Wednesday the jury failed to agree upon a verdict in the case of John Gilgannon, Thomas Molloy, and Thomas Donnelly, charged with having committed a mur- derous assault on William Hart, at Prescot, on the 2nd ult. Prisoners were remitted to the Assizes, bail being refused. At the sotto court the appeal of Frederick Greene, late licensee of the Bowling Green Inn, Leigh, against a sentence of a month's hard labour for assaulting his daughter Annie Rat- cliffe, was allowed, the evidence indicating that the girl had run away because she was accused of steal- ing money and clothing.—John Roddy, of no settled abode, pleaded guilty to a charge of having broken into the beer-house of Mrs. Ellen Hall, at St. Helens, on the 13th inst., and stolen therefrom four bottles of champagne, three bottle of ale, and other goods. lie was sentenced to four months with hard labour.—John Tatlock, for stealing a watch, the property of a fellow-workman at Newton-le- Willows, six months.—Ellen Davies, 19, laundress, for having done malicious damage to three plate- glass windows belonging to James Peace Thorpe, St. Helens, and worth .£5 Gs., six months.— John Latham, 27, hawker, for stealing a horse, cart, and harness at Windle, on the 11th June, the property of Thomas Cartwright, four months.—Wm. Whittle, 30, collier, for having at Ashton-in-Maker- field, assaulted Elizabeth Heaton, six months.—Jas. ; Ward, labourer, 16, was charged with having at ' Ashton-in-Makerfield. on the Bth July, assaulted Caroline Scott, 16 years of age, was bound over to appear for judgment when called upon.—Ellen Cos- tello (42), was acquitted of the charge of stealing a sheet at Parr, on the 16th ult.—Samul Grennan, 33, labourer, for assaulting Thomas Quinn at Widnes, on the 21st June, was sent to jail for one month.— James Ince, and John Farley, 18, labourers, charged with breaking into the warehouse of Mark Smith, at Widnes, on the Bth inst., and stealing 921bs. of lead and 701bs. of indiarubber were acquitted.

TRH BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, July 12th, 1890. —The mean temperature was 53-7 Fahrenheit, and therefore degree colder than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature 65 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the Bth inst, and the minimum temperature, 42 Fahrenheit, on the 12th inst. The rainfall measured '43ln. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 28th of the current year, 36 births and 18 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 18.72 per thousand, against 1404, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 24.8 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from scarlet fever, 1 from enteric fever, 1 from diptheria, 1 from rickets, 4 from old age, 5 from brain disease, 2 from lung disease. One case of scarlatina, and one of diphtheria were re- ported under the requirements of the Act of Parlia- ment. JouN U. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: NATURE'S SWEET RESTORER.
div.p: NATURE'S SWEET RESTORER.

"The Lady" says :—The Chinese have the credit of inventing one of the most dikbolical punishments that the human mind could imagink or human beings parti- cipate in carrying out. It is the deprivation of sleep, until the unhappy victim finds relief in the everlasting rest of the tomb. Guards relieve each other every two hours, night and day, whose sale duty consists in pre- venting the prisoner going to sleep, and this is kept up day after day, until at length he sinks beneath the fear- ful torture. Sleep may be defined as a state of physiological rest or natural unconsciousness, in which the voluntary powers are in a condition of insenibility, whilst the involuntary functions of nutrition, secretion, Ste., are going on, in- creased, diminished, or unaltered, according to circum- stances. The necessity for sleep arises from the fact that the exercise of the animal functions is in itself destruc- tive of the tissues of the organs which minister to them, so that if the waste produced by their action were not duly repaired, they would speedily become unfit for further use. The refreshing power of sleep depends on the nutritive regeneration of the tissues which take place during true healthy sleep. It will now be easy to understand why persons suffering from sleeplessness should, in a comparatively short time, become such com- plete wrecks, quite unfit for the ordinary duties of life. The normal function of the brain depends on the proper nutrition of the cerebrum, and if this nutrition is im- paired for any length of time by deficiency in the forma- tive power of the tissues caused by sleeplessness, insanity will in all probability supervene. The object of sleep may therefore be said to be the removal of the strain to winch consciousness is subjected durir°e, waking hours, and, generally speaking, the renewal of our vital or nerve-force. We have most of us suffered, at one time or another, from that most distressing ailment known as insomnia, when we lie awake in bed, tossing from side to side, and vainly endeavouring to obtain forgetfulness by those methods which are recommended in such circumstances. Imaginery sheep are counted as they jump over an imaginary stile, songs are sung, poetry repeated, the alphabet run through backwards and forwards, and still we are, if anything, less sleepy than when we went to bed . And then how hard the bed seems to become, and bow uncomfortable the pillow? How every little trivial sound is magnified by the silence of the night into a noise as loud and startling as thunder; and so hour after hour slowly passes away, until, as the grey light pro- claims the advent of dawn, we drop off, and obtain a

, short period of troubled sleep, awaking wearied and un- refreshed, and thoroughly unfit to resume the duties of the day. Who can blame the sufferer if he seeks a temporary re- spite in opium, morphia, chloral, or some other soporific, even if he does so with his eyes open, and is well aware of the hundred and one dangers attending the use of these narcotics? But, unfortunately, too many people get into the habit of taking these pernicious aruo'x, before they really know what they are doing, and what the cus- tom entails upon them. Medicines of this class should never be resorted to without the advice of a physician. In his hands they may prove useful; but the habit of taking them regularly having once been forn.ed, the sufferer from sleeples-sness soon discovers that to obtain the desired relief the dose must be gradually increased. and he thus exposes himself to the dangers of an overdose. Few patients, having once acquired the pernicious habit of taking narcotics regularly, possess sufficient strength of will to free them- selves again from this habit. Narcotics do not produce natural sleep, they simply cause a state of nnconciousness that may pass over into natural sleep, but this result is not often obtained. Narcotics exert a peculiar effect on the brain and the nervous system, they invariably affect the action of the heart by reducing its pulsation. They further modify the secretions, they check the flow of bile, and cause con- stipation, or, in other words, they create disturbances in the system which will in their turn produce sleepless- ness. In this circumstance we may find an explanation of the necessity of a gradually increased dose. This being so, it was with great pleasure that we heard of a new discovery, which, it was stated, would produce sleep, without any of the contingent disadvantages appertaining to opium and chloral; but as it does not always do to take what the promoters of a new invention say for absolute truth, we determined upon testing this new medicine before bringing it under the notice of our readers. . . _ .

Meuphrosine, for that is the name of the new specific, is guaranteed to contain neither chloral, henbane, aconite, Indian hemp, bromide, sulphonal, the amylic or paraldenyde compounds, or any preparation, or com- pound of opium. It is sweet and agreeable to the taste, with a strong flavour of peppermint. A teaspoon- ful given to an infant restless from teething appeared to give almost immediate relief, and produce a peace- ful slumber lasting all night. 4 dose of a wine-glassful gave an adult seven hours of restful sleep. The same dose banished all traces of a severe nervous headache, and a teaspoonful given to a child removed the evil effects of a too hearty indutence in unripe fruit. And in every case without any after effect, or unpleasant consequences whatever. These are sober facts, andour readers may accept them without reserve. Meuphrosine is sold by the Meuphrosine Manufacturing Company, 3, Jeffery's-square, London, E.C., and all respectable chemists. Price 2s. 9d. per bottle.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A FARM LABOURER'S HOARD.

At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, Patrick Crow, a farm labourer, hailing from Whitley,was chargad on remand, with stealing the sum of £2 54. from John Welsh on the previous Friday. Michael Connor and John Burke, also farm labourers, were charged with having received a portion of the money knowing it to have been stolen. The prisoner Crow had persuaded Welsh to bury his money in the ground, and after he had done so had gained possession of it. He had given Burke and Connor 4s. each. Crow, when charged with the theft, said that " the old lad must have tempted him to steal the money." Prisoners were remanded to the Daresbury Petty Sessioni.

THE BIRCH AS A PUNISHMENT FOR BOY THIEVES. The Warrington magistrates on Monday morning took a wise course in ordering the birch for two lads who had lapsed into the ways of thieving, in preference to relegat- J 47, the youngsters to jail. The boys—James Parry (13) and Elliott Harris (10)—were charged with having, on the Saturday before, stolen a pair of shoes and a pair of goloshes from Frisby's stall in the market, and five hand- kerchiefs from another stall kept by Alfred Peacock. They pleaded guilty, and according to the statements of their parents, had apparently- been good lads up to the time of the offence. Parry, who is the eldest of the offenders, was ordered to receive twelve strokes with the birch the same day, and another twelve on the fol- lowing day, and Harris was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod.
A BOY FINED FOR DRUNKENNESS.

A deplorable case of juvenile drunkenness was dealt with by the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday morning, on remand from the previous day. The prisoner, by name William Cunningham, is not yet sixteen years of age, and on Saturday night he was locked up on a charge of" drunk and disordnrly." He was formally charged with that offence on Monday morning, before the Mayor and other magistrates, to whom he stated that he met some navvies, with whom he had been working, on Satur- day night, and they gave him some beer to drink out of a bottle. "Not being used to loner," he added, "I got very drunk." The Constable who proved the case said that another lad was trying to persuade prisoner to go home. As prisoner appeared to be in a rather excited state, he was remanded until next morning, when he was seriously admonished as to his conduct, and fined 55., including costs.

DRUNK IN THE POLICE COURT. An elderly man named Henry Bithell was locked up by the Warrington police on Saturday morning in a state of drunkenness. In the evening he was admitted to bail, and had to appear before the magistrates on Monday morning. Perhaps with the idea of screwing up his courage, or perhaps because he was a good deal reckless as to the course matters might take, Bithell again got "on the drink," and when his case was called on he was utterly unfit to plead. He was therefore put back on remand. He was kept in durance until Tuesday morning, when he was fined ss. and costs for the original offence, and an additional ss. and costs for having been drunk when before the magistrates. At the same Court a young man named James Gleesou was charged with two offences of drunkenness. He was summoned to appear on Monday to answer a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on the 3rd July. He did appear, but as he, like Bithell, was under the influence of drink when asked to plead, he was put back until Tuesday, when he was fined ss. and costs.

AN EARLESTOWN MAN'S ADVENTURES AT WATIRINGTON. A man of respectable appearance, named George Baker, hailing from Earlestown, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday on charges of having been drunk, of having refused to quit the Central Hotel, and of haying assaulted Constable Singleton and Con- stable Hell. Evidence was given by Stephen Stirrup to the effect that the defendant, with others, came to the Central on Saturday night, and wanted to play billia'rds. Defendant was drunk, witness refused to allow hWto play, and an altercation ensued. Witness sent dA :for Constable Singleton. That officer swore thatl3aker6nck him in the face, and was very disorderly, and Constable Bell stated that the defendant kicked him on the wrist. In the course of a long statement, defendant stated that Stirrup assaulted him, and he (defendant) being rather ' dazed with the suddenness of the assault, struck out right and left. He resisted apprehension, because there was no reason why be should be locked up. The officers said that they would "put it in as hot as they could" for him. Frederick Waterman, fitter, Earlestown, gave evi- dence in support of the defence, and Alderman Davies remarked that apparently one circumstance had led to another. Defendant did not seem at all a man who would assault the police.—The Chief Constable : I think that is se..--Aldermati Harrison : Not unless you think be had some provocation.—Alderman Davies: No; I think he was dazed, and could scarcely help himself.— Defendant was ordered to pay a fine of 10s. and costs.

A VIOLENT GIRL'S ATTACK ON A POLICEMAN. . On Tuesday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a young girl named Winifred Jennings, who is well known to the police, was brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., and with having refused to quit the White Bear Inn. She was also charged with having assaulted Constable Hughes, when that officer was conveying her to the Police Station. In connection with the same case, a young fellow named Michael Kelly was charged with having attempted to rescue the female prisoner from the custody of the police. Hughes stated that Jennings both kicked and bit him, and the Chief Con- stable said that on the day previous she was charged with drunkenness, but the magistrates, wishing to try the effect of leniency, gave her a chance on her promis- ing to go to work. It might not be amiss if the magis- trates ordered her to find sureties for her good behaviour for six or twelve months, and, in default, let her lie in jail. He had known a dose like that to have a very good effect indeed. The magistrates sent the girl to hard lab- our for a month, and fined Kelly, who made his first ap- pearance, ss.and costs, or seven day's imprisonment in default of payment.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES ANDB ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES ANDB ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Murdoch, the Australian captain, still holds to his opinion that the team now on tour is "the strongest that has ever been sent over." He predicted that "when they showed their true form it would be seen that they were very powerful." The Australians will have to "hurry up" if they do not want to return to their An- tipodean homes before they have ever shown their "true form."

The Australians are another team that have some reason to complain of the weather, for they had an" easy thing" on with Gloucester on Saturday, the later county having only four wickets to fall and wanting 174 runs to escape a single-innings defeat. Gloucester was, there- fore, lucky in having this game declared a draw, instead of its being added to their lisb of six defeats, un- chequered by a single victory.

The match between Lancashire and Yorkshire had to be abandoned on Saturday owing to the persistent downpouring of the rain. This was rather hard on Lancashire, who, in all probability, had in store a deci- sive victory over their formidable rivals. When the game was abandoned the score stood—Lancashire, Ist innings, 161 ; second innings, 187; while Yorkshire were credited with only 88 for their first innings, and two runs for two wickets for their second attempt.

Briggs was the most effective batsman for the home team, running up 62 for his first innings and 54 for his second. Paul played well, too, for his 12 and 65. The Yorkshiremen hardly sustained their reputation in bat- ting, though their fielding was good.

The Australians met with the eighth defeat of their tour on Wednesday, at the hands of a team of the Players of England, got together by the Yorkshire Committee. On Monday the Players completed an innings of 221, and the Australians followed on with two innings of 91 and 161 respectively. In their second innings the Players easily made the number required to win with the loss of only one wicket. Turner (1, 35), Murdock (1,26), Trott (18, 17), Charlton (14,20), and Blackham (1, 38) did best for the Colonials. For the Players Shrewsbury was again at the head of the batting list with 65, Gunn following with 43, and Chatterton with 41.

Saturday's" Graphic" says :—Dr. W. G. Grace and Briggs were walking out from the pavilion at Lord's one day to take their stand at the wickets when a small child remarked to its father—" Pa, who's that big man ? " "That's Dr. Grace, my dear," answered the fond parent. " And who is the little man ? " continued the infant, "Oh, that's Briggs." "And is Briggs Dr. Grace's baby?'' said the youthful inquirer. The "Graphic" goes on to give same very well deserved praise of the Lancashire cricketer.

Two hours and ten minutes play at Old Trafford on Wednesday ended the Lancashire v. Middlesex match in a victory for Lancashire by seven wickets. A disas- trous start was made, as Barlow and Albert Ward were both out for an addition of three to the overnight score of 33. When Paul and Yates became associated a very different complexion was put upon the game. Both rnen hatted splendidly on a wicket which was none the worse for the two previous days play, and though seven mem- bers of the Middlesex team officiated with the ball, hit off the necessary runs. The Middlesex score was 164 for the first innings and 192 for the second ; and Lan- cashire made 188 for the first innings and 172 for the loss of three wickets in the second. In the second innings Paul and Yates put on 71 and 64 respectively without being displaced.

div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The county teams of Denton and Irlam met in the second series of ties, on Saturday, on the greens of the Ship Hotel, at Irlam, and the Old Soldier, Ashton, to contest for the leading prizes in the Lancashire and Cheshire Bowling Association. The Irlam bowlers were very successful on the home ground, and, despite the plucky play throughout of the visitors, succeeded in accomplishing a record score. At Denton the Irlam team scored 99, but on the home ground they secured 129, making a total of 225. The Denton players also did well on their own ground, 124 being the score, but at Irlam they fell behind with only 91, making a total of 215. On the Ship Hotel Green at Irlam. Irina'. Denton. Several Warringtonians competed in the open amateur handicap at the swimming gala held at Pendleton Baths on Monday evening. These were Fair Turner, J. Pem- berton, S. J. Beaman, W. Furnival, W. Henshall, and F. Garside. Garside was the only local swimmer who won his heat, but he was thrown out in semi-final by H. J. Hicks, of Manchester. Tie handicap was won by Tom Orr, of the Swan Club. with T. Harris, the Swan Club, second ;J. H. Hicks, third; and J. T. Rowan, Salford Club, four.

At the Amateur Athletic Championship meeting at Birmingham, on Saturday, H. Curtis shifted some records in the walking race. For five, six, and seven miles he knocked out the records-37min. 22sec., smin. 4sec., and 52min. 34sec.—made by H. Webster, of Knotty Ash, Liverpool, at the championship at Lillie Bridge n. years ago—April 7, 1879 ; and he is likely, when opportunity offers, to improve on the new figures, and accomplish what no amateur has yet done—eight miles in the hour.

It is some time since a championship went to Wales, but the principality can now boast of a very smart sprinter in N. D. Morgan, who won the hundred in fine style, Southerners only getting a fourth. Daft repeated his victories of 1885 and 1886 in the hurdles, beating the holder by a yard in the slowest time since 1879.
