THE _EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1890.
NAVAL AND MILITARY INTELLIGENCE.

LORD WOLSELEY'S NEW APPOINTMENT. The "St. James's Gazette "says :—As we annbunced some time 'since, it has long been settled that Lord Wolseley would be the next Commander-in-Chief in Ire- land if that appointment was not accepted by the Duke of Connaught. It is now understood that the Duke will not receive the post, and consequently Lord Wolseley, whose term of office as Adjutant-general ex- pires at the end of this month, will take the command of the forces in Ireland in October next.

div.head: PERPETUAL PENSIONS.
div.p: PERPETUAL PENSIONS.

The Lords of the Treasury have at length settled the terms upon which they propose to determine some of the perpetual pensions which still cling to the National Exchequer. The Duke of St. Albans receives a salary of £965 as Master Surveyor and Keeper of the Hawks. This is to be commuted at nineteen years' purchase. The Duke of Hamilton is Keeper of the Palace Gardens of Holyrood, a sinecure post which brings him £45 10s. a year. For this he is to receive twenty-two years' pur- chase. The Marquis of Downshire fills the office of Constable of the Fort of Hillsborough, in County Down, from which he draws an income of £54 3s. 4d. This is to be commuted at the rate of 25 years' purchase. The pensions of £2,000 a year severally enjoyed by Lord Exmouth and Lord Rodney are to be commuted for a fraction under twenty-seven years' purchase. Mr. Bradlaugh intends to oppose these two last proposals.
WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTITUTIONS.

The anniversary of the Institutions for Clergy Widows and Orphans and Clergy Daughters School was held on Thursday. In the, morning a meeting of subscribers was held at the Training College, Warrington, at which the president, Mr. G. Whitley, M.P., occupied the chair, and the others present were Bishop Cramer Roberts, the Ven. Archdeacon Bar- ber, General Sir Richard Wilbraham, Rev. Canon Maclure (Dean designate of Manchester), Canon Greenall ( hon. sec.), Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Rev. Canon Blundell, Rev. Canon Stowell, Rev. Canon Whitley, Rev. Canon Livingstone, Captain Whitingtan, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. F. W. Willis, Rev. W. D. Carter, Rev. J. Carson, Rev. J. A. M. Johnstone (Astley), Rev. F. E. Hopwood (Bury), Mr. E. Green- all, Mr. Fletcher Rogers, Mr. James Tinsley, Mr. Buckton, Rev. J. Phillips, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mr. H. Tinsley, Rev. E. T. Wigg (Royton), Rev. J. Holmet, and Dr. Watkins,

div.head: AN ABUNDANCE OF APOLOG /BS.
div.p: AN ABUNDANCE OF APOLOG /BS.

The Hort. SEC. (Rev. Canon Greenall) said he had re- ceived 159 apologies for non-attendance. (Laughter.) Should he read them, or might they be taken as read ? It was unanimously agreed to take them as read.

div.head: CLERICAL PRINCIPAL.
div.p: THE CLERICAL PRINCIPAL.
ArchdeacMiGona moved that the rule requiring tho appointment of a resident clerical principal be rescinded, and this being seconded by Canon PBI4IIHYN, was agreed to.
TN& PANSION FUND.

In his report as to this fund, Canon Greenell said that this, the oldest of their charitable institutions had now been carrying on its charitable work for 193 years, hav- ing been established in the year 1697. If the need lof such an institution was apparent then it was much more so now. Since the last anniversary two ladies had exceptional grants to the amount of £25. Four of the pensioners had died during the year. One Liverpool widow and two Manchester widows, feeling theze were so many others mere in need of help than themselves, had voluntarily withdrawn their names from the list. There were seven new applicants : five widows and two orphans. Ninety-six now stood in the list, namely, 21 widows and seven orphans from Chester diocese ; nine widows and ten orphans from Liverpool diocese; 31 widows and 13 orphans from Mancherter diocese. The free education of the girls in the Clergy Daughters' School had been provided for out of the funds a the institution. They Would be asked to sanction pensions, donations, and payments of free scholars in the clergy school to the amount of £2,075. The amount last year was £2,119. The income of the charity for the year ending the 31st. December last amounted to £2,260 3s. id. made up as follows :—Special donations, £64 103. 9d. ; interest on capital, £7OB 55.; collections £571 2s. 10d. ; subscriptions £766 6s. 6d.; unappropriated funds, £145 16. 3d. ; bank interest, &c., £4 Us. 4d.; total, £2,280 3s. Id. The total income of the previous year was £2,374 7s. M., £ll4 4s. id. more than last year's income. There had been a decrease in donations of £36 15s. 7d., in interest of the invested capital £44 16s. id.; in collections in churches £3l 16s. 3d. ; in subscriptions £lB 16s. id. ; in bank interest and odd money £7 16s. 4d.; altogether £l4O Os. 4d.; but an increase of £25 16s. 3d. from the unappropriated funds reduced the deficiency of £l4O Os. 4d• to £ll4 4s. Id. The Committee desired to call special attention to the serious falling off in the income of the charity. If this continued it must ultimately lead to a general reduction of grants which already were far too small, averaging from £3O to £lO. The Committee ventured to again call upon their clerical brethren to make known the existence, wants, and generous work of the institution in the several parishes. It was not sup- ported either so generally or so liberally as it deserved. The report then alluded to the changes in the Committee owing to the deaths of canon Hopwood and Dean Oakley. They were glad to announce that Canon Oakley would be succeeded by Canon Maclure, who, for many years, had rendered valuable service to those institutions. They offered their warmest congratulations on his pro- motion tl the Deanery of Manchester. (Applause.)— The report was adopted.

div.head: THB STATH OF THS SCHOOLS.
div.p: THB STATH OF THS SCHOOLS.

The report of the Rev. T. Stevens, M. L, of Magdalen College, as to his examination of the Clergy Daughters' School, was read, and in conclusion be said that as far as he was able to judge, the order, discipline, and tone of the school left nothing to be desired. The Rector of Warrington also read a report as to his work since his appointment as chaplain of the institutions, and stated that from an ecclesiastical, moral, and spiritual view he believed tho school to be very satisfactory.
TIII3 GRANTS.
The Rev. Callost GREENALL said that every application for assistance which had been received by the Committee had been carefully looked into and not one had been rejected.
TEN COMMITTEE! OF MANAGEMENT.
The Yen. Archdeacon Anson and the Rev. Srnethwick, of Seaforth, were appointed members of this Committee.
MIXT:2EAR% ARRANGEMENTS.
It was announced that the preacher of next year would be Bishop Cramer Roberts, and the president, Mr. Clement Royds.
TEE MEETINGS.

The Rev. F. E. Hopwood moved that the time of those annual meetings should be held on the first Thursday in August instead of the third in July. The Rev. Canon Penrhyn seconded this proposal,which was, however, not adopted. A vote of thanks to the president brought the meeting to a close.
After the business meeting a largely attended service was held in the Parish Church, the Archdeacon of War- rington preaching an eloquent sermon from 2 Kings, 4c., 3v.

_ Afterwards a luncheon was partaken of at the Clergy Daughters' School. Mr. E. Whitley again presided, and amongst those present was the Dean of Chester. The loyal toasts were proposed by the CHAIRMAN, and that of the" Bishops and Clergy of the three dioceses" of Ches- ter, Manchester, and Liverpool was proposed by General Sir RICIIARD WILBRAHAM. In responding to the latter toast the Brsuor of CHESTER referred to the increasing friendly feeling between the clergy and laity. He was sure that on both sides there was a desire to understand one another better, to co-operate more intelligently and more , sympathetically, and he felt certain they would welcome everything that tended towards union and mutual res- pect, and look coldly upon anything that tended to pro- duce disunion in the ranks of their church. (Hear, hear). There was one thiltr,. in reference to the clergy 'he should like to refer to. A very sad injury had been inflicted upon the simple and just rights of the clergy by the Tithes Bill being postponed. He hoped that every influence would be brought to bear on the govern- ment, so that their brethern, especially in Wales, would not be left with the difficulties of the winter upon them. (Hear, hear). He could not help saying in plain words that if that kind of treatment of the clergy and church by the present Government continued it would shako the loyalty of very inany. towards them. (Hear, hear and applause). Other toasts were proposed as follows : "The Archdeacon of Warrington, the preacher of the day," proposed by Mr. Fletcher Rogers and responded to by the Archdeacon of Warrington ; " Success to the Institutions." proposed by the Chairman ; "The Chair- man," proposed by Archdeacon Barber; and acknow- ledged by the Chairman; "'The lay friends of the insti- tution," proposed by the Rev. J. B. Jones, and responded to by Mr. W. P. Fullager ; "The town and trade of Warrington," proposed by Captain With ington and responded to by Mr. Buckton.

He anticipated that if the Liberals were again returned to power the Union would be in no serious danger. The danger' he thought, would lie in this, that every interest would be threaten- ed in turn.

NEW LINE OF STEAMERS TO THE ( ISLE OF MAN. There will shortly be placed before the public the prospectus of a new Company for establishing a line of steamers to ply between Liverpool and the Isle of Man, to be called the " Eiffel Tower Line." The Company was registered in Douglas in October last, and we understand that three first class steamers will be put upon the station in May, 1891. We gather from a preliminary circular that their will be 500 founders shares of ten pounds each, not ranking for dividend until ten per cent, is paid on ordinary shares. It is calculated the surplus will be at least £2,500, avail- able for distribution after payment of four per cent. interest to debenture holders, 10 per cent, to ordinary shareholders and providing for ample depreciation and insurance, one half or £1,250 will go the founders, equal to 25 per cent, to the ten pound founders shares, making their value at the end of the first year's working, assuming money is worth five per cent, per annum, "fifty pounds." With the 20 per cent. Co-operative tickets given to a ten pound founders share for each year for five years, the actual market value an founder's ten pound share will be at least seventy pounds. The founders likewise receive a free perpetual first class pass between Liverpool and Douglas transferable, similar to the debenture and ordinary shareholders. The founders guarantee to sub- scribe for five mortgage debentures ten pounds each, and 50 ordinary shares of one pound each, in proportion to one ten pound founder's share. Investors are requested to notice the advantages derived from the adoption of the co-operative system of trading, more especially as regards the working of passenger steamers.

div.head: "HANGING UP" COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE "HANGING UP" COMMITTEE.

The Committee of the House of Commons which had been appointed to consider the propriety or otherwise of suspending Bill& which had passed second reading until the next ensuing Session of the same Parliament met again on Monday. Mr. Goschen presided, and all the other members of the Committee were also present, with the important exception of Mr. Gladstone, who was in- disposed. The Committee proceeded to consider in detail ' the draft submitted by the Government, which had been read a second time at the previous sitting, and which embodied the proposed suspensory standing order, and gave reasons for its adoption l•y the House. The draft report consisted of eight paragraphs, and the prin- ciple discussion arose upon that one of them the language of which, it was contended, might be used as an argu- ment by the House of Lords for suspending in that House Bills which had already passed the Commons. Certain words of this paragraph were omitted, and others added instead thereof, on the motion first of Mr Chamberlain and next of Sir W. Harcourt, and as amended the paragraph placed on record the opinion that any attempt of either House on its own authority by standing order or otherwise, to postpone until a future Session of Parliament any Bill sent to it from the other House would be a breach of the constitutional usage of Parliament. The insertion of these words was agreed to, but the Opposition members regarded the paragraph as still containing something objectionable, and took a division against it, with the result tnat it was adopted by 11 to 8, An amendment, drawn by Mr. Gladstone, and proposing the addition of words setting forth that the House should do nothing under the standing order without the general concurrence of Parliament, was moved in his absence by Mr. J. Morley, and defeated by 31 to 8. The alterations made in the draft report, ex- cept that above mentioned, were purely verbal. A divi- sion was taken on every paragraphupon Mr. Gladstone's proposed addition, and finally, upon the report as a whole, the voting upon all questions of principle being on purely party lines, and the figures being in those in- stances 11 to 8. The Committee sat two hours. Its re- port was brought up at the meeting of the House, and presented by Sir Stafford Northcote, one of its members. Mr. Goschen, upon whom this duty would, in his capa- city as chairman, have fallen in the ordinary course, be- ing engaged out of the House at the time.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF -MR. STANLEY.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF -MR. STANLEY.

Enthusiastic excitement prevailed in the neighbour- hood of Westminster Abbey on Saturday afternoon; when Mr. Henry Morton Stanley, the eminent explorer, was married to Miss Dorothy Tennant, secOnd daughter of the late Mr. Charles Tennant, of Richmond-terrace, Whitehall, and Cadoxten Lodge, Neath, Glamorganshire. The nave and both transepts were also thronged with spectators, the north transept being thrown open at half-past one to the public. At a quarter to two o'clock two carriagesalrove up to the Abbey, sthe first contain"- ing the bridegroom, Count d' Arache, and Dr. Evsaril, who, in conjunction with Lieutenant Parkes, is attend- ing Mr. Stanley in his trying and painful illness. In the second carriage came the groomsmen, seated upon the box being Sardi, Mr. Stanley's faithful Zanzibari servant, who accompanied him throughout the memorable expedition. All eyes were now turned towards the west door, and in a few momenta Mr. Stanley entered the choir, walking with the aid of a stick, and leaning on the arm of his best man, Count d' Arache, who had been specially sent to perform this pleasing duty by the King of the Belgians. Following immediately behind the bridegroom came his no less distinguished and courageous staff of officers, Lieutenant Stairs, Mr. Mounteney Jephson, Surgeon Parkes, Captain Nelson, and Mr. Bonny, who acted as groomsmen,' Precisely at two o'clock a prelude from the organ announced the 'arrival of (the bride, and the vast congregation rose to their feet. The bride was accom- panied by her only brother, Mr. Charles Coome Tennant, and attended by two tiny bridesmaids, Miss Sylvia Myers, aged six, and Miss Finlay, aged eight, and a smart page, Master Leopold Myers (nephew of the bride), aged eight. The bridal dress was a very beauti- ful one. The front of the skirt was of white satin, richly embroidered in pearls, as were also the vest, the lower part of the sleeves, and the picturesque Medici collar. The train and bodice were of rich poult de soia, and a very pretty effect was obtained through the seams being sewn over with pearls. On each side of the front were large boquets of orange blossom, and there was another bunch on the bodice. The bride wore a double bandeau of orange blossoms round the coil of her hair at the batik, and a tulle veil. Her jewels included the miniature of the Queen surrounded by diamonds, the gift of her Majesty, a diamond necklace, and an aigrette and three stars Of diamonds and sapphires. And now the old, ever reverenced ceremony commenced. Confusion was stilled ;it was a moment of singular, almost intense devotion. Mr. Stanley rose— painfully enough—from his seat, and took his place by the side of his bride-elect, and there, under the lanthorn tower, the first part of the service was performed. Archdeacon Farrar descend- ed the steps from the sacrarium, and read the opening sentences of the marriage service. _Then the venerable cleric gave Place to the Bishop of Ripon. Mr. Stanley plighted his troth with evident fervour— leaning the while on the cane which had hitherto sup- ported him; Miss Tennant's reply was clear and unfalter- ing. 'then, amid the breathless deepened silence, the Bishop pronounced this twain man and wife. Then the e7splorer placed the ring on his wife's finger, and then the Bishop solemnly pronounced the first benediction. Slowly and sedately the bridal party followed the clergy to the sacrarium, and there'the remainder of the beauti- ful service was performed. The special hymn was sung with sweet tenderness and grace; the final words of blessing were spoken by the Dean; and then, to the swelling tones of the joyous "Wedding March," Mr. and Mrs. Stanley left the Abbey, and the carriage with difficulty made its way to Mrs. Tennant's residence, Richmond-terrace, Whitehall. Mr. Stanley was Om- ' pelled on his arrival to rest, being unequal to join his friends at the garden party which was subsequently given; but Mrs. Stanley and Mrs. Tennant were indefatigable, and gracefully performed the duties of hospitality. We regret to learn that on the presents at the Stanley wedding being finally collected and compared with the inventory it was discovered that several articles have been abstracted in addition to the two silver spoons which the thief was caught pocketing. Amongst the missing articles is a silver match-box, much valued by Mr. Stanley as the gift of an intimate personal friend. Wednesday's account from Romsey of Mr. 11. M. Stan- ley's condition is very hopeful.

TERRIBLE EXPLOSION OF POWDER
TEN PERSONS 'KILLED.

_ NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY MORNING.—As a cart load of giant powder was being driven out of a powder em- porium,at Lovelarid,Ohio, yesterday, the powder became ignited by some means at present unascertained and ten persons were killed arid thirty injured by the dreadful explosion which occurred.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. DAVID PUGH, M.P.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. DAVID PUGH, M.P.

Mr. Pugh, member for East Carmarthenshire, died at his London residence on Saturday. Mr. Pugh represen- ted Carmarthenshire as a Liberal, and voted in favour of the Home Rule Bill. He sat as member for the county from 1857 to 1868, .and for the Eastern Division since 1835. He was unopposed at the last election. In the last contest, which was in 1385, the figures were as fol- low :—Mr. D. Pugh (L), 4,487; Sir M. 0. Lloyd, Bart., (C), 2,122; Liberal majority, 2,365. ' The funeral of Mr. Pugh, M.P., for East Carmarthen- shire, took place on Thursday in Llandllo Churchyard. The cortege which left Manoravan, the deceased gentle- man's residence, at noon, was of great length, the funeral being of a public character.

div.head: DURHAWELECTION.--LIBERAL VICTORY.
div.p: THE DURHAWELECTION.--LIBERAL VICTORY.

Polling commenced in Mid-Durham on Thursday morning, for the election of a member of Parliament, to succeed the late Mr. William Crawford, Gladstonian Liberal, in the representation of the division. The can- didates are Mr. Adolphus Vane Tempest, Conservative, and Mr. John Wilson, Gladstonian Liberal. The electors came up to poll in considerable numbers at eight o'clock, and the election proceeded briskly. The result was declared about one o'clock on Friday I morning as follows : John Wilson (L) Adolphus Vane-Tempest (C)
Liberal majority 2,094 At the last general election Mr. Crawford was returned without opposition, while in 1885 the figures were :
W. Crawford (L) A. Vane-Tempest 3,245
Majority

Mr. John Wilson, of North-road, Durham, who thus succeeds to the seat held since 1885 by Mr. William Crawford, and now vacated only by his death, is the son of Mr. Christopher Wilson, labourer, of Greatham, Dur- ham, by his marriage with Hannah Spohton, daughter of• Michael Spenton, of Hamsterley, near Toft-hill, Durham, and was born at Greatham in 1837. He commenced work at Stanhope Quarries at the age of ten, and three years later,when he was thirteen, he went down the pit at Lud- worth Colliery, Durham. After working underground some years, he went at the age of nineteen to sea for a few years, but came back to England and worked in the Haswell Colliery. In 1863 he went to America, and stayed there 31 years, working in the mines at Penn- sylvania and Illinois. He assisted.; the formAtion of the , Miners' Association in 1869 ; was appointed in 1877 , secretary of the Durham Franchise Association ; and „ ' in MaylBB2, treasurer or the Durham Miners' Associa- tion. In 1863 Mr. Wilson married Margaret,daughter of George Frith, walminer, of Sherburn-hill, Durham. He is not quite new to Parliamentary life, having been returned for the Houghton-le-Spring division of the county in 1885, when he defeated Mr. N. Wood, Con- secvative. The following year, however, he was defeated by Mr, Wood.

div.head: LONDON POSTMEN'S AGITATION
div.p: THE LONDON POSTMEN'S AGITATION
END OF THE STRIKE.

The various deliveries of letters were sent out from the General Post Office on Saturday without hitch or incident of any unusual kind. Work at all the district offices also proceeded satisfactorily. In the East-end, however, police were employed to prevent postmen being molested. ' The men who struck in the Eastern district have peti- tioned for reinstatement, asking the Postmaster-General to be kind enough to overlooktheir misconduct, declaring that they have been misled : that their wives and chil- dren will be the greatest sufferers, and promising to have no further connection with the Postmen's Union. The petit on says they deeply apologise for their past miscon- duct. One of the men who struck is 50 years of age, with 30 years' service. He has a family,and was entitled to a. penSion of 18s. weekly. The authorities, are, :how- ever, at present determined not to reinstate any of the dismissed or suspended men. Up to Saturday 435 post- men had been dismissed for insubordination, 48 being first-class town postmen, 54 second-class town postmen, 24 first-clasS suburban postmen, 34 second-class suburban men, 20 third-class, and 255 unestablished.

There was no parade Of metropolitan postmen on Sat- urday.. Mr. Mahon, secretary of the ,Postmen's Union, denies that the struggle is ended, and declares that the men are not yet beaten. A meeting of postmen was arranged for half-past nine on Saturday night at , the Holborn Town-hall, but up to ten o'clock. only about 200 were present. Mr. Binhington, of the London Society of Compositors, presided, and amongst those present were Mr. Shipton, and M. Drummond, of the London Trades' Council. The proceedings were -private. The authorities at St. Martin's-le-Grand stated on Sun- day that everything was now working smoothly, and there was nothing further to report respecting the recent strike movement beyond the fact that one or two of their postmen had been attacked while on duty in the East-end. The assailants are not believed to be connected with the strikers.

div.head: RAINFORD TRAGEDY,
div.p: THE RAINFORD TRAGEDY,
THE REVOLVERS FOUND.

_ • An Important discovery in regard to the murder of Mr. Foster, was made on Saturday afternoon. This was the finding of a large five-chambered revolver, only one of the barrels of which had been discharged, the other four being loaded. It will be remembered that according to the confession of Mrs. Pickavance each of the prisoners carried a revolver, and that while the husband fired five or six times Mrs. Pickavance only fired once. Evidence was adduced at the Prescot Police Court on Friday, showing that the prisoners had formerly owned two' revolvers—a large jive-chambered one and a smaller weapon with six chambers. The presumption has been that the husband used the last-named firearm, while the wife carried that with five chambers. The discovery of the revolver on Saturday supports this view, and is a material corroboration of the published confession of Mrs. Pickavance in regard to the shots fired. Since the murder the police authorities were unremitting in their search for the missing weapons, and offfeers diligently searched the roads and fields from Rainford to Eccleston-lane-ends, Prescot, where the prisoners were apprehended. About midway between the two places, in a secluded and lonely part, the country road is bordered on one side by a dense plantation, forming part of Lord Derby's estate, and in the plan- tation, some yards from the footpath is a pond about twenty yards across. A channel was cut to run off the greater portion of the water into a drain, while the fire engine belonging to Lord Derby has also been at work pumping out the remainder of the water. On Saturday the whole of the water was cleared away, and it was while dragging ammo the thick, slimy mud, some feet in depth, that the searcher's were rewarded by bringing to view the weapon which is now in the possession of the police. The pond is situate about three miles from the scene of the murder.

On Monday, P.S. Smith, P.C. Carter and others con- tinued their search for the second revolver, and succeeded in finding it in the same pit. It is a six-chambered revolver, and two of the barrels were discharged. The weapon muat have been reloaded, as four bullets corres- ponding with this revolver have been found.

The Salt Union has received fourteen days' notice from the Winsford Saltmakers' Association that if certain grievances are not rectified the men will all be called out.
SUICIDE OF A SERGEANT-MAJOR.
Sergeant-Major Burrell, in charge of the canteen of the 7th Surrey Mile Volunteers shot himself at his residence at the Drill Hall, Upper Kensington-Lane, on Wednesday afternoon with a rifle.

THE CHOLERA IN SPAIN. The Austrian Board of Health is again deliberating upon what measure should be taken to protect the country from cholera, an increase of the epidemic in Spain having been reported. According to the inform- ation received by the Board, the epidemic is raging in 31 communes of Valencia and Alicante. Up to the 9th July there had been eight cases in the city of Valencia, and nearly 500 in the district, the proportion of deaths being 60 per cent.

div.p: SELECTED READIN GS.

Aix Aroun Erts.—The ways of eels are indeed mysterious, for nobody has ever yet succeeded in discovering where, when, or 'how they manage to spawn; nobody has ever yet tieen an eel's egg, or, caught a female eel in the spawning condition, or even observed a really adult undo or •feinale speci- men of perfect development. All the eels evesr found in fresh water are immature and undeveloped creatures. But eels do certainly spawn soma' where or other in the deep sea and every year, in the course of the summer, flocks of young ones, known as elvers, ascend the rivers in erlormous quantities, like a vast army under numberless leaders. At each tributary or affluent, be it river, brook, stream, or ditch, a proportionate detachment of the main body is given Off to explore the various branches, while the central force wriggles its way up the chief channel, • regardless •of obstaclers, with undiminished. • vigour. When the young elvers come to a weir, a wall, a flood-gate, or a lasher, they siMPIY squirm up the perpendicular barrier with indes acribable wrigglinge, as if they were wholly wise- quainted, physically as well as mentally, with Newton's magnificent discovery of gravitation. Nothing stops them; they go wherever water is to be found; and though millions perish hopelessly in the attempts millions more survive in the end to , attain their goal in the upper reaches. They even . seem to scent ponds or lakes mysteriously, at a die' tance, and will strike boldly straight across countran . to sheets of water wholly cut off from con-maraca* tion with the river which forms their chief highway. The full-grown eels are also given to Purneying , across country in a morn sober, sedate, and alga' 7 fled manner, as becomes fish which have fully , arrived at years, or rather months of discretion. When the ponds in which they live dry UP summer, they make in is bee line for the nearest sheet of fresh water, whose direction and distance s they appear to know intuitively, through some strange instinctive geographical faculty. On their way across the country, they do not despise the succulent rat, whom they swallow whole when caught with great gusto. To keep their gills wet during these excursions, eels have the power 01 distending the skin on each side of the neck, just n below the head, so as to form a big pouch for swell' fug. This pouch they fill with water, to carry a good supply along with them, until they reach the ponds for which they are making. It is the pouch alone that enables eels to live so long out of water under all circumstances, and so incidentally exposes them to the disagreeable experience of getting skinned alive, which it is to he feared still forinE the fate of most of those that fall into the clutchea of the human species. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
MR. ROGUE, M.P., ON "BALFOURISM."

T., 011 Sunday evening, under the auspices of the ineal branch of the Irish National League, a well- - attended meeting of Irishmen and others was held at the League Hall, in Orford-st., to hear an address by *4 . • onn Roche, M.P. for County Galway. The ' chair was occupied by Mr. F. Loughlin, president of the local branch, and amongst the gentlemen who I,l!PPorted him on the platform were Councillor - , 'eating, Dr. Gornall, and Messrs. Kiernan, White- Read, Chambers, Donnellan, &c. r The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a few introductory , enlarks, expressed his pleasure at seeing so numerous an I attendance, which he took as an earnest of their wish to , give Mr. Roche a hearty welcome as one of the work- ' !its on behalf of the cause of Ireland, and as a man who had done much for Ireland. Mr. Roche had taken more than one man's share in the work, and had beaten down I‘ill the methods of coercion that Mr. Balfour had set up. ..,e was now in England for the purpose of carrying on , e work that he had so successfully carried on in Ireland, to put the finishing touch to Balfourism, and he need hardly say that they were proud to welcome a Ina, a who had done so much for the cause that they had "cart. • (Cheers.) He then introduced Mr. Roche to the meeting. ,111 - ROCHE, M.P., who was accorded a hearty wel- ,7lne, made a speech of very great interest, during the "vdrse of which he was frequently applauded. "The greatest of Balfour's criminals," as he was described on I:de notices calling the..meeting, looked exactly opposite the generally accepted notion of a criminal, and his EPeech, delivered in a temperate and gentlemanly mau- ner, made a great impression on 40 hearers. • Mr. i.doche had a good deal of the brogue about him, and that by xio means detracted from the effect of his elo- quence. Having very gracefully thanked the large 13:0dience for the kind reception with which they met unni the member for Galway said that he believed the r asen for the heartiness of his welcome was because he estood before them as one of the humble representatives 1,4 the great party led by that distinguished leader Mr. smell. (Cheers.) He came from amongst a people— a3 a representative of a people—who had had to bear 9 the tyranny, and all the oppression, and all the vin- dictiveness, that a bad landlord like Lord Clanricarde, (.4Man unscrupluous Government like the present, "nid inflict. He hoped and trusted that now, as they "ere on the eve of battle, they would do all within .'• thei le_ r Power to put an end, once and for all, e) the struggles in Ireland, and that they would come to •;t . he rescue of the poor and oppressed people in Ireland, r Who were looking to them for help and for relief. , t taheen.) They had fought, and they had won, the ttle in Ireland. They had beaten Clanricarde to the 7lnst, and they had beaten Balfourisen and coercion be- , le_ eath the dust. Coercion had been tried against them z'''r. h, e believed it had never been tried during the whole ‘ory of the country in times gone by. It had been l' ?,Pecially levelled against the people of Woodford, and •', ',ter four years of that firm and resolute government that Was promised, what had Mr. Balfour to boast of? •,„ I had nothing to boast of. (Cheers.) He had hea- 'so, lied them, no doubt, time after time,- and in the Parish flora which the speaker came he had sent f , of their people to prison during the past Years. ("Shame.") After all that imprisonment, :110 alter all that tyranny and oppression practised "qaitiet them, the Irish people to-day stood firmer to- gether than ever. (Cheers.) They had beaten Balfour ilk luti Ida thercion beneath the dust; hence, he said, the iv .beld of battle had been transferred from Ireland to --regiland, and it now rested, with the Liberals of '-,ngland, and his fellow countrymen in England, to be tePared for the day of battle near at ,hand. That „ Y of battle was the day of general election, and he was tiroud to learn that in Warrington the people had looked he to the matter of registration—to such an extent that 8 believed there was scarcely a man to be found who .twnuld not he prepared to cast his vote for liberty and jeedom and against coercion and oppression. (Cheers.) ~,," did not think he ought to say any hard words about the present Government, for surely the Opposition could afford to be charitable and forgive the past, when they e,„enlembered that only the other night in the House of -seilmons Mr. Balfour wrote his own epitaph. (Laugh- et and cheers.) The Government had to admit that .. they were beaten, and they were preparing fast for dis- rlution. Irishmen had great reason to be anxious as to ;:he issue of the coming fight, and they appealed to the mberals to be prepared to strike a blow against coercion, and allow the Irish the same privileges which they Would not live 24- hours without in England. (Cheers.) On the Clanricarde estate at Woodford there were at the their time 110 families who had been evicted from Weir homes and there were 110 more to be evicted. ("Shame.") Woodford was only a small corner of the estate. The rental of the whole estate was £B,OOO a lla,v, and for the last four years the British taxpayer ' £lO,OOO in order to protect Lord Clanricarde's rulitia and emergency men in evicting tenants. P Shaine.") , With that expenditure of money they had no doubt succeeded in evicting the people, but they had not succeeded in getting one penny of Lord Clan- riearde's rack rents. (Hear, hear and Cheers.) No Matter how long the battle might have to go on, and no Matter what the people had to suffer, they were deter- :lined, at any cost or sacrifice, to stand loyal to one nether and never come to terms with that landlord until t he evicted tenants were reinstated in their homes. It Was the tenants who had built the places. Not one Penny of Clauricarde's money. had ever been invested in anything on the farms, but instead, whenever any im- P,,..,rovernent had been made, the rent was immediately '''„ lied. (" Shame.") The rents had been increased to an extent that after a few bad seasons many of the People who were unable to pay their rents became bank- Pt. That was the state of things with which the Irish tenants had to contend, and which forced them to 7,41.01 themselves under the banner of the Plan of •I'atnnaign. In August, 1886, Clanricarde attempted to !Viet four of his Woodford tenants. The spirit and illetermination of those people were such that it took , vteooo police and soldiers ten days to capture those four . I,onses. (Laughter and applause.) The defenders of , hose homes were dragged off to Galway prison and kept there , V from August until December :awaiting trial. .03nongst those who were sentenced to imprisonment was 4 ' te..7°llng man named Larkin, the only son of as brave, i•`,.'.45 honest-hearted an Irishman as ever trod the earth. it`,;•a,t Poor fellow died in Kilkenny goal, and he (Mr. , "cue) accompanied the father to the prison on receipt the Governor's telegram announcing the lad's death. . di "0 one knew how he ed. He had been suffering from Very bad disease, but instead of being removed to the •,, na,Pital and properly treated he was left in the prison and allowed to die like a dog. The features been so altered by sickness that neither -, to:)• the visitors were able to recognize the remains. iLne Would think that Clanricarde would be satisfied with ~'lie Wrong he had inflicted upon old Larkin, but what did ~: . •Ve audience think awaited him on his return from the itiLk tnneral? Nothing short of an ejectment process, request- him Vg him to give up the home he had himself created, and himself and his wife and daughters to go out upon ":,_le roadside. Only the other day the sheriff's agent and Zni.e bailiff of the estate visited him at any early hour of he morning and threw him with his family out on the • inadside, (" Shame.) That was only one of the many „ 'lastanees of what the people of Ireland had to put up With. In view of such occurrences he certainly thought !'t was not asking too much of English Liberals to do all la their power to try and remedy such a state of affairs, .litl allow the Irish that justice which they in England Insisted upon having. (Cheers.) It was often stated by lr. Balfour and the Tories that the people of Ireland ired under the same laws as the people of England, 0 doubt the law was the same,but how differently it was a; deninistered ! There was no more analogy between the t.tritninistration of the law in Ireland and in England '1,13n there was between the north and south poles. It Was the administration they had to complain of, and ~.. Z9iild complain of and fight against until they had it elllied out, and until they were allowed that right which v.erY free people ought to be allowed—the right to ad- Ic , mister their own laws. (Hear, hear.) From what he 'lad told them the audience would understand how the teople were treated in Ireland and the sufferings they had endured for some years past. They never would iave endured it so tamely or submissively were it not or the hope held out to them by the English Liberals ad their leader, that Grand Old Man Mr. Gladstone. ~.n heers.) They all turned to him. They believed he thealid redeem the pledges he had made them, and that ;jay of their deliverance was at hand. (Cheers.) t ' ll'ilt% Roche) was confident that the battle would be tght on the coming register, and he asked them to V . ae advantage of their opportunity and strike a blow tfainst coercion. (Cheers.) The Irish wanted nothing th ileearation. All they required -was liberty to make veil' own laws and to administer them. That surely has not much, and he asked the English people to allow etthem. If they did they might rest assured that instead ikoeParation they would create a bond of friendship 0 union between Ireland and England which centuries tied c . cr enturies of coercion could never dream or think of elting. (Loud cheers.) 4r. T. B. KIERNAN proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. „ elle for his address. He did not want to be locked for aiding and abetting one of Balfour's criminals, but of 0 was in Ireland he should be locked up for an offence „,....itilat kind. (Laughter.) He hoped. that every Irish Zit,,_ would take to heart the appeal made to them that rt' (Cheers.) I itie`•drelincillor FLEMING seconded the proposition, mad corn- e,em",•cl upon the necessity of keeping the register as „yiete as possible. • 110cAne motion having been carried with applause, Mr. Ul%4' briefly responded, and then proposed a vote of IN“ 8 to the Chairman. tar. GORNALL seconded this proposition, as an English ece ..c,a,t, with pleasure, and said that he should like to ec„ une time soon come when Warrington would be tilt:resented by a man who had at heart the interests of hi; People, and not one like the present, who did all in ?Ywer to trifle with the interests of the country, and Well n.,5 engaged in a traffic that was adverse to the l'elug of the town. te 4de vote having been heartily accorded, the meeting rminated.

div.head: CAPTAIN AND FOUR. MEN LOST.
div.p: CAPTAIN AND FOUR. MEN LOST.

The iron barque Inchcape Rock, 1,454 tons, belonging to Messrs. Comfort and Co., Glasgow, arrived at Queens- town on Sunday morning in a battered condition from San Francisco, in charge of Mr. Carson, chief officer, who reports the loss of Captain Armour, three seamen, and the steward, which occurred on the 12th and 13th April dur- ing a westerly hurricane. The vessel lay on her beam ends for sixty hours, the cargo having shifted. The steward, Robert Baird, of Dundee, was killed in the calm by a tremendous rush of water which wrecked the cabin.

div.head: COBDEN CLUB AfFETIN G.
div.p: COBDEN CLUB AfFETIN G.

The annual general meeting of the Cobden Club was held on Saturday, in the Council room of the National Liberal Club, Whitehall-place. Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., hon. secretary, presided. The report of the year's pro- ceedings stated that the foremost question which had occupied the attention of the Committee was the Sugar Bounties Convention. They ventured to think that the state of feeling in the public mind antagonistic to the ratification of that Convention had been largely due to the efforts made by the Cobden Club. The Chairman, in the course of a briet address, said the Cobden Club had now entered upon the twenty-fifth year of its existence. —Mr. Medley moved the adoption of the report, which, having been duly seconded, was carried unanimously.— Several other speakers addressed the meeting :and the proceedings closed in the usual manner.

div.head: KENTISH TOWN MURDER.
div.p: THE KENTISH TOWN MURDER.
A REPRIEVE,.

Mr. Freaks Palmer, the solicitor for the defence in the case of Thomas Harding, the Kentish Town murderer, has received the following letter from the Home Secre- tary :—" Whitehall, July 11th. Sir,—l am directed by the Secretary of State to acquaint you with reference to the petition which you submitted in favour of Thomas Harding, who was sentenced to death, that he has had this case under his consideration, and that he has felt warranted, under all the circumstances, in advising her Majesty to respite the capital sentence with a view to its commutation to penal servitude for life.—l am, &c. CHARLES S. MURDOCH, for the Under-Secretary." Harding was convicted of murdering FlOrence Varley, daughter of the proprietor of the ,Victory, public. house, Clarence-road, Kentish Town, on May '2lst, by shooting her.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. Ratcliffe, Hub- bert, Smith, Mather, Clarke, Turton, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Jolley, Gill, Owen, Dobson, Hood- Wright, 'P. Jones, Heaton, Davies, D. Jones; S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Pad- gate Schools). _ _

PAUPER PATIENTS AT TUE INFIRMARY. The thuramAx referring to his statement at the pre- vious meeting with regard to the admission of pauper patients to Warrington Infirmary, said the gentleman connected with the Infirmary whom he had consulted was Alderman Davies and not Major Litton, as some of the reports had mentioned.

div.head: INCREASE OF LUNACY.
div.p: THE INCREASE OF LUNACY.

The AssisvANT CLERK mentioned that for some time past there had been a continuous increase in the number of lunatics in the Union, and during the quarter just passed there had been an expenditure in regard to lunatics of £l2B in excess of the sum paid in the corres- ponding quarter of last year. This increased expendi- ture was entirely due to the increase in the number of lunatics, as he might safely say, taking the asylums all round, that there had been a reduction in the charges.— The CHAIRMAN said the increase might arise from the fact that people were now taken to the asylums who were formerly left at the Workhouse.—The ASSISTANT CLERK said that no doubt accounted for a few of the cases, but the increase was not materially affected by it. They had been sending lunatics to the asylums by the score, some- times two and three in a week.—Mr. CLARKE said the increase in lunacy had taken place all through the coun- try. This year was commenced with 1,727 cases over last year.—Mr. WARD said there were 21 imbeciles in the Workhouse just now.—The subject then dropped.

div.p: GIFTS.

Mr, MINES reported that " The life of the Queen of England," in four volumes, had been presented to the Padgate Industrial schools, by Mr. W. B. Roberts, of NVilderspool Causeway ; and The History of Europe," in five volumes, by Mr. Salmon, of Lovely-lane. Gifts of books for the library, and pictures for the rooms, would, headded, be very much appreciated.

THE SCHOOL BAND. The Padgate Schools Committee recommended that the School band be allowed to "go to Stockton Heath on the occasion of the Walking Day there. The Committee also recommended the purchase of twenty new band instru- ments from Messrs. Ingham and Company, Manchester, for the sum of £52 6s. The relief cases were then taken.

div.head: ORANGE CELEBRATION AT HALTON
div.p: ORANGE CELEBRATION AT HALTON
CASTLE.

The annual picnic in which the Orange body of Liver- pool are wont to indAlge to commemorate the victory of their hero, King William 111., took place on Monday, in- stead of on Saturday, the 12th inst., the spot chosen for the event being Halton Castle, near Runcorn. There were about 3,000 men, women, and children present, re- presenting in all seventy lodges. This body of excur- sionists left Lime-st. early on Monday morning, and at eleven o'clock they started to march from Runcorn to Halton Castle, to the "music," of a dozen bands, and with the embellishments of an almost innumerable num- ber of banners of the most pronounced and glaring hues. The procession was led by a carriage, in which were Messrs. Harry Thomas, G.T. ; W. Touchstone, G.S. ; W. Shaw, D.G.M. ; R. Murray, D.G.M. ; J. Lynch, P.G.S. ; Q. Y. Lawson, D.G.S. ; W. Gilbert, D.P.G.M. : T. R. Connell, and Platt. Upon the arrival of the party at Halton Castle, the procession broke up, and vanous spoits and games were entered into. In the afternoon a meeting was held in a ficld near the Castle, and in the evening all that was left of the original procession re- formed and walked back to Runcorn Station. At the meeting which was held in the afternoon,Mr. 11. Gilbert presided, and others present were Colonel Sandys, M.P., Mr. T. B. Hoyden, M.P., Mr. Thomas M'Cracken, and Mr. J. Thompson. Mr. Touchstone first moved a resolution, expressing "time thankfulness of those present in participating in the anniversary of the battle of the Boyne, when the great, glorious, and immortal Prince William of Orange delivered their fathers from Popish thraldom, and handed down the priceless heritage of civil and religious liberty, and they pledged themselves, by God's help, to maintain those priceless privileges by all lawful means." Mr. T. M‘Cracken, in seconding the resolUtion, said they were in critical times at present. The Orange body must remember that they belonged to the Constitutional party; they were Conservatives, for a man could not be an Orangeman if he was a Radical. Colonel Sandys, M.P., in supporting the resolution,said they had assembled that day to commemorate the Battle of the Boyne, where the English people settled once and for all the question whether the Government of the country should be that of the Pope of Rome and that Was the question which was at issue at die present time. (Applause.) The questions to which he had referred ought to be taught to the children in schools, but they were not, because in this country people were so desperate afraid of injuring the feelings of Roman ' Catholics that they dared not teach their children the lessons of English history. (Applause.) At the battle the question of Protestant ascendancy was settled, but they had to look whether those principles for which their forefathers fought and died were kept intact. They were not, and he was sorry to see it; but what they had got to do was to see that they kept what they had got, and that their opponents did not take any more from them (loud applause.) Two hundred years ago the patriots had surrounded the Protestant Constitution with a triple rampart ' • they said that the Sovereign should be Protes- tant, and that there should be a Protestant Legislature and a Protestant electorate. He was glad to say that the first rampart still remained ; hut was it the case with the second and third rampart (" No no ") ? If they swept away the rampart of a Protestant electorate, he did not see how they could restore the rampart of a ProtestantiLegislature. Much rested, however, upon the electors themselves, who would have an opportunity of speaking before twelve months were out to say whether or not the men who were to represent them in Parlia- ment should be those who upheld the Protestant princi- ples, such as those upheld by the Orange Order, before they elected them to Parliament. (Applause.) Those were the men they ought to elect, and they ought to ask whether a man was a Protestant first and a party man afterwards. (Applause.) He said the time had come when they ought not to allow a man to represent them in Parliament unless he would pledge himself to main- tam the Protestant Constitution. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and was unanimously adopted. Councillor A. H. Holme next moved a resolution ex- pressing confidence in the Government, and this was seconded by Mr. Harry Thomas. Mr. '. B. Boyden, M.P., in supporting, apologised for the absence of the other local Conservative members, and said that, beset as the Government were with obstruction, which had lowered the dignity of the house, they were unable to attend. He could assure them, however, that they all had the glorious Protestant cause at heart. (Applause.) In their course of obstruction the Opposi- tion cared nothing whatever for the benefits a measure proposed would confer on the country or on the working classes. All they sought was to prevent the Government passing useful measures •, but when the Conservatives asked again for the confidence of the people they would be able-to say that the Government had passed many useful measures in spite of this desperate obstruction. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was afterwards adopted, and upon a vote of thanks to the chairman being carried, the meeting broke up.

div.head: Ettttrs to the Odor.
div.p: Ettttrs to the Odor.
LOCAL VOLUNTEERS AT BISLEY.

--- Sir,—As an old subscriber to the Volunteer Prize Shooting List, can you give me any information whyl the best shots have not been sent to represent our local regiment at Bisley this year? Is it true they have sent men to represent them, who, at the competition at Altcar for places to Bisley, scored 61 points below those they re- fused to send? And is it true they have sent one that could not make 40 points out of 80, 2nd Class, before they would send marksmen? Is it also true they paid eight entrances for the Queen's and St. George's, and went hawking the tickets about before they would send the good shots, and they could only find five to g.? What have they done with the other three tickets ? Yours truly, Horsemarket-st., July 18th, 1890.

div.head: INQUISITIVE.
div.p: INQUISITIVE.

THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS' ELECTION. Sir,—ln view of the forthcoming election of Newton Commissioners, I think it only fair to the ratepayers that they should know how the three retiring Commissioners have attended to their duties during the past three years. Let the Surveyor prepare a statement showing the aver- age number of attendances made each year at the fu I Board, and also in Committee, and this table of atten- dances, could, with advantage, be placed in view of all who enter the Town Hall, on Wednesday next, to record their votes. It is important that we should have men to represent us who attend to their duties regularly, and not "when fancy pleases "or " pleasure calls." I bring this matter under your notice because I am given to understand that two out of the three retiring Commissioners have not attended.one-half the meetings .they ought to have done. —I am yours truly, Earle,stown, July 14th, 1890.
A CITIZEN.

FLOWERS IN CHURCHES. Sir,—At Runcorn Parish Church a small company of ladies possessing more money than sense, i.e., sense of the teaching of the Church of England and the New Testament (see Articles six and thirty-five) are subscrib- ing three pence per week to buy flowers to fill the vases over the communion table. We read that the Church o England requires her flock "To believe only what can be proved from the Scriptures." I read therein that " God is to be worshipped in spirit and in truth," not with flowers, and that bread, wine, and water are the only symbols or emblems Christ left to His church, the two former to keep us mindful of His Passion. Water emblematical of the believer's new birth (not infant sprinkling). Not a word about adorning the chancel with flowers. The Article thirty-five, mostly composed by Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and Jewell, says "We know that now in the time of clear light of Jesus Christ the Son of G.el, all shadows, figures, and significations are utterly gone, all vain and unprofitable ceremonies both Jewish and heathenish, fully abolished ; and therefore our churches are not set up for figures and significations cf Messiahs and Christ to come, but for other godly and and neces- sary purposes." These men could see a little further than Vicar Wood,and they would now no doubt pronounce deckinr, of churches with flowers unprofitable. Perhaps he will be able to explain the meaning of this waste on his return from the land of pomp and ritual. The saintly Bishop Beveridge, of St. Asaph, said, ."For my own part, I know not how anything should be worthy of God's accepting, that is not of God's commanding." Well might Bishop Calfield ask "Who required these things at your hands ?" Are there no waifs for whom this probably five shillings per week could be laid out on education, or sick ones to whom kind relief could be rendered, or ragged ones to cover? We are, alas! tra- velling backward, not forward. "The holiness of beauty is the modern substitute for the beauty of holiness—the sacraments for Christ, the clergy being looked upon as a sacredotal rather than a ministerial order." Follow the example of the noble Bereans, and submit the practices and preaching of these men to the test of the BIBLE. Runcorn, July 16th, 1890.

div.head: GLIMPSE AT IRELAND'S HISTORY SINCE
div.p: A GLIMPSE AT IRELAND'S HISTORY SINCE

Sir,—l ask your kind permission to put this letter in next week's "Examiner." All Ireland was confiscated. Under Elizabeth one million acres had been taken away; under Cromwell three millions additional, and under William eight millions. Nearly twelve million acres had been taken, and there did not remain a single Catholic proprietor on Ireland's land. They were allowed to expatriate themselves—forty thousand Irish soldiers were allowed to join the armies of France and Spain. The able-bodied men were encouraged to leave; the young people had &en kidnapped to the Barbadoes Island. Now what was the conduct of England with regard to that land ? Scotland has become a prosperous land by the union. Scotland was united to England in 1707. Hence many people, have argued that since the Scotch could gain by Union the Irish could have gained also. Let us see what was given to the Scotch, and what was given to the Irish. I now wish to show how unjust England was to Ireland. She might make Ireland a peaceful and prosperous country, and we to-day would net recall these harrowing scenes. They would have been forgotten, because we are living in days of prosperity, and would not like to go back to misery. Things were granted to Scotland that enabled that land to rise. Even Scotch historians admit that, up to the time of the Union, Scotland was far behind Ireland; her land was much less fruitful; her people were more ignorant. Scotland was a land where dissension and czvil war and blood shed were far more common than in Ireland, yet Scotland rose out of all that misery to become a great country. And how? First, because the church of the people was recognised in the Union as the established church of the land. The kirk of Scotland became the Established Church of Scotland, and so the people, identified with their national church and guided by it, had no bitter memories to call up. There were no persecutions except of the Episcopalians. In Ireland it was the very contrary. The church of the majority was crushed to the ground. Nine-tenths of the Irish people were Catholics, yet the Catholic Church was banned and her priests were taken from her. Her abbeys were ruined ; her churches despoiled; and her people threa- tened with the penalty of a felon if they should listen tol a priest of their faith. The result was that the church had to hide as in the early days of Christendom. The priests had to go into the bogs, and that church, that might have directed the Irish nation was not allowed to bringher civilising influence upon the immense majority of the people that believed in her. Consequently the people who loved the Church were obliged to hate thel Law that banned that Church. Their consciences that obliged them to submit to the Catholic Church made them ' feel that the law that banned that Church should not be obeyed. Naturally they grew up to hate the Govern- ment that banned their Church. The Church of one- tenth of the people was made the Established Church, and to that minority all the property of the Catholic Church was handed over. Foreign Bishops were given to them. The people did not recognise these Bishops. There were actually Bishops of Ireland who never saw their diocoses in a score of years, yet they drew from the starving poor people—from the nine-tenths that were crushed to the earth—their tithes and income, and all - ' went to England. The next thing was that parochial schools were estab- lished in scotland and her people were educated. The Scotch people had not to sacrifice conscience when they went to the Scotch school. Hence young Scotchmen soon found places of every position in life. They rose in their own land, and they rose in foreign lands, because they had education. With the Irish people it was differ- cnt. No schools were allowed in all Ireland. It was felony to keep a school—Ave pounds for the head of a schoolmaster and for the head 0 a priest. Not only were they forbidden to have Catholic schools in Ireland, hut the people were forbidden to send their children to France or elsewhere to be educated. The Catholic who sent his child abroad forfeited all claims to his property and to his child, and the child lost all claims to any in- heritance. This las sad subject. The historian tells us that, even as late as 1809, he maw an old Isisbman

pass one of the charter schools in Dublin and call down terrible maledictions upon it. The third matter by which Scotland was benefited was in the land laws. There was no new race of landlords put over the Scotch people. In Ireland all the old land- lords were rooted out, and a new race was set over the people, with no bond of sympathy between the two. 1 They came as enemies to the Irish people. They treated ' them as such, and the slavery introduced by Irish land- lords has never been surpassed for cruelty and horror by that of the Pashas of the Turks over the eastern Christians. No slaveholders in the south of America ever dared to perpetrate the atrocities on their slaves that the Irish landlords considered themselves perfectly free to adopt against their Irish tenants. The power of the landlords continues to the present day. They can :still evict and disposess and throw out to die on the road side their poor tenants, and the law has very little 'to say against them. In old days the power of the land- lord even extended to the households of the tenants ; and historians tell us that the landlord considered him- self entitled to even send for the wite or daughter of his tenant. It was the father of a girl that had been ruinsl by Lord Leitrim that caused that landlord's death. Finally, Scotland gained by the Union because she entered at once into a full equality of commercial privi- leges. She was allowed to trade with England and with the colonies, and Scotland grew prosperous. Scotch merchants had their ships in every sea, whereas every effort was made to crush out any attempt of the Irish people to enrich themselves in trade or manufacturing of any kind. The cattle trade that was so profitable in Ireland had been destroyed by English law. The Irish people started into the woollen• industry. In this they prospered for many years, until in 1698 a law was passed prohibiting the manufacture of woollen fabrics because it hurt the trade of England. 'rwo years after the passage of this law,there were 30,000 paupers in the streets of Dublin who had been woollen weavers, and famine followed famine; scarcely a year passed when there was not a famine. , These famines did not come from accident or from thel visitation of Providence, but from the operation of British law. In the famine of 1741, out of a population of a million and a half, it was said that about 400.000 perished for want of food. When the first gun was fired at Bunker's Hill, the spirit of liberty leaped up once more in the Irish breast. Grattan came to the front, and an Irish Parliament was established. It was said even now, that Ireland was insatiable, that she was always demanding some- thing. Grattan had answered that, a hundred years ago by saying that Ireland asked for nothing but what England had robbed her of, and Grattan won Independ- ence one hundred years ago, and for nearly eighteen years Ireland governed herself as she has a right to do tp-day. Though that Parliament was not a perfect one, yet during eighteen years it made Ireland prosperous. That Protestant Parliament gave freedom to Catholics. It opened Universities to Catholics. It intended to emancipate Ireland; but England, seeing that Ireland was becoming too prosperous, fomented the rebellion of 1793.

We have had a Union for a long number of years and now we can ask the testimony of the world whether the prediction of Grattan has not been fulfilled. Ireland has been crushed worse than before. What has Ireland gained by the Union? Her commerce was destroyed, her cities have gone down, her population has dwindled. We look over Ireland, and her plains are deserted, her sons and daughters are banished by cruel and wicked landlords, and still the British Government aids those landlords. Nothing will satisfy the Irish people but Home Rule, led on by Mr. W. E. Gladstone and his party. Home Rule for Ireland is therefore our motto. I remain yours &c.,
PHILIP O'BRIEN. 38, Naylor-st., Warrington, July 15th, 1890.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
DAMAGING PROPERTY AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. Brundrit and Dr. Steele, at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Riley, John Gilligan, Isaac Bothwell, Samuel Green, Ernest Bentley, and Robert Jones, boys, were charged with damaging the property of the executors of the late Mr. T. A. Walker, contrac- tor to the Ship Canal Company. The defendants pleaded guilty.—Mr. A. Linaker, prosecuted.—P.C. Boyle said on the 2nd July at 5 p.m. he was on duty on the Ship Canal railway opposite the Belvedere when he saw the defendants interfering with a stack of new bricks there. They had made" houses" of the bricks, and had thrown many on the metals in such a way as to bo a danger to the trains passing along. Many of the bricks were smashed.—Mr. Linaker said the damage and annoyance caused by boys such as the defendants, had become so great tlAt the contractors felt ccmpelled to take pro- ceedings to put a stop to it. They did not wish to punish the defendants severely but to inflict such a penalty as would deter them and others from future de- predations.--Mr. Brundrit severely reprimanded the defendants and ordered each to pay 4s. 6d. costs. He pointed out that they had rendered themselves liable to A fine of £S, and that any future offenders would be severely dealt with.

div.head: NATIONAL RIFLE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: NATIONAL RIFLE ASSOCIATION.
THE BISLEY MEETING.

The first meeting held by the National Rifle Association at Risley was inaugurated, on Saturday, by the Prince and Princess of Wales, who proceeded thither by special train, with the Princesses Victoria and Maud, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, and the Duchess of Edin- burgh. The Princess fired a shot at the five hundred yards range, the rifle having been sighted by Sir H. Halford, and hit the bull's eye. Lord %Vantage then I presented her Royal Highness with the Gold Medal of the Association. After inspecting the targets and the camp, the Royal party returned to town. The shooting proper commenced on Monday with the Alexandra competition. The first day's meeting on the new ground was quite as successful as the most sanguine official could have expected. At the meeting at Risley, on Tuesday, the first stage of the competition for the Queen's Priro was entered upon.l The top scorers so far are Captain Pergusson, of the In- , verness Rifles and Lieutenant Wakeman, of the let Wilts,who made 34 each. In the " Graphic " competition, which is shot from the standing position, Major R. Wil- liamson, of Oxford, succeeded In scoring within one of the highest possible. On Wednesday the meeting was again favoured with fine weather, and shooting was well up to the average. The principal competition was the Queen's, the range being 500 yards. In the evening it was found that Lieut. Atkinson, 3 V.B. Durham Light Infantry headed the list with a total of 67, having made 33 on Tuesday, and 34 on Wednesday. Sergeant Mackenzie, 4th V.B. Scots; and Private McLachlan, Bth La nark,tied for second place, with 66. In" The Daily Graphic " competition at 200 yards, seven competitors made 34 each; and at 500 yard twenty scored the highest possible. THE QUEEN'S PRIZE. The competition in the first stage of the Queen's Prize, 600 yards was completed on Thursday, and resulted in a tie between Corporal M'Lachlan (3rd Highland Light Infantry), Lance-Corporal Fletcher (3rd Hants), and Corporal Wellington (2nd Manchester), their aggregates being 98 each. THE ST. GEORGE'S COMPETITION. , In the St. George's competition at Bisley, yesterday, Corporal Scott, of the Border Rifles, and Captain Gibb, lof the Bristol Engineers, tied for first place with high- est possible score and tie shots totalling fourteen, Private Fisher, 2nd Welsh, comes third, and Sergeant Holies, Ist Somerset, fourth. The ties will be shot off to-day.
