div.head: COUNT KILLED.
div.p: A COUNT KILLED.

- - - 13Baux, Taunsnex.—Count Conrad Stolberg, while wild duck shooting yesterday, was accidentally shot, and sustained such injuries that he died almost immediately. Count Conrad was only eighteen years of age, and was the son and heir of Count Stolberg, Werni- gerode, one of the wealthiest of the noble land propne- tars in Germany.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1890
LYIIII.

ROOFING THE TowEn.--The work of putting the roof On the new tower is being proceeded with, and a flag pole 45 feet long has been erected. GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—The result of the South Kensing- ton examinations in mathematics shows that the students of the Lyn-1m Grammar School have passed 100 per cent., all in the first class. _ _

OUGHT-MSG-TON CHIIRCH. - The Rev. J. Edwardes- Evans, master of the Lymm Grammar School, occupied the pulpit of Oughtrington Church, on Sunday, and will act as locum tenens until the second week in Angust, when the Rector, the Rev. NV. G Knocker, returns from his holidays in the south of England. SPECIAL MEETING OF THE LOCAL BOARD.—A specia meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, Mr. Cameron presiding. There were also present Messrs. Daniel Rogers, Hugh Harrison, James Gibbon, Frederick Swallow, William Mullard (clerk)., and Charles Severs (gas manager). The chief business was to sign a cheque for Messrs. Tattersall, of Elland, for the new purifiers at the gas works.—The Gas Manager reported that the purifiers were now in working order, though there, as yet, had not been much time to test whether they had been properly put together.—A cheque on account was signed. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.-At the Sale Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. R. H. Joynson and other magistrates, Thomas Davies, of Sandy-lane, Lymm, was charged with travelling on the London and North. Western Railway, between Oxford-road and Heatley, on the 15th June.—Mr. Fenna represented the Railway Company. Defendant pleaded guilty.—lt was stated that the defendant was seen at the Oxford-road Station, Manchester, on Sunday evening, about 6.15. The station- master of Heatley was on the platform, and watched the defendant, who was seen to get into the 6.40 London and North-Western train. The stationmaster got into the same train. When the train arrived at Heatley, de- fendant was seen by the stationmaster to go to the gate where the tickets were collected, and he told the collector that he had only come from Sale, and paid the fare from that place. Imme- diately after he had gone the stationmaster followed him, and told defendant he had come, from Oxford- road. He denied it, and the stationmaster said he was at Oxford-road and saw him get in the train. He then admitted the offence, and offered to pay the fare, which was refused. The Chairman said the case was similar to one already disposed of. It was evident that this thing had been going on for some time, else they would not have watched defendaut.—A fine of 20s. and 17s. 6d. costs was imposed.

div.head: WARRINGTON EXTEN-
div.p: THE WARRINGTON EXTEN-
SION, &c., BILL.

A report of the proceedings in regard to the War- rington Extension, Water, and Improvement Bill, I which has this week been befote a special Committee of the House of Commons, will be found on another page, but a few details as to what has been granted and refused by the Committee will be of interest to the public. With regard to the extension of the borough the Committee have allowed the clauses providing for extension on the northern side of the borough, in the limits of which in future part of Orford, Polley- lane, the barracks, and Longford works will be included. The proposed extension in the direc- tion of Liverpool-road and Sankey Bridges, where are situate the large works of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., is not, however, taken in. The Cheshire portions sought to be added, which were rejected by the Committee, include the mea- dows at Arpley and Appleton, Lower Walton, and part of Latchford. Among the clauses that have been left in the Bill is one providing for a re-ar- rangement of the wards, and their representajon ; and in regard to the purchase of the Water Works undertaking the promoters have secured an important concession. This is the suspension of the Sinking Fund for a period of five years, which practically means that the purchase can be effected without laying any burden at all upon the rates. In the case of the Gas Act, the suspension of the Sinking Fund was only for three years. The clause providing for the extension of the library rate is also passed. Power Is also given to extend the infectious diseases hospital, and to borrow money for the extension of the baths. Another portion of the Bill gives power to pur- chase gas annuities at the market price, instead of at 25 years' purchase. With regard to the with- drawal of the sanitary clauses, we understand that the Government are bringing in a Bill under which the Corporation will be enabled to obtain the powers originally sought for in the Bill.

div.head: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA.
div.p: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA.
WARRINGTON DISTRICT.

Another outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia having been discovered amongst the herd of cattle owned by Messrs. Bennett, of Bruche Farm, Padgate, the animal which was suffering was immediately slaughtered. Arrangement are, we understand, being made for the slaughter of 95 head of cattle with which the deseased animal had been in con- tact. It will be remembered that a previous out- break of pleuro-pneumonia on the same farm, a few weeks ago, resulted in the slaughter of 44 cattle.

_ An animal suffering from pleuro-pnemonia was, on Thursday, destroyed on the farm of Mr. Dean, the Poplars, Orford, and other two animals which bad been in contact with the diseased cow will also be slaughtered.
PLEURO-PNEUMONIA. IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, William ' Mercer, and Henry Mercer, of Marsh Gate Farm, Norton, were summoned for having, on the sth May, removed seven cows from Lancashire into Cheshire which are declared infected areas under the Con- tagious Diseases (Animals) Act without having a movement license.—P.C. Fryer proved the case, and the defendants pleaded ignorance on the subject.— Superintendent Large said the order had been in force since November last and over a hundred cattle had been slaughtered in Runcorn district within the past month.—Mr. Brundrit said this was a very serious matter and a stop must be put to the removal of cattle without the necessary authority. Persons engaged in business like the defendants ought to have known what they ought to do. A tine of 10s. and costs Bs. ad. was imposed upon each defendant.

div.head: LOWTON.
div.p: LOWTON.

On Friday an outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia occurred at Lovrton on the premises of Mr. Henry Marsh, farmer. One of the cows was found to be affected with the disease, and it was shot, after inspection by Mr. Harwell, veterin- ary surgeon, Leigh. The other cows, four in number. were ordered to be destroyed. An outbreak of the disease also occurred on the farm of Mr. James Boardman, of Kenyon Hall Farm, Kenyon, and a bullock purchased from Mr. Bennett, of Padgate, about two months ago, was shot on Sunday. The re- maining eight cattle had to be slaughtered.
WIFE DESERNON BY A ST. HELENS EX-COUN CILLOII. A MONTH IN GAOL.

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Friday, William John Kirkham, ex-town councillor of St. Helens, was charged in custody with deserting his children. Mr. J. O. Swift, who prosecuted, stated that the prisoner was arrested on a warrant issued by the guardians of the Prescot Union, for deserting three children in October, 1888, since which period they had been chargeable to the union. Kirkham formerly carried on business as an auctioneer at St. Helens, and was reported to have absconded to America, but had for some time carried on business under the name of Dalton at Sunderland. Mr. Bar- ton, relieving officer, said .£5O had been expended on the relief of the prisoner's children.—Mr. Riley, who defended, said when the prisoner went away he left sufficient money and clothing with friends to keep the children. The case was the result of vindictive action by the prisoner's wife, between whom and Kirkham there had been divorce proceed- ings, in which prisoner was successful.—The Bench remanded Kirkham. On Friday, at the Woolton Petty Sessions, before Mr. J. Bingham (chairman), and Major Gaskell, the charge preferred by the Prescot Board of Guar- dians against William Kirkham, an ex-town coun- cillor of St. Helens, came up for hearing, the prisoner being charged, on remand from l'rescot, with haying deserted his wife and family, thereby leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union Workhouse. The case for the prosecu- tion was conducted by Mr. J. V. Swift, the prisoner' being defended by Dlr. H. L. Riley. lr. J. P. Mearns watched the case on behalf of Mrs. Kirkham.— The prisoner on being charged said, "I am advised to plead guilty."—The Clerk: We don't know anything about your advice. Are you guilty or not guilty?— Prisoner : I plead guilty.—Mr. Swift, in stating the case for the prosecution, said that he was instructed by the guardians to prosecute the prisoner under the vagrancy act, which provided that any person running away and leaving his wife and family should be punishable as a rogue and a vagabond, the penalty prescribed being im- prisonment for a term not exceeding three months witk or without hard labour. Up to Septe:nber, 1888, the prisoner had lived in St. Helens, where he had carried on business as an auctioneer. As a result of divorce proceedings, he and his wife had separated. He had then in his house a lady who was considered to be the housekeeper, and there also lived with him his eldest daughter—a girl of 14 or 15—and three younger children—toys. About thetime mentioned the prisoner and his housekeeper, Miss Adamson, an- nounced their intention of leaving St. Helens for a short holiday. They went away, taking the eldest girl with them, and leaving the other children in the care of the servant. They also left a good many people interested in their whereabouts. Nothing was heard of them, until the 10th of this month, when the prisoner was discovered in Sunderland and was taken into custody under a war- rant which was issued shortly after he left St. Helens. The parish had continued to maintain the prisoner's family from 9th October, 1888, up to the present time, the cost incurred in their maintenance having been about £5O. Mr. Riley having addressed the court for the defence, the Chairman, after a short consultation with his brother magistrate, said—We will take as lenient a view of this matter as possible, but we have come to the oonclusion that the prisoner must go to gaol for a month with hard labour. Kirkhara:was weep- ing bitterly while the case was proceeding, and he was so deeply affected that he turned his back on the court, and stood facing the wall with his handkerchief to his eyes.
The United Methodist Free Church Conference, sitting at Leeds. decided, on Wednesday, to raise a fund of £12,000 for aggressive missionary operations at home and abroad.

SCHOOL TRE AT AT STOCKTON HEATH. Yesterday was what is observed in Stockton Heath as the annual Walking Day. The scholars attending. St. Thomas's Church, to the number of about 500, attended service in the church early in the afternoon, and afterwards marched in procession round the village, headed by the Padgate Industrial school band. They then had tea at the schools, after which they proceeded to a field near Wilderspool brewery which was lent by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. Unfortunately, rain began to fall during the afternoon, and completely spoiled the out-door enjoyment of the children. They had, however. some consolation on each receiving a bag con- raining sweets and nuts. Those who principally had charge of the treat arrangements were Mr. William Butterworth. superintendent; Miss Badde- ley, superintendent of the girls' school ! Miss fib- ' hert, superintendent of the infants' school; and Mr. W. James headmaster of the day school. The ser- vice at the church wa.s conducted by the Rev. C. J. Rolfe.

div.head: AMBULANCE CLASS.
div.p: AMBULANCE CLASS.

At a meeting held on Thursday evening, in the Lymm Grammar School, the certificates and badges of the St. John's Ambulance Association were distributed to those who passed at the examination held in April, in what is called "The first aid to the injured class." The chair was occupied by the Rev. G. W. Guest, rector, and the distribution was undertaken by Mr. C. Lister C.C. There were also present Miss Fox, Mrs. Dr. William- son, Mrs. Addenbrooke, Mrs, Masters, Miss Brown, i Mrs. Lister, Mrs. Edwardes-Evans, and Miss Hard- man.—The Chairman incidentally mentioned that during the last few months there had been a class held in that room in connection with South Kensington and all the boys who sat for that examination had passed. That he thought might be a stimulus to other young men in the neighbourhood. It was Mr. Evans' intention to organise similar classes during the coming winter, and if this were generally known he thought they might have a larger number of members than last winter. He named that because he wished the neighbourhood to be benefited as much as possible by such classes.—Mr. Lister said that a class like that was formed to ameliorate suffering. They were informed that in England there were 1,000 drowned every year and 1,000 killed on the railway, with a corresponding number in Scotland and Wales, so that the necessity for such classes was evi- dent. In Manchester Infirmary there were about 41,300 cases treated in a year, and something like 5,360 serious accidents. What,then,must it be in more populous places? They could not but say that the signs of the tunes were promising, and if he met with an accident in this neighbourhood he should like to come under the hands of one of the ladies present. (Laughter.) He was glad to see two of the police force present. He had a report from the Chief Constable stating that since he gave permission to the officers to become members of the St. John's Ambulance Association, 183 had undergone instruction, and out of these 168 had passed. (Applause.) There were now 215 members of the police force of this county who held certificates out of a total force of 376. jApplause.) That was very pleasing to the magistrates and they would be asked for permission for the officers to wear badges on their arms. Mr. Lister then presented the certificates.—Mr. C. E. Ardern proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Fox for the part she took in connection with the classes, and also with the nursing classes, which was seconded by Mr. Jones, and heartily carried.—The Rev. Edwardes-Evans then pre- sented a handsome riding cup to Dr. Williamson for the voluntary services rendered by him to the class.—Dr. Williamson responded and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Lister for making the presentations.

div.head: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
YESTERDAY.—Before C. Lister, Mr. H. Stanton, and
Dr. Braba.zon.

DRIINKENNESI.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—John Kilcannon. at Lymm, on the 28th ult., ordered to pay the costs, 4s. 6d.; Joseph Whitehead, at Lyinm, dismissed on payment of costs, 45. 6d.; and Pat Mitchell, at Lymm, on the 13th inst., fined ss. and costs.
BAD LANGUAGE.—For the offence of using obscene language in the streets at Lymm, Eunice Asprey, Thos. Jury, and Margaret Buxton, were each fined Is. and costs.

CARE r.Ess DRIVER. —Thomas Baskerville, for riding in a lurry without using reins, at High Legh, on the 2nd inst., was cautioned and dismissed. THE DOGS' ORDER.—Edward Clarke was summoned for allowing a dog to be at large unmuzzled, and was fined ss. including costs. Thomas Brundritt and Arthur Bomphrey, for similar offences, were also each ordered to pay Sc., including costs. THE Onsynnc•rioN QuEsTioN.—Samuel Silcock, of Warrington, was summoned on three informations for having, on the 29th, 30th, and 31st. May, obstructed the free passage of the highway at Lvmm by erecting swings, poles, and ° a cocoa-nut sheet. Mr. Ridgway, law-clerk to the Lymm Local Board, conducted the prosecutioa, the intention of which was, he said, to have it made clear to the public that the land near the Cross, in the centre of the village, was a highway. He stated that the land had benn used by the public for a long period, and in 1866 it was paved by the Local Board. No claim had been made by any lord of the manor to the use of the land, and he submitted that if such a claim were to be now made the lord of the manor would only be entitled to mineral rights under the land. The Chairman said that the Bench were satisfied that the land was part of the public highway, and Mr. Ridgway then called evidence as to the obstructions. He also in- formed the Bench that a memorial had been submitted ! to the Board complaining of the obstructions near the Cross. The Chairman said that the magkrates were Prepared to declare the road a highway, under the con- trol of the Board, but they should only inflict a nominal penalty of is., and costs.

AILLGED Ctinsury TO A Cow.—John Harrison Warren farmer, Bollington, was summoned for having ill-treated a cow by allowing it to be overstocked with milk. On the 4th of June Sergeant Cook watched two cows belong- ing to the defendant, to see that they were not removed from a field in contravention of the pleuro-pneumonia regulations. He commenced his watch at five o'clock in the afternoon, and kept it up until three o'clock next morning. During the time so occupied the mulch cow in question appeared to be in great pain, and bellowed con- stantly. Its udder was hard and full, and very much inflamed. At three o'clock in the morning he knocked the defendant up and the cow was milked. The defend- ant, who asked why the sergeant let the cow remain in pain all night without informing him sooner, was fined Is., and the costs, which were heavy.

div.head: LADY CP=IIEI7E-RS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE LADY CP=IIEI7E-RS AT WARRINGTON.

Warrington was visited on Saturday by the team! of lady cricketers who are touring the country. The afternoon's game on the Arpley cricket ground was spoiled by wretched weather,, but play was continued until the score had reached 48 for the loss of seven wickets. There was a considerable attend- ance of spectators, and the general opinion was that the ladies were not bad players, though the novelty of the performance and not the cricket was undoubtedly the chief attraction. It: the evening the lady cricketers gave an entertainment in the Public Hall before a large audience. The entertain- ment opened with musical drill and barbell exer- cises, which were well executed. Subsequently Mr. M'Anney went through some cycling manceuvres, and Ondah's pupils gave a gymnastic performance on the rings. There were also some exhibitions of fencing and the singing of comic and sentimental songs. THE NEW RECTOR OF WINWICK. _

The Re; Canon Penrhyn, late of Iluvton, offici- ated on Sunday in Winwick Church, of which he was lately appointed vicar in succession to the late Canon Hopwood. The rev. gentleman "read him- self in" in the forenoon, and in the afternoon preached a short sermon from Romans 6, v. xi. In the course of it, Canon Penrhyn said he did not feel as if he were coming among them as a stranger among strangers,. but rather as returning among men and the children of men amongst whom he laboured as a curate some thirty years ago. A generation had passed away since then, and pro- bably few of those present could recollect when he was there as curate. Canon Penrhyn concluded with a fitting reference to the memory of the late rector, and with a fervent appeal for the hearty and prayerful co-operation of the congregation. Arrangements are being made to place a stained- [glass window at the west end of the south aisle of the church to the memory of Canon Hopwood, the late rector.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR ACTON BRIDGE.

On Monday night, the engine of one of the trains running from Crewe to Liverpool ran off the rails near Acton Bridge. The main up-line to the north was fouled for some hours and traffic dislocated. No one was hurt. A break-down gang from Crewe arrived and repaired the damage.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, LA.TCHFORD. On Sunday afternoon and evening, the Rev. R. Hall, of Burnley, preached the annual sermons in Wash-lane Baptist Chapel. Special hymns were used, and two anthems sung by the choir. The con- gregations were large, and the collections, which were in aid of the chapel funds, realized £2l 3s. 6tl.

div.head: _ LATCHFORD WESLRYA.N SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: _ LATCHFORD WESLRYA.N SUNDAY SCHOOL.

Anniversary services in connection with this school were preached on Sunday, by Mr. J. Bennett Jun., of Bewsey. In the afternoon a musical ser- vice was held, and Mr. Bennett gave an address to the children. At each service special hymns were sung by the children, and the choir rendered two anthems. Mr. Ford was at the organ. Collections were made in aid of the Sunday School funds.

FUNERAL OF A POLICE CONSTABLE. The funeral of the late Police Constable Paice. of the borough force, whose death occurred yesterday week, took place on Monday afternoon, the remains being interred at the Cemetery in the presence of a large gathering of people who had known and re- spected the deceased. Among those who followed the body to the grave were the Chief Constable (Mr. S. Hunt), Inspectors Spinks and Cox, Sergeants Rowbotham, Cheney, and Bowen, and thirty con- ' , stables. Mr. John Connor, of 81, Legh-st., had charge of the funeral arrangements.

A YOUTHFUL ORGANIST. Frederick Jones, a boy of eleven years of age, who is a pupil of Mr. R. H. Pearson, officiated at the organ at St. John's Presbyterian Church, on Sunday. Although he is so young, this is not the first occasion on which he has acted in that capa-

city. Me has also played at several social meetings of the church, and as a regular thing conducts the musical service at the Sunday School. Jones, who is the son of Mr. William Jones. clogger, of Win- wick-road, is said to display wonderful talent for a boy of his years. THE SHOCKING DEATH AT COCKHEDGE MILLS. The inquiry as to the death of Charles Pairbrother, the lad who met with a shocking death at Cock- hedge Mills last week, was held on Saturday fore- noon, at the Police Station, before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner. The evidence was similar in effect to the particulars given last week in our columns. The lad had climbed to the top of one of the boilers that was not being worked, and in ' attempting to swing from one of the coal hoppers it gave way and fell on his head, which was crushed in a dreadful manner. A verdict of "Accidental Death" was returned. LICENSING CHANGES IN THE BOROUGH.

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Alder- men Harrison and Davies granted the following transfers of the licenses of publichouses :—Rope and Anchor, from Thomas Gibbs to Henry Summerscales ; Ring o' Bells, Wilderspool-rood, from George Brooks to Thomas Boskow ; Travellers' Rest, from Thomas Forster to Betsy Forster. An off-license held in respect to premises in Battersby-lane was trans- ferred from Edward Plinston to John Norbury. Peter Baguley received temperory authority to sell at the Green Dragon Inn, and James Taylor to sell at the Alexandra beerhouse.

div.head: TRIPPERS AT CROFT.
div.p: TRIPPERS AT CROFT.

On Saturday, --heirVieen-46-al-ni.o Of the employds of Messrs. John Morris and Sons, fil.e engine builders, Sze., of the Regent Works, Salford, had a picnic to the General Elliot Hotel, Croft, where they arrived at 12 o'clock, and partook of dinner pro- vided by Mr. and Mrs. Owen, the host and hostess. Afterwards the party adjourned to a field opposite the hotel, and engaged in cricket. On Sunday morning a picnic party of thirty-two persons from Heywood, and a party of 26 from Manchester, wore conveyed to the Horse Shoe Inn, Croft, where they dined. Other picnics visited the parish in the afternoon. Sr. ANNRS CHURCH CHOIR PICNIC.

The adult members of this choir on Saturday had their annual picnic, going to the popular resorts of Chatsworth and Haddon. Luncheon was partaken of at Bakewell, and the excursionists left for Chats- worth, where they arrived at 1 p.m. After viewing the rooms open to visitors, the village church ot Edensor was visited. Hadon Hall was next reached, the drive from Edensor being much enjoyed, and a pleasant hour was spent in viewing the many inter- esting relics to be seen at the Hall. The party returned to Bakewell in the afternoon for tea, and afterwards a visit was paid to the church at Bake- well. A start for home was made soon after eight, Warrington being reached about ten. CHOIR EXCURSION TO CHESTRR.

The members of the Bevvsey-rd. Wesleyan Chapel choir, together with some friends, to the number of GO, had their annual excursion on Tuesday, Chester this year being selected as the destination. They started in 'buses from the Lion Hotel shortly before 8 a.m., and airived at Chester, after an enjoyable drive, at eleven o'clock. On reaching the city, the party dispersed, but again assembled at one o'clock, and proceeded by boat to Eaton Hall. Other places of interest in Chester were viAted, the return jour- ney being commenced at 8 p.m. Warrington was reached at midnight. The weather was tine. The arrangements were admirably carried out by Messrs. Place, Parkinson, Muir, and Whitehouse. THE WORKINGMEN'S 9PEN-AIR TOTAL ABSTINENCE

div.head: MISSION.
div.p: MISSION.

On Saturday, the Rev. J. J. banghain, of Padgate, gave the above mission a garden party, and though the weather was very unfavourable, a pleasant afternoon was spent. After tea, the members gave a very interesting entertainment. Mr. J. Price, the president of the mission, presided. The entertain- ment was opened with singing, and the chair- man addressed the meeting upon the progress of the work done by the mission since its' start. Mr. J.
iiinTy and Mrs. Houghton maal;a presentation, on behalf of the workingmen's mission, to the Rev. J. J. Langham and Mrs. Langhatn, for their good work done in the temperance cause. The Rev. J. J. _ _

Langham responded, and said he would always take great care of the presents,coming from the working- mon. He also wished the mission every success.— On Sunday morning there was a meeting at Sankey Bridges. SCENE IN THE SANKEY-ST. CIRCUS.

A scene of some excitement occurred on Saturday night during the progress of a variety entertainment that was being I.eld at the Circus in Sankey-st. Three items of the programme had been carried out satisfactorily, when a rather prolonged "wait "took place. The audience, beginning to get impatient, gave expresiion to their displeasure by hooting and hissing with a considerable amount of vigour. Bottles and other things were thrown on the stage, and a couple of the "gods " relieved the tedium of the interval by indulging in a little sparring. After the lapse of about half-an-hour, one of the promoters of the entertainment came to the front, and told the audience that during the previous week the manage- ment had suffered a pecuniary loss of about £25, and that since then they had experienced another loss of the same amount. In consequence of these adverse circumstances, they _lied not been able to pay the members of the Company the salaries that were due to them, and now they declined to proceed with the entertainment. Considerable excitement followed this announcement, but ultimately it was stated that a compromise had been arranged between the promoters and the Company, and the perform- anc. was proceeded with. EXHIBITION OF WILD FLOWERS AT BURTONWOOD. The second annual exhibition of wild flowers took place at Burtonwood, on Saturday, and proved a success. It was held in a marquee erected on land adjoining the Bridge Inn. The exhibitors were children attending St. Michael's (Church of Eng- land) and St. Paul's of the Cross (Roman Catholic) schools. Messrs. John Anderton, James Woodward, and P. Jones officiated as judges, the list of awards being as follows :—Class 1, for children between the ages of 12 and 15 years (32 exhibitors) : Hester Porshaw 1, Mary A. Isherwood 2, Kate Martin 3. Class 2, for children between the ages of 9 and 12 years (45 exhibitors): William Griffiths 1, James Isherwood 2, William Gleave 3. Class 3, between the ages of 5 and 9 years (58 exhibitors) : Maggie Gleave 1, Sarah E. Travers 2 Edith Shipton 3. Tea was afterwards served. it had been provided through the exertions of Mr. Anders, to whom the credit of originating. the show and carrying it to so successful an issue IR due. Addresses were after- wards delivered by Messrs. Anders, Simcock, Beffield, Woodward, and others, and the proceedings closed with a dance. On Monday afternoon the children were given another treat, as the weather on Satur- had been unfavourable for outdoor enjoyment. Upwards of 200 put in an appearance, and amongst them 4-cwt. of sweets and 121bs. of nuts were dis- tributed. Racing, jumping, and a variety of sports took place, prizes being given fcr the different events. In the evening dancing took place, the Burtonwood string band supplying the music.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE DUNCAN DIVORCE CASE.

In the celebrated Duncan divorce case yesterday, the jury found that Mrs. Duncan had committed adultery with Lieutenant Engelheart, and assessed the damages at £5OO. His Lordship delivered judgment accordingly. The jury disagreed in regard to the co-respondent Hill.

SUICIDE OF A PROMINENT POLITICIAN. Mr. Tom Howson, timber merchant at Appleby, and well-known throughout the north as a prominent Liberal politician and speaker, committed suicide on Thursday night by throwing himself in front of a train. He had before attempted suicide. He was a wealthy man and an Oxford Wrangler.

div.head: BLEEDING A WITCH.
div.p: BLEEDING A WITCH.

DANTZIC, FRIDAY.—A disgusting instance of the super- stition which is still prevalent amongst the labouring classes, has been brought to light. A well-to-do mason named Martin Stankewitz accused an old woman of the name of Nixdorf, of having betwitched his wife. He accordingly extracted blood from the arm of the supposed witch, and gave it to his wife to drink, in order to counteract the witchery. This the unfortunate woman did with fatal results, and her husband has now been sentenced to a months' imprisonment, for his treat- merit of Nixdorf.
PRINCE BISMARCK AND SIR ROBERT MORIER MORE ACCUSATIONS.

BERLIN, FRlDAY—Prince Bismarck has repeated the accusations made some time ago against Sir Robert Morier, English Ambassador at St. Patersburg. The ex- Chancellor says that Sir Robert conspired in 1860 with an English woman(the Crown Prince.ss Victoria)to ruin him. It will be seen that this is a variation of the previous attack by Prince Bismarck. On the former occasion he alleged that Sir Robert Morier supplied the French with important information during the great war of 1870. Commenting on this new phase of the controversy the Liberal section of the press says that if the Prince knows anything against the Empress Frederick he had better out with it, and the Empress will then defend herself against any open accusations of conspiracy against Prussia.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS, YESTERDAY.

TEMPERANCE IN Nom—Lord Caoss. in reply to ques- tions, said the temperance canteens in India formed part of the regimental system. MISCELLANEOUS—The Irish Light Line Railway Bill was withdrawn. The second reading of the Bill to re- peal the English and Scotch Government Acts,moved by Lord Denman, was negatived. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—YESTERDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE PELICAN CLUB —Mr. MATTHEWS, replying to Mr. Coghill, said the Society of the Pelican Club denied absolutely that prize fighting or boxing in any form was carried on on Sunday evenings. If specific information was given inquiry should be made. THE CALLIOPE.—TIIS FIRST LORD of the ADMIRALTY informed Mr. T. M. Healy that though the traditions of the navy forbade special recognition of gallantry of officers of H.M.S. Calliope during the hurricane at Samoa, those connected with the affair had been pro- moted. _

THE PARTNERSHIPS BILL.—Upon the Partnerships Bill, Mr. HUNTER moved the adjournment to allow of a full consideration of the application of the Bill to Scotland.— The motion was defeated by 167 to 85, and the Bill read a second time. THE Inisri ESTlMATES.—Consideration of the Irish Esti- mates was them resumed in Committee.—On the first vote, relating to Irish prisons, Mr. T. M. HEALY made detailed criticism of Irish prison administration. Mr. FLYNN complained of the general treatment of prisoners and of the action of Tralee gaolers in violently cutting off the moustache of Mr. E. Harrington M.P. He likewise took exception to the general massing of the Crimes Act prisoners in Tullamore. Mr.. SHAW LEFEVRE said that his views remained unaltered that the treatment of prisoners under the Crimes Act was contrary to the practice of civilized countries. He called attention to the restrictions imposed upon visits to Crimes Act prisoners,and to the fact that the visitors were compelled to conduct their conversations with bail prisoners in the presence and hearing of a warder. That, he thought was contrary to the spirit and intentions of the Prisons Act.—Mr. W. O'BRIEN said the Irish prison rules were a mass of inconsistency and chaos. He and his friends never asked to be better treated than their honourable colleagues. All they asked was for a classification of prisoners. They objected to the Belfast swindlers being , treated virtually as first class misdemeanents, and the Irish peasant and the Irish men convicted under the Crimes Act treated as burglars and footpads. LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDIY.—There is a strong tone In the market with an attempt in most departments to get more money, which only succeeds in exceptional cases. Cotton is steady, but it has not yesterday's buoyancy, the da,'s business being covered by the first estimate of 10.000 bales. Spinners are not making much progress. Twist is very firm, especially good marks, but common sorts are not any dearer, and ord,•rs would be welcome in many quarters. Wefts about 50's are ptrong, and command full prices. Bun4ilas aro not active, but some India qualities are wanted, and a fair trade might be done if spinners were more pliable. In cloth things are various. Best shirtings both for India and China are moving at advanced prices. Lower qualities are strong, but trade at quotations is very moderate. LONDON PRODUCE, PRIDAY.—SIIOr : Pieces full up ; dry goods and crystals steady • foreign quiet ; beet slow— July-August buyers 128 80 and sellers 12s 9d ; September buyers 12s 4id mid sellers 12s 51-d ; new crop buyers lie lid and sellers 12s ; cane steady. Coffee slow on the spot ; futures inactive ; Rio—September 77s 3d and December 745. Tea steady. Rice, jute, and hemp quiet, but steady. Linseed oil, 23s 9d to 245. Turpentine 32s 3d. Petroleum American 5 7-16 d to 50. GLASGOW METAL, FRlDAY.—Market strong, with a good business done at 45s 9d to 45s fild and 46s 'lid cash ; also at 45s lid to 46s 3d one month ; buyers 465 id cash and 468 3d one month ; sellers id more. Middlesbrough 43s 3d one month; buyers 43s 2d cash . • sellers 43s 4,1 cash. Hematite 52s id to 528 6d cash, and 52s 34 to 525 7d one month; buyers 528 6d cash and 52s 7id one month; sellers Id more. Market closed till Tuesday next. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY.—For Beef the inquiry keeps slack, hut. there is no alteration to note in values. Pork is steadily held. Holders of Bacon are firm in their demands for full prices, short boneless being partially 6d per cut' dearer than yesterday. Hams continue steady, and Shoulders firm in value at unchanged rates. Cheese rules quietly steady, Butter quotations are nominal. Lard closes weaker intone.

I.O.G.T.—TEMPERANCE :MISSION LODGE. On Wednesday evening what was. termed a "strawberry festival" was held in the ACadern. Y:St. room, in connection with the Temperance Mission Lodge of Good Templars. About 70 members and friends were present. An open air mission for Sunday evenings has been started, and last Sunday a meeting was held in Bank-st. Mr. Ilewitt pre- sided, and addresses were given by Messrs. Gandy, - F. Dixon, and C. H. Mills. MORE ASSAULTS ON CHILDREN. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- • day morning, Michael Burns, an elderly man, charged with having, on the 14th July, attempte to criminally assault Lucy Michaels, a girl under the age of sixteen. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was afarm labourer and lodged in Bay Horse-yea' Winwick-st. About half-past four on Monday after noon a married woman named Ellen Hilton. wife Richard Hilton, of 124 Ad miral-st., saw the prisoner conducting himself in Howley fields, in a very improper manner in the midst of a crowd of beYs and girls whose ages ranged from 8 to 14. girls ran away, but Burns followed, and seizing Michaels threw her on the ground and attempted. rc; assault her. She having got' away, he next seize'. another girl named Cunningham, nine years of age' and then Mrs. Hilton and others interfered, and the police were informed of the circumstances. IroPee.: tor Spinks and P.C. Monoghan arresting the Prit soner. The girl Michaels said that prison threatened to throw her in the river for mak!ng t noise. Prisoner was committed to take his trial a the assizes.

ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS FOR THE TOWNSHIP OF NEWTON-IN MA.KERFIELD. TO THE ELECTORS. LADIRS lEDGENTLBMIIN,-At a meeting of ratepayers held in the Co-operative Hall, Bane-street, Barlestown, on Mon- day evening last, we were publicly nominated as candidates for the three.vacant seats on the Board of Commissioners, and in responee to the unanimous wish of that meeting we beg to place our services at your disposal. With the necessities and requirements of the township we are well acquainted, and we I shall. if wehave the honour of being elected as your ropre sentatives, always advocate such measures as are likely to be benettetarto the inhabitants of Newton, Barlestown, and War- grave. Roping to be favoured with your votes, and assuring you that, if successful, we will bestow diligence and REGULAR attention to the duties devolving upon us, we have the.honour to be, ladies and gentlemen, your obedient servaata, T. ORMAND, P. McMAHON, and E. T. EVANS. Newton-le-Willows, July 16th, 1890.
